Fourth, by the preceding vibration, he shakes the palaces of Māra, causing them to be struck with fear.
Within the second mouth, there are likewise four aspects:
first, it is able to destroy the heterodox.
"Tearing asunder the net of heterodoxy" refers to the destruction of false teachings.
"Eliminating all views" teaches the severing of the false mind.
These two remove [the obstacles of] views.
"Dispersing all defilements" means to destroy the realm of desire.
The objects of the five desires have the power to soil and vex sentient beings; therefore, they are called "defilements" (*rajas-kleśa*).
To speak of emptiness as a means of refutation and dismissal is termed "dispersal.
"Destroying the moats of all desires" teaches the relinquishing of the mind of desire.
Because the mind of craving and desire is deep and difficult to cross, it is described as a moat.
Teaching cessation is called "destruction.
These two eliminate craving.
These four pairs, taken together, constitute the first [section], clarifying the ability to subdue what is heterodox.
The second section, "Guarding with Adornment" and below, clarifies the ability to penetrate the correct [Dharma].
"Guarding the City of the Dharma" refers to preventing others from slandering it.
Because the Dharma can provide protection and defense, it is described as a city.
Praising the good and ceasing slander is called "adornment" and "protection.
"Opening and elucidating the Dharma-gate" refers to hearing the exposition of the true teaching.
In general, "Dharma-gate" (dharmamukha) carries the meaning of a gateway through which one enters and proceeds toward realization; therefore, it is called a "gate."
To unfold and expound [the teaching] so that others may enter it is called "opening" and "elucidating.
From the section on "washing and cleansing" downward, this concludes the first meaning: the subduing of heterodoxy.
The afflictions of views and craving are termed "defilements and impurities."
The instruction is to remove the name and wash [the stain].
Regarding the section beginning with "Manifestly Clarifying" (xiǎnmíng) below, it elucidates the meaning of the second preceding point concerning the penetration of the correct.

It states, "Manifestly clarifying and purifying, the light fuses with the Buddha-dharma. This refers to the preceding text’s description of solemnly protecting the city of the Dharma and removing the heterodox to manifest the correct; therefore, it is called "manifestly clarifying" (xiǎnmíng).
The Dharma manifested therein transcends false slanders and is thus called "pure and white.
It illuminates and exalts the True Dharma, emerging from all that is deviant and delusive; therefore, it is called "light."
To smelt and refine [the Dharma] until it is pure is called "smelting the Buddha-dharma.
"Proclaiming and circulating the transformation of the Dharma" clarifies the opening and expounding of the Dharma-gates mentioned in the preceding text;
because one proclaims and circulates it to transform others, it is termed "opening and expounding."
This concludes the first section.
Within the third body, "entering the country for *piṇḍapāta*" refers to beginning the practice of begging for food.
In the vernacular language, *piṇḍapāta* is called *fenwei*; here it means "begging for food."
Having obtained various abundant foods, he received alms by begging for food.
Regarding the phrase "storing merit" (*guṇa-saṃcaya*) below, it refers to generating merit through enjoyment.
"Storing" (*zhu*) means accumulating.
To accumulate many virtues is called "storing merit.
To manifestly receive material offerings is therefore termed "demonstrating" (*śāstra*).
To produce worldly blessings and goodness is like a field producing crops; hence it is called a "field of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*).
In the fourth section, "Desiring to Manifest a Smile," the introduction to the discourse is established, followed by the actual exposition.
Within this, the initial statement—“To heal the three types of suffering with the medicine of all dharmas”—is intended to cause beings to transcend birth and death.

The suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)—these are the three types of suffering.
Their meaning is as explained in a separate chapter; this should be discussed in full detail.
Bestowing the teachings of the Dharma to effect severance is called "Dharma-healing."
From the section beginning with "Manifesting" (*prabhāvanā*) onwards, the text leads people into the Path.

Within this, the initial phrase "manifesting the intention for the Path" (*mārga-citta-prabhāvanā*) instructs people to generate the resolve; it manifests the bodhisattva's generated intention for the Path so that people may likewise generate it.
"Immeasurable Merit" teaches people to initiate practice.
From "Bestowing upon the Bodhisattvas" onwards, it ultimately leads them to attain the fruit.
Bestowing the prediction (vyākaraṇa) upon the bodhisattvas is the skillful means for attaining that fruit.
When causes produce their effects, it is like the mind recording an object; therefore, it is called "recording" (*vyākaraṇa*).
When the Sages teach and reveal this to others, it is termed "bestowing" (*ādeśana*).
"Attaining Equal and Perfect Enlightenment" specifically clarifies the realization of Buddhahood.
From here below is the tenth section, the characteristics of *parinirvāṇa*.
"Manifesting extinction" correctly reveals the attainment of cessation;
what follows demonstrates its benefits.
"Saving and delivering without end" demonstrates that the benefit is vast and expansive.
"Eliminating the outflows" (*āsrava*) and so forth demonstrates that the benefit is complete.
By eliminating all outflows, they manifest cessation; this causes people to grow weary of existence, sever the cause of birth and death, and plant the roots of manifold virtues.
Because its manifestation and cessation cause people to rejoice in tranquility and cultivate the causes for *nirvāṇa*,
the preceding section has extensively praised the two virtues of the provisional and the real.
From here on, the third section concludes by pairing these two together.
"Endowed with merit, subtle and immeasurable" concludes the preceding discussion of his real qualities (*dharmatā-guṇa*).
"Wandering through the lands of all Buddhas, universally manifesting the teachings of the Way" concludes the preceding discussion of his expedient qualities (*upāya-guṇa*).
The above has discussed the two virtues of provisional and ultimate reality.
Below this, secondly, is the praise of his merits of self-benefit and benefiting others:
conduct that is able to benefit oneself is called self-benefit;
Practice that is able to provide simultaneous benefit and moisture is defined as benefiting others.
The conduct of a bodhisattva does not go beyond these two; therefore, they are praised.
Within this, first, there is a brief praise of the bodhisattva scriptures.
From "Jiuchang" (Thoroughly Elucidating) onwards, there is an extensive eulogy.
Within the brief section, first comes the individual exposition, followed by the general conclusion.
Within the individual exposition, there are four parts:
First, the purity of one's own practice;
second, from "For example" onwards, the skillfulness in transforming others' practice.
First the simile, then the application.
In the analogy, the initial phrase "for example, like a magician" illustrates the creation of an emanated person.
The subsequent description of "manifesting various different forms, as male or female," and so forth, illustrates the characteristics of the emanation.
"Fundamental learning and clarity" (*benxue ming*) and so forth metaphorically represent the virtue of initiating transformation.
"Fundamental learning and clear understanding" (*benxue mingliao*) metaphorically represents the practice of the methods of transformation.
Because learning serves as the foundation for transformation, it is termed "fundamental" (*ben*).
To practice the Buddha’s transformative Dharma thoroughly and skillfully is what is called "learning for clarity.
Regarding "what is intended by the mind," this refers to the arising of function once learning has been perfected.
Since its accomplishment resides within the mind, it is termed "intended by the mind."
Acting at will for the sake of transformation, it is therefore called "that which is done.
The following section harmonizes with and clarifies the Dharma.
"The Bodhisattva is thus" harmonizes with the preceding illusionist.
“Learning all” and so forth collectively give rise to the virtue of transformation.
“Learning all dharmas” collectively refers to the original learning; that is, learning all dharmas for the sake of transforming others.
"Piercing through, synthesizing, and refining" corresponds to clear understanding.
To penetrate thoroughly and practice comprehensively, knowing the Dharma with meticulous scrutiny, is therefore called "refining.
"Abiding securely and with certainty" corresponds to mental focus.
Regarding the dharmas in which one dwells, settle the mind in profound discernment.
"There is nothing that does not lead to transformation" means that this accords with what is to be accomplished.
"Mi" (靡) means "none"; "chi" (致) means "to bring forth" or "to transport."
There is nowhere where he does not exercise his transformative power.
Furthermore, "to cause" (*chi*) means to induce; it refers to causing all sentient beings to be moved toward transformation.
"Manifesting universally throughout countless Buddha-lands" combines with the aforementioned characteristics of transformation, wherein various forms are manifested as men, women, and so forth.
This is the second skillfulness regarding transformative conduct (*nirmāṇa-caryā-kuśala*).
Third, from the section beginning with "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) below, it reveals the first [topic]:
the purity of one's own practice (*sva-caryā-viśuddhi*). Because one does not become arrogant or indulgent regarding what has been attained, one's conduct is pure.
4. From "Compassion" (*kṛpā*) onwards, the second skillful means of transformative conduct (*nirmāṇa-caryā-kuśalatva*) is revealed.
"Compassion" refers to pity (*karuṇā*).
Because the mind possesses compassion and takes pity upon sentient beings, one is able to manifest various transformations for the sake of others.
The preceding section was a specific praise;
"this Dharma is fully complete in all respects" concludes it as a whole.
The above has been a brief praise.
The following provides a broad eulogy of this, which consists of four parts:
first, practicing one's own portion of the path based on the Bodhisattva-dharma;
second, from "Innumerable Buddhas all protect him together" onwards, clarifying the practice of superior progress based on the Buddha-dharma.
3. From "Making Offerings to the Buddha" onwards, one extensively cultivates and accomplishes virtues based on the previous stage of self-benefit (*svārtha*).

4. From "Receiving and Upholding the Profound Dharma of the Tathāgata" onwards, one distinguishes the cultivation and accomplishment of virtues based on the previous stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*).
Within the first section, one first cultivates self-benefit and subsequently gives rise to the benefit of others.
"Thoroughly mastering the essential subtleties of the Bodhisattva scriptures" constitutes self-benefit.

To have thoroughly investigated and mastered the Bodhisattva teachings, attaining their essential core and understanding their subtle purport—this is why it is called "thoroughly investigating and elucidating the essentials and subtleties.
That "renown reaches everywhere, guiding and governing the ten directions" refers to benefiting others.
In the second section, there is likewise first the benefit for oneself.
The passage beginning with "The Tathāgatas, through their transformative teachings, each can proclaim [it]" refers to the benefit for others.
Within the benefit for oneself, there is the protection of immeasurable Buddhas.
Those of superior virtue encompass those below; as their practice enters the realm of the Buddhas, they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas in common.
These Buddhas protect them so that they may abandon evil thoughts and cause their wholesome thoughts to increase.
Regarding the passage beginning with “The abodes of the Buddhas,” this describes the progressive cultivation of higher stages in accordance with the path.

Within it, the initial statement, “Those who abide in the abodes of the Buddhas have all already attained such abodes,” demonstrates that their practice is identical to that of the Buddhas; they abide in the same Dharma as the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas dwell together therein.
Furthermore, all Buddhas abide in the practice of suchness, and Bodhisattvas likewise abide therein.
"That which the Great Sage has established, they have all already established"; thus, their teaching and practice are identical to those of the Buddha.
The Great Sage is the Buddha; the various perfections (pāramitās) of the dharma-realm are established by the Buddha and likewise established by the Bodhisattvas.
Within the section on benefiting others, the first part explains the characteristics of benefiting others.
From the phrase "penetrating all dharmas" onwards, it clarifies the virtues of benefiting others.

Within the characteristics of benefiting others, "the Tathāgata’s path-transformations are each able to be proclaimed" means that as a teacher of bodhisattvas, he benefits people through the teachings of the Dharma.
"The Tathāgata’s path-transformations are each able to be proclaimed" means that his preaching of the Dharma is identical to that of the Buddha.
"To act as a great teacher for all bodhisattvas" means that in benefiting others, he is equal to a Buddha.
Because he manifests the transformative activity of a Buddha, he serves as a great teacher for bodhisattvas, guiding the multitude through profound meditative concentration and wisdom.
Realizing the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, one transforms through profound meditative concentration and wisdom, acting in accordance with the Buddha.
Although the practices of meditative stillness (*śamatha*) and wise insight (*vipaśyanā*) are manifold, they do not transcend these two essentials.
Guiding and instructing the multitude, one benefits others as the Buddha does.
Within the section on disparaging the virtues of others, it is explained that one is able to transform sentient beings by possessing the practice of the three kinds of mastery.
To penetrate the nature of all phenomena is the practice of mastery of wisdom and perfect enlightenment.
This means being able to penetrate the dharma-nature of the two truths, and to realize the characteristics of sentient beings—the sovereign activity within the world of sentient beings.
Because sentient beings frequently die, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*).
The multitude of phenomena constitutes sentient beings, who are also called "sentient beings.
Whether in form or substance, all their various characteristics and appearances are fully known.
To clearly understand all lands is the sovereign practice regarding the vessel-world.
The first phrase is called "penetrating" (tōng), the second "reaching" (dá), and the third "elucidating" (shuōmíng); these terms refer to the left and right ears [of wisdom].
These three are explained in detail as they appear in other sutras.
From here below is the third section: the extensive cultivation and accomplishment of virtues based on the preceding stage of self-mastery.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, the means of cultivation;
second, from "nor is there any action" onwards, the virtues accomplished through causal practice.
3. From "Abiding in profound meditative concentration" (*samādhi*) onwards, the subsequent stage clarifies the arising of cultivation.
4. From "Transcending all that belongs to the world" onwards, it explains the virtues accomplished through that cultivation.
The first part further consists of four sections:
first, the cultivation of self-benefit;
second, from "shattering and tearing" (*huài liè*) onwards, clarifying his benefit for others.
3. From "Transcending" (*atikrama*) onwards, it further clarifies self-benefit.
4. From "Well-established" (*susthita*) onwards, it again clarifies benefiting others.
In the first section on self-benefit, it clarifies the cultivation of the practice of the teachings.
The second is benefiting others by teaching people to abandon faults;
the third is self-benefit by clarifying the practices of cultivation and realization;
the fourth is benefiting others by instructing them to cultivate goodness.
Thus, there are four distinctions.
Within the first [section] on self-benefit, the passage "making offerings to all Buddhas, manifesting his body like a flash of lightning" clarifies the cultivation of meritorious conduct.
Making offerings to all Buddhas brings about vast merit.

The manifested bodies (nirmāṇakāya) are like lightning; their activity arises with swiftness, such that in the space of a single thought-moment, these manifested bodies reach everywhere to make offerings to all Buddhas.
From "well-trained" onwards, the cultivation of the practice of wisdom is elucidated.
"Well-trained and fearless" refers to the cultivation of the skillful means of wisdom.
"Thoroughly understanding illusions and transformations" signifies the perfection of the practice of wisdom.
Furthermore, one studies fearlessness and is not timid toward others;
having clearly understood illusion and transformation, one is able to know all phenomena.
To discern the heterodox and adopt the orthodox is called "skillful study."
Reaching the correct and transcending the deviant, one is thereby without fear.
Because the wisdom of fearlessness governs and encompasses all phenomena, it is called a "net.
Furthermore, one may study this to employ it for the purpose of gathering in others; thus, it is described as a net.

To clearly perceive that all phenomena are free from the nature of existence and non-existence, being like illusions—neither existent nor non-existent—is called "thoroughly understanding illusory phenomena.
If a phenomenon were definitively existent, it would not be called "illusory existence";
if a phenomenon were definitively non-existent, it would not be called "illusory non-existence."
When non-existence is taken as existence, it is called illusory existence;
when existence is taken as non-existence, it is called illusory non-existence.
When non-existence is taken as existence, that existence is not truly existent.
There are phenomena that are non-existent; yet that which is non-existent is not [absolutely] non-existent.
Illusory phenomena are like this, and thus they are taken as a metaphor;
transformations are also like this.
The Sūtra sets forth ten parables, which are cited here in their entirety.
The preceding section on self-benefit is concluded;
the following section concerns benefiting others.
"Tearing asunder the net of Māra" means causing one to leave behind wrong actions.
"Unbinding all fetters" means causing one to leave behind the afflictions (*kleśa*).

The "fetters" refer to the ten fetters: shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), torpor (*styāna*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), resentment (*upanāha*), anger (*krodha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*); these are the ten.
Because they entangle sentient beings and bind the mind, they are called "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*).
"Binding" refers to the four bonds: the bond of desire, the bond of existence, the bond of ignorance, and the bond of views; these are the four.
The various fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm, excluding ignorance and views, are called the "bond of desire" (*kāma-bandhana*).
All afflictions (*kleśa*) within the two upper realms, excluding ignorance and views, are called the "bond of existence" (*bhava-bandhana*).
Ignorance within the three realms is called the bond of ignorance.
All views within the three realms are called the bond of views.
They are termed "bonds" because they bind sentient beings and fetter the mind.
Furthermore, all afflictions and fetters may collectively be termed "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*); when a Bodhisattva teaches others to sever and abandon them, this is termed "liberation.
These two sections are concluded.
From here below is the third section, which again clarifies self-benefit.
"Transcending the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas" refers to the excellence of what is practiced.
This clarifies the etymological meaning of the term "Śrāvaka. Generally, there are three ways to explain it:
first, the verbal teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are called "sound" (śabda); because one awakens to understanding by consuming these sounds, one is called a "Sound-Hearer" (Śrāvaka).
The two—the self and sentient beings—and so forth, are merely names without reality;
therefore, they are said to be "sounds. As the *Dilun* states:
"Observing this understanding, it is explained that their meaning constitutes 'hearing'."
The sound of the Mahāyāna Dharma taught by the three Buddhas is called "sound" (*śabda*).
Because they cause all beings to hear the sound of the Buddha-way, they are called *Śrāvaka* (Hearers).
This is as explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The former two are the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and the latter one is the Greater Vehicle (Mahāyāna); the present treatise concerns the Lesser Vehicle.
Such are its name and meaning; as for its essence and characteristics, how are they?
There are two ways of distinguishing them:
There are two types of śrāvaka-śrāvakas: first, those who hear from the voice [of others]; second, those who are pratyekabuddha-śrāvakas. Their meanings have been explained above.
Regarding the term "pratyekabuddha," there are three aspects to its name and meaning:

first, the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) are called "conditions" (pratyaya); because one attains awakening by contemplating these, they are named "condition-awakened" (pratyekabuddha).
As stated in that *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*:

"The causal conditions of the phenomena of the two present lives are called 'conditions' (*pratyaya*); because one attains awakening by relying upon these, they are named 'Pratyekabuddha' (Solitary Realizer)."
As stated in the *Pratyekabuddhamārgaprāptisūtra*:

"The dependent origination of the three Tathāgatagarbhas and the Dharma-realm is termed 'conditions' (*pratyaya*); because one awakens to or becomes deluded within them, one is called a 'Pratyekabuddha' (Solitary Realizer)."
Among these three, the first two belong to the Hīnayāna and the last one to the Mahāyāna; this treatise now concerns the former.
Such is the meaning of the names; what are their characteristics?
There are two types of analysis:
First, the pratyekabuddha-pratyekabuddha; second, the śrāvaka-pratyekabuddha. Regarding the pratyekabuddha-pratyekabuddha:
such a person originally seeks the path of a pratyekabuddha, constantly delights in contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, and thus perfects the nature of a pratyekabuddha.

In their final body, they do not encounter a Buddha during their lifetime; rather, they attain realization of the Way by relying on present circumstances. For this reason, they are called "Pratyekabuddhas by conditions.
As for those who are both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, these individuals originally sought the path of the Śrāvaka and thus established the nature of a Śrāvaka.
Encountering the Buddha, he was taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and attained the first fruit of enlightenment (*srotāpanna*).
Because his faculties were dull, he did not achieve the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and was reborn seven times among gods and humans.
In their final existence, they do not encounter the era of a Buddha; rather, they attain realization of the Way by relying on the conditions of present events.
Because these original śrāvakas attain awakening in their final existence by relying on the conditions of present events, they are described as śrāvaka-pratyekabuddhas.
The Bodhisattva completely transcends all these; therefore, it is said that he "surpasses" them.
Regarding the phrase "attaining the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness," the depth of what is attained is profound; this clarifies that which is entered.
Sentient beings and all phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; therefore, they are called "empty.
Even their causes and conditions lack any defining characteristic; thus, they are described as "signless."
This is free from the grasped object and far removed from the deluded mind that grasps; therefore, it is called "wishlessness" (apraṇihita).
Samādhi is a foreign term; in this language, it means "right concentration" (samyaksamādhi).
Because one dwells correctly and without distraction within these three emptinesses, it is called samādhi;
it is named according to this principle.
Its meanings have many aspects, as detailed in other chapters, which should be discussed in full here.
These three sections are concluded.
From here below is the fourth section, which further elucidates benefiting others.
"Skillfully establishing expedient means" refers to the wisdom for transforming others.
Regarding the meaning of *upāya* (expedient means), there are generally four types:
first, the expedient means of progression.
This refers to the seven stages of expedient means prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth; they are called "expedient means" because they progress toward the fruit.
Second is the skillful means of cultivation,
such as the *upāya-pāramitā* among the ten *pāramitās*, so called because it involves the skillful practice of various deeds;
third is the skillful means of expedient adaptation.
As in the case of the two types of wisdom, such as the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), it is called "skillful means" because it skillfully gathers and guides sentient beings.
It is called "skillful means" because the four aggregates (*skandha*) are integrated through skillful means, for all phenomena share the same essence and are skillfully assembled.
Therefore, the *Dilun* states: "This Dharma is skillfully accomplished; this is called 'expedient means' (*upāya*).
Furthermore, other sūtras explain the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) as expedient means; this, too, constitutes the integration of expedient means.
What is now being discussed concerns skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
Within these skillful means, there are three types of expedients:
first, the expedient of physical action (*kāyakarma-upāya*).
Their provisional forms manifest diversely, such as the power of the skillful means of Avalokiteśvara.
What are these matters?
To those who should be saved by the body of a Buddha, he immediately manifests the body of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma for them.
All such instances constitute the two types of expedient means of vocal action (*vākkarman-upāya*).
Adapting to the transformation of sentient beings through various different explanations is termed "expedient means."
Just as there are no two vehicles [in reality], they are spoken of provisionally;
all such cases are like this.
The third is the skillful means of mental action, which refers to the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
In accordance with the transformation of sentient beings, there are various and diverse understandings.
What is discussed here is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the mental karma (*manas-karman*) within his provisional teachings.
Because he skillfully establishes the three types of karma and employs clever expedients to deliver beings, it is called "skillful means."
The section below, "Manifesting the Three," concerns the practice of transforming others.
"Manifesting the three vehicles" refers to explaining the causes of the three vehicles.
From the perspective of the greater encompassing the lesser, it is called "manifesting the three vehicles."
"Manifesting parinirvāṇa within this [world]" refers to the fruits of the Hīnayāna.
Among these, the Pratyekabuddha is termed "middling" and the Śrāvaka is termed "inferior"; it is said that there is nirvāṇa within these two, which is called "manifesting parinirvāṇa."
These constitute the skillful means (*upāya*) of vocal action (*vākkarman*).

The preceding four sections together form the first [section], the "Compendium of Cultivated Practices" (*bhāvanācaryā-saṃgraha*); from here below is the second, "Virtues Accomplished through Cultivation" (*bhāvanā-niṣpanna-guṇa*).
Within this, the first part clarifies the merit of self-benefit;
from "proclaiming" onwards, it clarifies the merit of benefiting others.
Regarding the former, there are four sections:
First, the equality realized;
second, from "endowed with" (*samanvāgata*) onwards, the manifold qualities accomplished;
third, from "vast and universal" (*vipula-samanta*) onwards, the profound and expansive realization.
4. From "attaining Buddhahood" downwards, [the text discusses] the excellence of what is accomplished.
Within the context of that which is realized and so forth, "there is also nothing to be done" means there is no cause to be produced;
"there is also nothing that exists" means there is no fruit to be found.
To say "non-arising" means there is no purity that can arise;
to say "non-extinction" means there is no defilement that can be extinguished.
This sets forth the underlying principle.
“Attaining the Dharma of Equality” is explained in terms of principle as realization.
That which is termed “non-action,” “non-existence,” and so forth, is called the Dharma of Equality; to realize and accord with it is called “attainment.”
Among the many qualities thus accomplished, "fully accomplishing immeasurable dhāraṇīs" refers to attaining dhāraṇīs, whereby one's practice and virtues become manifold, as explained in other sūtras.
Regarding the phrase "a hundred thousand samādhis, faculties, and wisdoms," other virtues are numerous as well.
Faith, diligence, mindfulness, and so forth are called the "faculties" (indriya); if discussed generally, all wholesome dharmas are termed "faculties," as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Within the profound and vast nature of what is realized, "vast and universal quiescent concentration" refers to the vastness of realization.
To give rise to no deluded thoughts regarding any phenomena is called the vast quiescent concentration.
"Profoundly entering the treasury of the Dharma" indicates the profundity of what is realized, for one is able to enter deeply into the true treasury of the Dharma.
Among the excellences of what is accomplished, "attaining the Flower Ornament Samādhi of the Buddha-Tathāgata" indicates the excellence of virtue.
The Flower Ornament Samādhi (*Avataṃsaka-samādhi*) is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
This single samādhi encompasses the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), such that all Buddha-dharmas enter therein.
The preceding section clarifies self-benefit;
it should be understood that the subsequent exposition of all things clarifies benefit for others.
Below this, the third section further elucidates the arousal of cultivation.
“Abiding in the gateway of profound meditative concentration, one beholds all the immeasurable Buddhas of the present,” and so forth; this refers to the cultivation and realization of self-benefit.
“Abiding in the gateway of profound meditative concentration” constitutes the basis for initiating practice.
There is no coming or going with a [discursive] mind; it arises solely through the power of the samādhi dharma-gate, and therefore one must abide in meditative concentration.
The following clarifies the arousal of practice:

"Beholding all the present immeasurable Buddhas" indicates the vastness of the encompassing practice; by seeing many Buddhas, one generates merit through making offerings and generates wisdom by receiving the Dharma.
"In a single moment of thought, there is nothing that is not universally pervaded," indicating the swiftness of the arousal of practice.
The following clarifies the benefiting of others:
"To rescue those in various extreme hardships, whether in leisure or non-leisure," meaning to support people so they may leave suffering behind.
There are eight difficulties of separation:
three pertain to the three miserable realms;
among humans, there are four:
First, those who are blind, deaf, mute, or speech-impaired; second, those who are wise, eloquent, and intelligent; third, those before and after the Buddhas; fourth, those in the realm of Uttarakuru.
Among the heavens, there is one [exception], namely, the long-lived devas of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
Among these eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), the three miserable realms (*durgati*) are the most severe; the Bodhisattva rescues those therein.

The sufferings of humans and devas are slight and are termed "leisure" (*kṣaṇa*); yet because the Bodhisattva exhorts and transforms them [to transcend this state], they are called "non-leisure" (*akṣaṇa*).
“Distinguishing and manifesting” and so forth refers to bestowing wholesome dharmas upon others.
“Distinguishing and manifesting the limit of reality” refers to realizing the Dharma to teach others.
The rational nature is reality; the point of attainment is called the “limit” (koti), and bestowing it upon others is called “manifesting.”
The passage beginning with “Attaining the eloquence and wisdom of all Tathāgatas” concerns the teaching that benefits sentient beings.

“Attaining the wisdom of the eloquence of all Tathāgatas” refers to the attainment of the capacity for exposition; that is, attaining the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) of the Tathāgata to fully comprehend all phenomena.
"Entering the various sounds of speech" refers to the understanding of preaching.
"Entering" means understanding;
that is, understanding the various sounds of speech of sentient beings and employing them to give rise to preaching.
"Transforming and enlightening all" correctly clarifies the arising of the teaching.
From here below is the fourth section, which further clarifies that which is accomplished.
Within this, it first clarifies the accomplishment of one's own virtues.
From "In all" below, the virtue of benefiting others is established.
Within that, the initial statement, "surpassing all mundane phenomena," establishes its excellence.
"Because the mind is eternally true," and so forth, that which is accomplished is immovable.

Furthermore, it transcends the mundane world, clearly accomplishing the virtue of cessation; this means it transcends all phenomena of the mundane world, both those of the fragmented birth-and-death (*pariccheda*) and the transformational birth-and-death (*pariṇāma*).
"The mind constantly and truly abides in the path that transcends the world" clarifies the accomplishment of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).
"Truly" (*di*) means peaceful stability; it refers to always dwelling peacefully in the true, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) path that transcends the world.
Regarding the benefit of others among the [four immeasurables], "having mastery over all things according to one's will" constitutes the virtue of benefiting others.
Because one has accomplished supreme supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one can transform all objects at will; thus, being able to benefit sentient beings, it is termed "mastery."
For the sake of all ordinary beings, he gives rise to altruistic activity.
"Acting as an uninvited friend for all classes of beings" refers to the skillful means of transformation and benefit.
"Ordinary beings" (shu) refers to the common masses; "classes" (lei) refers to their various categories.
There are two kinds of "not requesting":
first, those who have long lacked the roots of the Path and yet look up to move the Bodhisattvas; this is called "not requesting.
Second, those who lack the desire for present happiness and do not know how to seek the Sage; this is called "not requesting."
The Bodhisattva forcibly acts as a friend in this regard.
"Bearing the burden of all living beings as a heavy load" precisely clarifies the benefit of transformation.
Śrāvakas abandon material things and do not take sentient beings to be a heavy burden; [the Bodhisattva does so].
Because Bodhisattvas take up the burden, they regard sentient beings as their heavy load.
There are four distinct types of such burdens, as explained in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
This concludes the third [section].
From here on, the fourth section relies on the aforementioned superior progress to distinguish the virtues accomplished through cultivation.
Within this, the first part initially distinguishes that which is cultivated;
the passage beginning with "All roots of goodness are transcended" and following clarifies that which is accomplished.
Within the preceding section on practice, the first part clarifies self-benefit.
The second part, beginning with "arousing great compassion," clarifies the cultivation of benefiting others.
Within the section on self-benefit, the phrase "receiving and upholding the Tathāgata’s profound treasury of Dharma" clarifies the cultivation of resolute understanding (*adhimukti*).
The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is the profound Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Since the veils of darkness have been removed and clarity has manifested within the mind, it is called "upholding.
"Protecting the Buddha-lineage so that it never ceases" clarifies the cultivation of sublime practices.
The various perfections within the dharma-realm constitute the lineage of the Buddha.
To protect them so they remain free from hindrances and to give rise to wholesome states without interval is called "constant non-interruption.
Regarding that which does not benefit others, the Dharma is presented first, followed by the analogy.
Within the four phrases of this teaching:
first, "arousing compassion," clarifies the arising of the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*);
second, from "expounding compassionate eloquence" onwards, clarifies the arising of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Speaking based on the arousal of a compassionate mind is called "expounding with compassion.
Causing understanding to arise through the teaching is called "bestowing the Dharma-eye.
Third, "closing the three evil destinies and opening the gate of goodness" reveals the prior benefit of compassion.
"Dù" means to block off.
Because it teaches people to distance themselves from evil, it blocks off the three miserable realms;
because it teaches people to cultivate merit, it opens the gates of goodness.
4. Regarding "bestowing the gift of Dharma upon the masses without being requested," this clarifies the aforementioned benefit of compassion.
It consists of two phrases in the analogy.
The first, "like a filial son who loves and respects his parents," demonstrates the aforementioned profundity of compassion.
The passage beginning with "Toward all sentient beings" reveals the profundity of the aforementioned compassion.
The preceding section clarifies that which is practiced; the following section clarifies that which is accomplished.
The phrase "All roots of goodness have crossed to the other shore" clarifies what has been accomplished.
"Attaining" (*du*) means "reaching.
Reaching the other shore of *nirvāṇa* is achieved through the practice of causes; thus, the causes are fulfilled.
The phrase "all have attained Buddhahood," etc., clarifies that the fulfillment of the fruit consists in the possession of merit and wisdom.
"Attaining all the immeasurable merits of the Buddhas" clarifies the attainment of the Tathāgata’s adornment of merit and virtue.
"The holy brilliance of wisdom is inconceivable" clarifies the attainment of the Tathāgata’s adornment of wisdom.
His wisdom is profound and vast; its emotional conditions are unfathomable and beyond the reach of verbal measurement, hence it is called "inconceivable.
The preceding section was a praise of his virtues.
This present section, which states that such qualities are beyond calculation or reckoning, is the fourth part, manifesting their magnitude.
All these have come together because they manifest the Dharma through their influence;
they have gathered at one time because their minds are unified in their devotion to the Dharma.
The above constitutes the second section, which distinguishes and enumerates the assembly of followers.
From here below is the third section: the Tathāgata manifests signs to inspire [the discourse], and Ānanda requests instruction.
Within this section, there are six textual units, which are subsumed into three pairs.
Regarding these six units: first is the manifestation of signs by the Tathāgata to inspire, and second is Ānanda’s inquiry; this constitutes the first pair.

The third pair consists of the Tathāgata’s thorough inquiry as to whether the request was made by Ānanda himself or at the request of those to be converted, and Ānanda’s truthful reply that it was his own personal request.

The fourth pair consists of the Tathāgata’s praise and command for him to listen and permit the teaching, and from the words "He replied" onwards, Ānanda’s compliance with the command and manifestation of his own desire to hear. These constitute three pairs.
At the beginning, the phrase "at that time" indicates the moment when the signs appear.
The term "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) identifies the person who manifests these signs.
Because the Buddha is endowed with all virtues and is revered by the world, he is titled the World-Honored One.
Regarding the foreign (Hū) pronunciation, *lōuqiātóqié* translates here as "World-Honored One" (*bhagavat*).
The phrase "the faculties are gladdened" and so forth clarifies the manifested signs.
"The faculties are joyful" indicates the manifestation of the sign of joy.
The five faculties, beginning with the eye, all manifest a sign of joy; this is termed "delight.
"Pure and serene appearance" indicates the manifestation of a joyful countenance.
Because the physical form is free from gloom or distress, it is called "pure."
The phrase "the light is lofty and majestic" further clarifies the color of his joy.
The phrase "the countenance is grand and imposing" further clarifies the physical marks of his joy.
"Grand and imposing" describes the appearance of his sublime excellence.
Why does the Buddha rejoice?
There are two meanings to this rejoicing:

first, he rejoices because the practices and virtues accomplished by Amitābha Buddha are worthy of celebration; second, he gives rise to joy because the time has come for sentient beings to receive his benefits.
In the second section, "Venerable Ānanda" identifies the person who makes the request;
"receiving the Buddha’s holy intent" clarifies the basis upon which the request is made.
"Intent" (zhì) refers to the underlying purpose.
This inquiry was undertaken through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s intentional power.
The phrase "immediately from his seat" and so forth indicates the skillful means of making the request;
the phrase "and addressed the Buddha" and so forth represents the actual delivery of the words.
There are three parts within this discourse:
first, the restatement of what he has perceived;
second, from "So be it" (*evam*) onwards, the manifestation of what he has contemplated.
Third, from "For what reason" onwards, the purpose of the inquiry is concluded.
In the first part, there is first the teaching (*dharma*), next the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and finally the application (*upanaya*).
From "Never before beheld" onwards, he expresses his astonishment that the present is different from the past.
Within the Dharma, this refers back to what was previously manifested.
Regarding the metaphor of "the mirror's reflection appearing on both sides": the light of the mirror shines outward, which is called the "reflection on the surface."
The light that shines outward, appearing clearly within the mirror, is called the "reflection within.
Likewise, the Buddha’s body emits such radiance that the outward manifestation of this light reveals the Buddha’s body; this is called the "reflection both within and without."
The analogy may be understood through this synthesis.
"Never before have I beheld such exquisite excellence as now" expresses the wonder that the present differs from the past.
From here below begins the second section, which reveals what he himself was contemplating.
Within this, the initial statement, "Indeed, Great Sage, such is what I think," generally proclaims one's own mind.
"Indeed" (唯) carries the sense of exclusivity.
It is called "indeed" to manifest one's exclusive mindfulness.
"Ran" (然) means "so it is.
To manifest that what is conceived in one's own mind is indeed so, one says "weiran" (唯然).
To inform the Buddha so that he may know [this], one addresses him as "Dashingeng" (大聖, Great Sage).
To proclaim one's own mind is called "my recollection and thought.
Below, this is specifically elucidated.
Within that, first is the recollection of what has been attained by the Buddha.
Below the section on “past, future, and present,” the purpose of the Buddha’s mindfulness is explained.
Within the preceding [section], there are five phrases; their characteristics are obscure and difficult to discern, so they shall be briefly discussed.
The first phrase is the general [statement], while the remaining four are specific [details].
In the initial statement of the summary, "Today the World-Honored One," the word "today" indicates a specific object of mindfulness.
It is used to distinguish him from other Buddhas; thus, it says "today.
This same principle applies to the word "today" in all subsequent phrases.
Regarding "abiding in the extraordinary": the Dharma attained by the Buddha transcends that of all others and is non-existent among those in the world; therefore, it is called "extraordinary.
The following four points specifically clarify this: the first phrase refers to his own virtue, the second to benefiting others, the third to his own virtue, and the fourth to benefiting others.
What is the distinction between the first and third [aspects] regarding one's own virtue?
The former is *nirvāṇa*, while the latter is *bodhi*.
What is the distinction between the second and fourth regarding the benefit of others?
The former refers to his practice of benefiting others, namely the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and so forth;
the latter refers to his qualities for benefiting others, namely the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four kinds of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), and so forth.
At the beginning, "Hero of the World" (*lokanātha*) is an epithet of the Buddha.
Because the Buddha is the most heroic and powerful in the world, he is called the Hero of the World.
"Abiding in the abode of the Buddhas" refers to the eternal fruit of *nirvāṇa*, wherein all Buddhas dwell together.
Today the World Hero abides in that which he abides in—abiding in Great Nirvāṇa—and is able to initiate transformative activity; therefore, we now contemplate him.
In the second phrase, "Today the Eye of the World" is an alternative epithet for the Buddha.
He is called the "Eye of the World" because he can open the eyes of worldly beings, enabling them to see the true path.

Regarding "abiding in the conduct of a guide": the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and so forth constitute the Buddha’s conduct as a guide for transforming sentient beings; the Buddha now abides in these.
Abiding in this practice, he now wishes to guide others to enter the Buddha-dharma; it is for this reason that he is remembered.
In the third phrase, "the Hero of the World today," this is an epithet of the Buddha.
The Buddha is the most preeminent and excellent in the world; therefore, he is called "World Hero" (Lokanātha).
As for "abiding in the supreme path," unsurpassed bodhi is the most supreme path.
The internal realization of the true Way is the path of bodhi; the Buddha now abides therein.
Because he abides in this path, he knows the virtues of all Buddhas; therefore, we now contemplate him.
In the fourth phrase, "Today the World-Honored One" (*t'ien tsun*), this is an alternative name for the Buddha.
There are five kinds of "heavenly beings" (*deva*), as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The first is the worldly heaven (*laukika-deva*), referring to the kings of men in the world who are called "sons of heaven" (*devaputra*).
Second is the heaven of birth, referring to the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.
Third is the heaven of purity, referring to those from the Stream-enterer up to the Pratyekabuddha.
Fourth is the heaven of meaning, referring to all Bodhisattvas, because they understand the meaning of the emptiness and quiescence of all phenomena.
Fifth is the *paramārtha-deva*, referring to the Buddha-Tathāgata, because he understands and realizes the meaning that the Buddha-nature is not empty.
Since the Buddha is supreme among these five types of devas, he is called the "Heavenly Honored One" (*devātideva*).

"Practicing the virtues of a Tathāgata" refers to the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, the five eyes, the six supernormal knowledges, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and so forth; these are the merits of a Buddha.
"Entering the practice of renown":
because one enters these virtues, one becomes capable of delivering sentient beings; therefore, one now recollects them.
The preceding section concerns the recollection of what has been attained through mindfulness of the Buddha.
The object of their lower-level mindfulness surpasses that of all Tathāgatas; this is what they practice.
The phrase "the Buddhas of the past, future, and present mutually mindfully contemplate one another" serves as an illustration for other similar cases.
Regarding the phrase, "I wonder if you now keep the Buddhas in mind," the word "ye" (perhaps) is used to measure this remembrance of others.
"Ye" is a term of uncertainty;
because one measures it by means of principle and does not yet dare to reach a definitive conclusion, one says "ye."
From "For what reason" onwards is the conclusion of the inquiry regarding its purpose.
"For what reason is his majestic spiritual power so radiant?"—this concludes the first response.
Below this begins the third section: the Tathāgata’s formal interrogation.
"Tell me: how [did you know]? is the general question.
"Was it taught to you by the devas, or did you see it through your own wisdom? is the specific question.
From here below is the fourth section, Ānanda’s actual response.
“No deva taught me,” he said in reply to the Buddha’s previous question.
“I asked about this meaning based on what I myself had seen”; with these two replies, the section concludes.
From here below is the fifth section: the Tathāgata’s praise of the question, his command to listen, and his permission to speak.
Within this, first he praises the question itself;
from the passage "Ānanda, you should know that the Tathāgata is perfectly awakened" onwards, he sets forth the Buddha’s merits, commands one to listen, and grants permission to speak.
In the initial part of the praise, it says, "Excellent, Ānanda!
Your question is most refreshing"; this is a general praise.
"Excellent" (shàn) simply means "good."
The particle "zai" (哉) is an expletive.
To accord with the capacities [of beings], to be appropriate to the Dharma, and to coincide with the time is called "joyful.
The section beginning with "profoundly manifesting" (發深) below provides a detailed classification.
"Generating profound wisdom" refers to praising his wisdom in posing the question;
the preceding contemplation of the five kinds of merit of the Buddha is called "generating profound wisdom.
"Truly wondrous eloquence" praises the phrasing of his question.
Looking forward, he praised the Buddha for abiding in five virtues, which are called "true and wondrous eloquence" (*pratibhāna*).
To speak of reality is called "true"; to speak with skill is termed "wondrous.
Because his speech can discern and clarify, and his discourse is skillful and artful, it is called "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*).

Out of compassion for sentient beings, he inquired about the meaning [of the teachings] and praised his intention in asking; this may also be termed praising the purpose for which the inquiry was made.

Previously, Ānanda raised the five virtues of the Buddha as the basis for his questions; since these five virtues take wisdom (*prajñā*) as their primary element, it is called "inquiring into the meaning of wisdom."
From "The Tathāgata" onwards, there is a praise of the benefits of the inquiry.
This section contains four parts:
first, the Tathāgata manifests his own compassionate heart and takes pity on sentient beings.
The Buddha’s compassion is so preeminent that nothing else can surpass it or eclipse it; thus, it is called "unobstructed compassion" (anāvaraṇa-karuṇā).
There are also manuscript versions of the sūtra that emend this to "inexhaustible" (akṣaya), but "unobstructed" is correct and need not be altered.
"By means of this 'Great Compassion' (mahākaruṇā), he takes pity upon the three realms.
"Pity" (jing) is synonymous with "compassion" (lian).
The realms of desire (kāmadhātu), form (rūpadhātu), and formlessness (ārūpyadhātu) constitute these three realms.
Second, from "The reason why" onwards, the Tathāgata reveals that he has appeared in the world for the sake of sentient beings.
"The reason why he has arisen" poses a question to initiate the discourse, which is then answered and clarified below.
"To brilliantly expound the Way of the Teachings" means desiring to rescue all living beings, using the Dharma to benefit people.
Bestowing true benefit through compassion, one realizes the Dharma to aid all things.
Its principle is ultimate reality; it teaches people what is beneficial.
3. From "Immeasurable billions" onwards, it clarifies that a Buddha is difficult to encounter, first by means of the Dharma and subsequently by means of a simile.
4. From "What you have now asked" onwards, it demonstrates the benefit of the question by correlating it with the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*).

The present inquiry is beneficial in many ways; "generally clarifying what is beneficial" refers to the overall benefit, while "transforming and enlightening all beings" specifically clarifies that benefit.
The preceding section praises the question asked, while the following section cites the Buddha’s virtues, commands the listeners to attend, and grants permission for the teaching.
Within this, the first section extensively enumerates the Buddha’s virtues, recounting what was previously extolled.
From the words "Ānanda, listen attentively" downward, he commands the audience to listen, grants permission to speak, and sets forth that which he has contemplated.
Furthermore, the preceding section extensively enumerates the Buddha’s virtues to demonstrate his own capacity to preach;
the subsequent command to listen and permit the preaching demonstrates his own desire to preach.
Within the preceding section, the excellence of the fruit is first elucidated.
The section beginning with "For this reason" distinguishes the cause to manifest the fruit.
Within the clarification of the fruit, it first addresses what Ānanda was contemplating above, thereby clarifying the superiority of the Buddha’s wisdom.

From "With a single meal" onwards, [the text] contrasts the aforementioned instances such as Ānanda’s observation of the various faculties being joyful and contented, thereby clarifying the excellence of the Buddha’s body.
Within the clarification of the excellence of his wisdom, the phrase "Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One" generally enumerates the Buddha’s gnosis.
His wisdom is difficult to equal, distinguished by its manifest excellence.
"His wisdom is immeasurable" means his clear wisdom is profound.
Because he has thoroughly realized the extremely profound *dharmatā* of *nirvāṇa*, his wisdom is immeasurable; thus, his clear wisdom is profound.
This, then, is the immeasurable wisdom in which the former Buddhas dwelt; the realization of the Dharma is called "dwelling.
"Guiding many" refers to the vastness of brilliant wisdom.
This is precisely the conduct of the Guide in his previous abodes.
"Wisdom-vision is unimpeded" manifests mastery in wisdom; knowing and seeing all dharma-gates without obstruction—this is the Tathāgata’s virtue resulting from those previous practices.
"Unable to be obstructed" reveals the excellence of his wisdom, showing that he cannot be surpassed or hindered by others.
This manifestation of his superior characteristics is termed "unobstructed."
This refers to the supreme path of the preceding dwelling.
The following section clarifies the excellence of the body; by stating that "the power of a single meal enables one to sustain life" and so forth, it reveals the reality through its manifestations.

By manifesting the power of receiving a single meal in accordance with his transformations, he is able to remain for many kalpas without his body undergoing decay; this clarifies that the Buddha’s essence is eternal.

This may also be termed "revealing transformation through the real," because since the real is eternal, he manifests the reception of the power of a single meal in accordance with his transformations, thereby remaining for many kalpas without his body undergoing decay.
In the text, the initial statement that "by the power of a single meal one can sustain life for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas" demonstrates the permanence of life.
The passage beginning with "the faculties are joyful" clarifies the permanence of the body.
"The sense faculties are joyful and not impaired" clarifies the permanence of their faculties based on the joy of the faculties manifested above.
"The physical appearance remains unchanged" clarifies the permanence of their life-force based on the purity of the physical appearance manifested above.

"His radiant countenance was no different [from before]" means that, based on the aforementioned manifestation of his radiant and majestic countenance, it clarifies that he is constantly in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Thus far, based on the fruit, it has been clarified that both the Buddha’s body and wisdom are preeminent.
The subsequent citation of the cause serves to clarify and establish the preceding result.
As for the phrase "Why is this so?", it functions as an interrogative inquiry to initiate the explanation.
Why is it that the Tathāgata has attained this supreme wisdom and eternal body?
The following section explains this in contrast [to other teachings]:
"The Tathāgata’s concentration and wisdom are thoroughly perfected and infinite" clarifies that they are superior because they have been cultivated to full completion.
Concentration is cessation (*śamatha*) and wisdom is insight (*vipaśyanā*); these two are the primary practices, and thus they are singled out for mention.
All others followed him; therefore, they are omitted here without further discussion.
Because his concentration and wisdom were ultimate, he was called "Jiu" (Ultimate).
Because his penetration was unimpeded and free, he was called "Chang" (Unfettered).
Vast and boundless, it is called "the infinite.
This refers to the practice of his mind’s mastery.
The phrase "attaining mastery over all dharmas" clarifies that he is superior because of his mastery in what he has studied.
This is the practice of mastery over phenomena.
Skillfully entering the gateways of all dharma-realms, the power of these dharma-gates manifests in everything; this is called mastery (*vaśitā*).
The preceding section has extensively enumerated the Buddha’s virtues, recounting what was previously praised.

From the words "Ānanda, listen attentively" onwards, he commands the audience to listen and grants permission to speak; he speaks of that which he contemplates, namely, his mindfulness of Amitāyus Buddha in the Western Quarter.
"Listen attentively" is an injunction;
"for you" is a promise.
This concludes the fifth section.
The sixth [section], Ānanda’s receiving and upholding of the teaching,
is clear in its text and may be understood accordingly.
The introduction is hereby concluded.
Within the main body of the text, there are three distinct sections:
first, the clarification of what is practiced;
second, from "Ānanda said to the Buddha: 'The Dharma-treasury Bhikṣu has entered parinirvāṇa for the sake of his own Buddhahood'" onwards, the clarification of what is accomplished.
3. "He told Ānanda: 'As for those sentient beings who are born in that land, they abide in right concentration. The following clarifies what is encompassed [by this teaching].
These three [points] are all spoken with reference to Amitābha Buddha.
The phrase "that which is practiced" reveals the immeasurable vows and practices cultivated by that Tathāgata in the past;
the phrase "that which is accomplished" reveals the fruits of the body and land currently attained by that Tathāgata;

and the phrase "that which is encompassed" reveals how that Tathāgata currently gathers immeasurable sentient beings from the lands of the ten directions to go together to that land for the purpose of teaching, transforming, benefiting, and aiding them.
These three constitute the main body of the sutra.
Within the section concerning practice, the initial listing of many Buddhas clarifies the conditions for initiating practice.
The passage beginning with "At that time, there was a king who heard the Buddha’s teaching" demonstrates how that Dharma-treasury serves as the basis for initiating practice.

In total, fifty-four Buddhas are enumerated; the first fifty-three are listed together in one place, while the final Buddha, who personally received the Dharma-treasury, is listed separately in another place.
Within the first fifty-three Buddhas, the phrase "In the past, inconceivable kalpas ago," and so forth, clarifies their temporal setting;
the phrases beginning with "Dīpaṃkara appeared," and so forth, list them in successive order.
"All such Buddhas have already passed away" concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one.
Next, the name of the Sovereign King Buddha (Vaiśvānara-rāja) is listed;
"Sovereign of the World" (Lokavaśavartin) is his specific epithet.
“Tathāgata,” “Arhat,” and so forth, are his universal epithets.
Since the virtues of a Buddha are immeasurable, names are bestowed in accordance with these virtues; thus, the names are likewise limitless.
This sutra follows a specific numerical scheme and briefly enumerates ten such types.
Among the ten [perfections], the first five are the Buddha’s own virtues, while the latter five concern benefiting others.
Within the first five, there is a pair consisting of the first two: the former is the perfection of the Path, and the latter is the ultimate of Cessation.
Of the three subsequent pairs, the first two refer to the perfection of the cause, while the last one refers to the ultimate fruit.
Within the first pair, the term "Tathāgata" is used to manifest the perfection of his path.
Because he has traveled upon the path of reality as it is and come to achieve perfect enlightenment, he is called the Tathāgata.
As for the term "Arhat" (Worthy One), it manifests the perfection of his cessation;
because he is in accord with the realization of cessation, he is named Arhat.
Furthermore, because he has realized cessation (*nirodha*), he is worthy of offerings; thus, he is called "Worthy of Offerings" (*Arhat*).
Within the latter pair [of epithets], the first two represent the perfection of the causes.
Among these, the term "Perfectly Enlightened One" (*Samyaksaṃbuddha*) manifests the perfection of his understanding (*jñāna*).
In other sūtras, he is also called the "Perfectly Complete Knower" (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
"Perfect" (Samyak) refers to the principle (dharma);
because he exhaustively illuminates that principle, he is named the "Complete Knower" (Saṃbuddha).
The term "equal" (*sama*) mentioned here refers to its pervasiveness (*vyāpin*).
It is called "equal" because it accords with principle (*yukti*); "correct" (*samyak*) likewise refers to what is correct in other sūtras.
As for the term "awakening" (*bodha*), it refers to that which knows (*jñāna*).
Regarding "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*): it signifies that his conduct is perfected.
"Knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers to realized conduct; because the realization of the Dharma is clearly manifest, it is called "knowledge.
There are three types of this, as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
First is the illumination of a bodhisattva, namely the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Second is the illumination of all Buddhas, namely the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).
Third is the illumination of non-illumination, referring to the eleven kinds of emptiness; because these are not [ordinary] intellectual understanding, they are called "non-illumination."
Because it can produce the clarity of wisdom, it is further called "clarity" (*vidyā*).
Of these, the former two are that which realizes, while the latter one is that which is realized.
Furthermore, Nāgārjuna said:

The Buddha possesses the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); therefore, these are called the three insights (*vidyā*).
To practice these teachings is what is described in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
"Calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are called 'practice' (*caryā*)."
Furthermore, Nāgārjuna says:
Precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth are termed "practices" (*caryā*); because these two [the practices and their fruits] are perfectly complete, they are called "feet.
The term "Sugata" clarifies that his fruition has reached its ultimate limit.
"Good" (*śubha*) means excellent, and "gone" (*gata*) means departed.
Because the Tathāgata has gone excellently, he is called the Sugata.
Since the Buddha’s virtues are fully perfected, where else could he go such that one would speak of him as having "gone well"?
Although there is no place to which one goes, it is not that one cannot go.
It is like the fire at the end of an eon (*kalpa*): although there is nothing for it to burn, it is not that it cannot burn.
Therefore, one may say that there is going.
Among the latter five, the first four are specific and the last one is general.
Within the first four specifics, "Knower of the World" refers to the wisdom that transforms others.
Being well-versed in the world, he is called the "Knower of the World.
The two titles "Unsurpassed Man, Tamer of Men" and "Teacher of Gods and Humans" refer to his mastery over the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
That Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, is able to tame the minds of beings; having tamed himself, he tames others. He is the ultimate among tamers, and is therefore called "Unsurpassed.
"One" (*śi*) is a specific designation for such a person.
This Unsurpassed One is able to skillfully employ expedient means to subdue sentient beings; thus he is named the Charioteer of Men.
As the Teacher of Gods and Humans, he is able to bestow the Dharma.
Because he is able to closely instruct gods and humans through the True Dharma, he is named the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
He transforms beings across all six realms, and among gods and humans, those benefited are exceedingly numerous; for this reason, he is singled out for mention.
As for "Buddha," it refers to his virtue of transforming others.
This term is translated as "Awakened" (Jue); because he awakens himself and awakens others, and because his practice of awakening has reached ultimate fulfillment, he is called a Buddha.
Regarding the term "World-Honored One" (Bhagavat), this title is general.
Because the Buddha is endowed with all virtues and is revered by the world, he is titled the World-Honored One.
The preceding section clarifies the conditions for the arising of the Buddha’s practice; the following section clarifies how the treasury of the Dharma arises based upon those conditions.
Within this, the first part clarifies mundane practice.
From the passage, "The Buddha told Ānanda that the Bhikṣu Dharmākara spoke these verses," onwards, supramundane practice is clarified.
That which is practiced prior to the stages (bhūmis) is termed mundane; [that which follows is supramundane].
Regarding the mundane and supramundane, within the practices of the world, there are three successive stages:

first, hearing the Dharma and generating the aspiration for enlightenment; second, leaving the household life to cultivate the path; and third, approaching the Buddha’s presence to pay homage, offer praise, and generate the vow-mind.
At the beginning, the phrase "at that time there was a king" introduces the practitioner.
"Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, his heart was filled with joy" means that his mind rejoiced upon hearing the Dharma.
"Immediately he gave rise to the aspiration for the Way" correctly clarifies the arousal of the mind.
The meaning of *bodhicitta* is explained extensively in a separate chapter; this should be discussed in full detail there.
In the second section, "abandoning his country and relinquishing his kingship," clarifies that which was renounced.
"Practicing as a śramaṇa" clarifies his conduct.
This is translated as "Resting," because he brings all evils to rest.
"Named Dharmākara" lists his personal name.
The phrases "high talent and courage" and so forth distinguish his character and conduct.
"Talent" refers to skillful ability; because his talent and virtue surpass those of others, he is called one of "high talent.
A strong will is termed "courage," and a clear mind is designated as "wisdom."
This virtue emerges in solitude, hence it is named "Transcending the World.
In the third section, first he approaches the Buddha's dwelling, and next, having arrived, he pays respect.
"Bowing one's head" (*kāśī*) signifies respect.
To humble oneself and receive those of low station is therefore used to express reverence.
"Circumambulating to the right" signifies affection;
because one circumambulates without abandoning them, it is used to express affection.
From "kneeling with long legs" (*jang-kwei*) onwards is the praise and the making of vows.
"Kneeling with long legs and joining the palms" constitutes the skillful means for offering praise.
"Spoke in verse" is the general summary provided by the compiler of the sutra.
Why are verses (gāthā) employed?
Because their meaning and expression are exquisite and beautiful, those who offer praise generally use verses.
Furthermore, verses are skillfully concise; within few syllables, they are able to encompass many meanings.
The Bhikṣu Dharmākara, wishing to encompass the Buddha’s virtues extensively through concise words, therefore expressed them in verse.
The following presents the verses.
There are seven initial verses which praise the Buddha’s virtues and clarify that which he seeks.
The final thirteen verses express vows to seek Buddhahood, clarifying the capacity for such seeking.
Within the preceding seven verses, the first five and a half verses specifically praise the Buddha’s virtues,
while the final one and a half verses conclude by praising his virtues.
In the preceding section on the formal praise, the first two and a half verses praise the Buddha’s physical activity (kāyakarma);
the next half verse praises the Buddha’s verbal activity (vākkarma);
and the final two and a half verses praise the Buddha’s mental activity (manaskarma).
Within the eulogy of the Buddha’s physical actions (*kāyakarman*), the phrase "the radiance is magnificent" praises the excellence of the Buddha’s light, constituting one gate.
The phrase "the countenance is magnificent" praises the excellence of the Buddha’s body, constituting another gate.
The term "wei-wei" has already been explained above.
Furthermore, there are seven phrases that manifest the wei-wei radiance.
Its majestic spiritual power is infinite, and its light issues forth from its basis.
Because the Buddha’s majestic virtue and spiritual power are infinite, he is able to emit light.
Such blazing brilliance refers precisely to the substance of the light itself.
"There is none equal to him" manifests his superiority in contrast to others; the bodily radiance of other people cannot match it.
“The sun, moon, and mani-jewels are like a mass of ink” refers to the manifestation of superiority through contrast with specific objects.
When these various lights are compared to the Buddha’s light, they are all eclipsed and obscured, just as a mass of ink placed beside a conch shell or mother-of-pearl.
The following two lines reveal the majestic countenance of Yan and Wei:
"The Tathāgata’s countenance transcends the world and is peerless," thus his countenance is majestic (*weiwēi*).
"Peer" (*lún*) refers to a match or equal.
Next, the verbal karma is praised: "The great resonance of the Perfectly Awakened One flows throughout the ten directions.
Below this, the mental karma is praised.
Within this section, there are initially two verses that praise the Buddha’s virtues of practice;
The latter half-verse praises the Buddha’s virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*):
"Practice is *bodhi*; cessation is *nirvāṇa*.
Within the former [half], the first verse praises the excellence of the Buddha’s virtues.
The latter verse praises the profundity of the Buddha’s virtues.
"Superior" refers to the practice of teaching, while "profound" refers to the practice of realization.
Within the preceding praise for superiority, the passage "precepts, learning, diligence, samādhi, and wisdom" enumerates the essential substance of his virtues.
"His majestic radiance is peerless, supreme, and rare" refers to his excellence as manifested through virtue.
His majestic power is without equal, such that no other can match it;
it is supreme and rare because the Buddha's virtues transcend all others.
Later, he sighed deeply within himself, saying: "Profoundly and truthfully contemplate the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas," which refers to the skillful means for attaining realization.
"Truthfully" (*di*) means with thorough examination.
By contemplating the ocean of Buddha-dharmas with profound and truthful mindfulness, one is thus able to attain realization.
The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is the ocean of the Buddha-dharma.
To "exhaust its depth, exhaust its mystery, and investigate its furthest limits" refers to the accomplishment of realization and practice.
This praises the virtue of practice; what follows praises the virtue of cessation.
“Ignorance” (avidyā) is delusion; “desire” (rāga) is greed; “anger” (dveṣa) is hatred.
Because the Buddha has severed these forever so that they no longer exist, his severance is supreme.
The preceding section has separately extolled the merits of the three types of karma;
from here on, the praise is concluded. "The Lion among Men, whose divine virtues are immeasurable" is the general concluding praise.
The "vastness of merit" is a concluding praise according to its specific distinctions.

Regarding "the vastness of merit," this concludes and praises the preceding [section on] speech: because the great resonance of the Perfectly Awakened One flows throughout the ten directions, the Buddha’s merit in transforming others is vast.
"Wisdom profound and subtle" concludes by praising the preceding meaning.
Although there were many virtues mentioned previously, the text specifically concludes with its wisdom because it is the primary practice.
"Profound" refers back to its depth, and "subtle" refers back to its excellence.
"Radiant Majesty" (*Prabhāsa-tejas*) and so forth conclude the eulogy of his previous life.
Having finished the eulogy above, from here on he makes vows to seek that which was previously praised.
Within this section, there are initially ten verses of text that formally give rise to the aspirational mind;
The final three verses request that the Buddha bear witness.
Within the preceding ten verses, the first five seek the Buddha’s Dharma-body,
while the latter five seek the Buddha’s Pure Land.
Within the section on seeking the Dharma-body, the first verse expresses the aspiration for the fruit of Buddhahood;
the next two verses express the aspiration for the causes of Buddhahood;
and the final two verses provide a comparative evaluation to manifest its excellence.
Within the pursuit of the fruit, "May I become a Buddha, a Sage and Dharma King" seeks the Buddha’s own virtues;
"Transcending birth and death, there is none who is not liberated" seeks the virtue of benefiting others.
Regarding the search within the causes, there are initially one and a half verses seeking the practice for one's own benefit;
below that, there are half a verse seeking the practice for the benefit of others.
Within the search for one's own benefit, the first verse sets forth those practices of the six perfections.
“Generosity that disciplines the mind” refers to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Cultivating generosity to remedy stinginess is called “disciplining the mind.

“Precepts” refer to the perfection of morality (*śīla-pāramitā*); “patience” is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); “vigor” is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*); “samādhi” is the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); and “wisdom” is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
Wisdom that excels is called "superior"; in contrast to this inferior state, one gives rise to a vow:
"I vow to attain Buddhahood. This is the destination toward which one directs one's practice.
To "universally carry out this vow" means to seek the causes and proceed toward that goal.
The lower seeking of the benefit of others is clear from the text and thus easily understood.
The upper seeking refers to the seeking of the cause;
the two verses below this [the preceding section] employ comparative analysis to manifest its superiority and thereby strengthen the resolve for the vow.
"Even if there were hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas" cites the Jewel of the Buddha;

The phrase "making offerings to these" and so forth refers to making offerings to the preceding Jewel of the Sangha.
"To all these Buddhas" refers to making offerings to the preceding Jewel of the Buddha.
The section beginning with "not as good as seeking" contrasts the aspiration with the former acts to demonstrate that [the former] falls short.
"Què" means "to retreat.
Although one may provide for many sages, it is not as good as seeking the Way oneself without retreating; therefore, this is emphasized to strengthen the resolve.
Such comparisons in the sutras are so numerous that they cannot all be recounted in detail; for while offerings are limited, the mind seeking the Way has no such limit.
In the section on seeking the land below, the first three and a half verses concern seeking a pure land for oneself;
the final one and a half verses concern seeking a land that gathers others.
Within the pursuit for oneself, the initial two verses generally cite many lands.
Next follows a half-verse clarifying what is sought by oneself, which is the foremost among all lands;

Within the preceding general enumeration, the phrase "like the sands of the Ganges" and so forth extensively cites many lands.
