The phrase "pervading this land" clarifies the adornment of the light of the Buddha-Tathāgata.
"The vigor and majestic spiritual power are thus immeasurable" clarifies the adornment of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
That the Buddha diligently manifests transformative deeds in that land is termed "vigor."

Regarding the phrase "causing me to become the foremost among Buddha-lands," this refers to the land currently established as Amitābha’s realm, which is the most supreme among all the lands previously enumerated in terms of its various marks of adornment.
Below there is a verse that reveals the first characteristic.
"The assembly is wondrous and marvelous" clarifies that the assembly is foremost.
"The site of enlightenment is transcendent" clarifies that the location is foremost.
"The land is like nirvāṇa and has no equal" clarifies that the land is foremost, and it may also be called the foremost in bliss.
Nirvāṇa and nibbāna are originally one name; the difference lies only in the phonetic transmission.
Therefore, the text below states: "In the land of Amitābha, sentient beings experience bliss and subsequently enter nirvāṇa.
The preceding section concerns seeking [enlightenment] for oneself;

The phrase "I shall compassionately deliver all" clarifies that when he himself attains the Buddha-way in the future, he will liberate all beings.
The passage beginning with "Those who come from the ten directions shall have joyful and pure minds" clarifies that those born in his land in the future will all equally obtain supreme benefit.
Those coming from the ten directions are many; their births are numerous.
Their hearts are joyful and pure, for they have returned with single-minded devotion.
By saying "I have already arrived," and so forth, they obtain superior benefit.
The ten preceding verses properly give rise to the mind of aspiration;
the three subsequent verses request the Buddha to bear witness.

In the first half-verse, "幸" (xìng) signifies a wish; it is a prayer that the Buddha may believe my request is not in vain.

At the beginning, there is first the request, followed by the Buddha’s response.

The passage beginning with “and addressed the Buddha” reveals the words of that request.
"I have resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment" serves as a transition from what precedes to what follows.
In the preceding verses, seeking the body and seeking the land was termed "resolving to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
The mind is the root of practice; by manifesting that one possesses this root, it clarifies the capacity to initiate practice and gives rise to the request.
"I pray that the Buddha will extensively expound the Dharma for me" is the formal request for its proclamation.
The phrase "I shall cultivate," and so forth, clarifies the purpose for which the request is made.

"I shall practice" is the first gate, which constitutes the cause for practicing the pure land of the Dharma-body.
"Having grasped" and what follows is the second gate, clarifying that which has been accomplished by oneself.
Regarding "the land formed by the body," such as "taking up the pure adornments of the Buddha-field" and so forth, this refers to the land that is formed.
"Quickly accomplishing [it] in the world" refers to the body that is formed.
“Extricating from birth-and-death” and so forth constitute the third section, clarifying what has been encompassed by oneself.
It describes the gathering in of sentient beings and their instruction and transformation so that they may emerge from the root of the suffering of birth-and-death.
To "uproot birth-and-death" means to produce the fruit of transcending birth-and-death, to uproot the source of suffering, and to depart from the causes of birth-and-death.
Because one undergoes the suffering of birth-and-death repeatedly due to these causes, those causes are termed the "source of suffering."

There is no contradiction between these two; this is precisely what is meant by this.
"Hong" (弘) means "great.

Principle transcends all marks; therefore, there is nothing to which one clings.

Ānanda asked first, and the Buddha answered afterward:

Therefore, that Dharma-treasury, within a single body, practiced for five kalpas in the presence of that Buddha.
A question is asked:

The commentary states:
Other people perceive the exhaustion of the kalpa, whereas those such as Dharmakara perceive that land as peaceful, secure, and unmoving; thus, they are able to initiate their cultivation.

This corresponds to what is said in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "When sentient beings see the end of the kalpa and are scorched by the great fire, my land remains peaceful and secure, always filled with devas and humans."
The meaning is similar [to what precedes].

Within the first section: "Having practiced thus" concludes the preceding and introduces what follows;

"I have already, throughout the first five kalpas, undertaken the pure practices for adorning the land.

Because that treasury of Dharma has itself expressed its vows, it causes the assembly to share in the joy of aspiring to be born in that land; thus it is called "initiating that which pleases the entire assembly."
The passage beginning with "When the Bodhisattvas hear" is for the benefit of the Bodhisattvas.

Because that treasury of Dharma itself proclaims its own vows, it causes all Bodhisattvas to study them and likewise resolve to attain them; therefore, it says that having heard them, they practice this Dharma and fulfill their great vows.
“Having heard it, one practices” marks the beginning of the arising of the vow.
“Bringing [the conditions] to fulfillment,” and so forth, indicates the accomplishment of the aspirational mind.
From here below is the third section, in which the Bhikṣu Dharmākara himself proclaims his own vows.
"Please deign to listen and examine," he requested so that the Buddha might speak.
"May you explain fully according to my vow," he said, and the Buddha granted his general consent to proclaim them.
Below follows the actual exposition; therein there are forty-eight vows in total, which in substance comprise three points, though they are distinguished into seven sections in the text.
The essential meaning consists of three types of vows: first, the vow to encompass the Dharma-body; second, the vow to encompass the Pure Land; and third, the vow to encompass sentient beings.
Among the forty-eight vows, the twelfth, thirteenth, and seventeenth are those that encompass the Dharma-body;
the thirty-first and thirty-second are those that encompass the Pure Land.
The remaining forty-three [vows] are for the purpose of gathering in sentient beings.
As for the seven distinct categories of text: first, the eleven vows are for gathering in sentient beings;
next, there are two vows which constitute the second category, for gathering in the Dharma-body.
Next, there are three vows; this is the third [section], which extensively gathers in sentient beings.

Next, there are thirteen [vows]; this is the fifth [section], for the purpose of gathering in sentient beings.

below are sixteen, which constitute the seventh, for the further purpose of encompassing sentient beings.
Within the first section, there are initially two vows: the first is the vow to be born where there is no suffering;
the subsequent nine vows are the vow to be born and obtain happiness.
Within the category of being free from suffering, the first vow is the wish that one's own country be free from suffering.
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals in my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
To "not attain perfect enlightenment" means that if these vows are not fulfilled, one shall ultimately not become a Buddha.

"Suppose my vow were not fulfilled; I would rather never attain enlightenment. For this reason, it is said: 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts in my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'"
The others are also like this.
As for what is called "hell" (dīya), it refers to a prison beneath the earth that is a place of suffering; therefore, it is called hell.
As for what is called a "hungry ghost" (preta), hunger and thirst are termed "hunger."
They are called "ghosts" (*preta*) because they are timid, cowardly, and full of fear.
As for "animals" (*tiryagyoni*), this is a name derived from being raised and kept by a master; since all worldly people raise these beings either for food or for labor, they are called animals.
The latter vow is the wish that all sentient beings within one's own country shall not suffer in another land after their lives end.
These two vows are the wish to be born where there is no suffering.
Among the latter nine vows for attaining happiness upon rebirth, the first two vows aspire to the happiness of the body;
the latter seven vows aspire to the happiness of the mind.

Within the mental happiness, the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are each treated as one, while the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is divided into two; thus, there are seven vows.
The following consists of three sections, the textual characteristics of which are easily understood.

Regarding the first two verses within the section on the virtues of transformation: "The power of spiritual transformations radiates light that illuminates boundless lands" refers to the transformation of bodily action (*kāyakarman*).

To eliminate the three impurities and rescue those from calamities and hardships refers to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, which transform beings by severing the three poisons; this is called "removing the three impurities.

"Merit and fortune" (in the single verse) cites the Buddha's own virtues.

“Majestic brilliance and clarity,” and so forth, refer to the functional manifestations of the Buddha’s virtues.
For now, the function of light is cited as an illustration, while the others are omitted for brevity.
“Majestically illuminating the ten directions” refers to the vastness of that light.
"The brilliance of the sun and moon is withdrawn and the light of heaven does not appear"—this refers to the superiority of [the Buddha's] light.
When the Buddha’s radiance eclipses them, the sun and moon withdraw their light so that it can no longer shine outward; this is called "withdrawing the double radiance."
The single verse beginning with "For the sake of the multitude" reiterates the virtue of transformation; its meaning is clear and can be understood from the text.

The first of these verses clarifies that the Buddha attained the fruit through the perfection of the causes.

The ten preceding verses establish the solemn vow and self-restraint.

Within the preceding discussion on the cause for abandonment, the phrase "not giving rise to thoughts of desire, thoughts of anger, or thoughts of harm" specifically clarifies that which is to be abandoned.
There are eight types of vitarka, as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
first is the vitarka of desire, which consists of thinking about wealth and thinking about forms;
second is the vitarka of anger, also called the vitarka of resentment, which consists of desiring to harbor ill will toward others.
Third is the perception of harm, also called the perception of vexation, which involves the thought of wishing to inflict injury upon others;
fourth is the perception of kin, which is the recollection of one's relatives;
fifth is the perception of the realm, which is the contemplation of the security and peril of the world.
Sixth is the perception of immortality, which means thinking that one will not die and thus extensively accumulating the necessities of life;
seventh is the perception of lineage, which involves contemplating the high or low status of one's clan;
eighth is the perception of disparagement, which involves thinking of looking down upon others.
Among these eight types, the first three are the most serious faults and are therefore singled out for mention.
The phrase "not giving rise to thoughts of desire or thoughts of anger" reiterates this point.
Not giving rise to thoughts of desire is called being free from sensual perceptions (*kāma-vitarka*).
Not giving rise to thoughts of anger is called being free from the perception of anger;
not giving rise to thoughts of harm is called being free from the perception of harm.
Alternatively, the preceding statement regarding the non-arising of the three perceptions may be understood as indicating freedom from them at their very inception.
One does not give rise to thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, or thoughts of harm; this is based on the ultimate clarity of detachment.
To pre-emptively give rise to improper reflections before encountering an object is termed "vitarka" (applied thought).
When the mind arises in response to conditions, it is described as the three types of "saṃjñā" (perceptions/thoughts).
All of these are abandoned.
Below, the objects of delusion are abandoned: "not being attached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles," and so forth.
This concludes the first section.

“Wisdom is unimpeded” refers to the excellence of the practice of insight (vipaśyanā).
The four preceding sections together constitute the benefit for oneself (svārtha).
The following section clarifies the abandonment of afflictions through the benefit of others.
"Having no mind of hypocrisy or crookedness" clarifies the abandonment of faults of the mind.
The term "gentle countenance" clarifies the abandonment of faults of the body.
"Kind speech begins with inquiry," which clarifies the avoidance of verbal transgressions.
Because there are no afflictions (*kleśa*), errors do not arise within body, speech, or mind.
The preceding section was the first, clarifying the avoidance of afflictions; from here on is the second, clarifying the cultivation of virtue.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, generating the mind of aspiration;
second, from "with reverence" onwards, initiating practice based on that aspiration; [and third, the conclusion].
3. Below the section "Abiding in Emptiness," practice is perfected and entry into realization occurs.
Within the initial arousal of the vow, the passage "With courageous diligence and tireless aspiration, he seeks the pure and white Dharma" constitutes the vow for self-benefit.
"Benevolently benefiting all living beings" refers to the vow for the benefit of others.
Within the second section, self-benefit is explained first, followed by the benefit of others.
Regarding the former, within self-benefit, "revering the Three Jewels and serving one's teachers and elders" constitutes the skillful means for gathering [practices].
"Revering the Three Jewels" encompasses the skillful means for accumulating merit;
"serving teachers and elders" encompasses the skillful means for acquiring wisdom;
and "great adornment," etc., manifest the perfection of practice.
"Greatly adorned" means that one adorns oneself with the two types of adornments: merit and wisdom.
"Possessing all practices," when categorized individually, refers to possessing all practices such as *dāna* (generosity) and the rest.
The following clarifies benefiting others.
By practicing and teaching others, one causes sentient beings to achieve the accomplishment of merit.

Regarding the third realization, it says: "Abiding in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, which are unconditioned and unarisen. Because all dharmas do not exist and persons and dharmas lack intrinsic nature, this is called emptiness.
Since both the person and phenomena are provisional, their characteristics do not exist; this is called signlessness (*animitta*).
Within these two, the absence of any mind that seeks or takes delight in them is called wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Furthermore, being free from conceptual construction is also called "wishlessness" (*apraṇihita*).
Among these three, that for which no fruit can be produced is called "non-action" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Although one practices non-action, one manifests the reception of a body. Therefore, we know that non-action is discussed in terms of its fruit.
Among the three preceding [categories], that which cannot arise due to a cause is termed "non-arising" (*an-utpāda*).
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Although one practices non-arising, one gives rise to wholesome conduct. Therefore, we know that "non-arising" is spoken of in reference to causes.

However, the principles taught throughout the various sūtras are not fixed; sometimes they speak of a single emptiness, such as the "solitary emptiness" (du kong) described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Because it distinguishes one [emptiness] rather than many, it is termed "solitary."
Some speak of two kinds, namely the two types of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Some speak of three kinds: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Some speak of four kinds, as taught in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, namely emptiness, non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), signlessness, and non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:

there is the emptiness of existing phenomena (*bhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existing phenomena (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of transformed phenomena (*nirmāṇa-śūnyatā*). These are likewise four kinds, which are explained in detail in a separate chapter.

Alternatively, five kinds are taught as explained here: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), and non-arising (*anutpāda*), all of which have been fully explained above.
Alternatively, seven kinds of emptiness are taught, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Some speak of nine emptinesses, as explained in the *Abhidharma*;
some speak of eleven, as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*;
and some speak of fourteen, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Some speak of eighteen [emptinesses], as taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Others speak of twenty-five emptinesses, as taught in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; if expanded, they are immeasurable.
Now, based on one gate, we shall briefly discuss five kinds.
To realize and comprehend this principle of the Dharma is called "contemplating phenomena as like illusions," wherein the realization of the Dharma is not non-existent.
This concludes the second section; from here below, the third section clarifies the departure from evil karma.
Within this, the first part clarifies the avoidance of faults;
from "cultivating the wholesome" onwards, it demonstrates the practice of gathering and correcting.
In the preceding section on avoiding faults, "staying far away from coarse speech" clarifies the avoidance of verbal misconduct.
"Avoiding harm to oneself, harm to others, and harm to both" clarifies the abandonment of physical misconduct.
Within the subsequent section on "cultivating wholesome speech," one remedies the aforementioned verbal misconduct.
"Benefiting oneself and benefiting others, so that both self and others are benefited" refers to remedying past bodily evils.
This concludes the third section; hereafter begins the fourth, which again clarifies the cultivation of goodness.
Within this, the first part clarifies his self-benefit: "Abandoning his kingdom and renouncing kingship, he utterly cast away wealth and beauty," which clarifies what he relinquished;
"He personally practiced the six perfections," which demonstrates what he cultivated.
The following clarifies benefiting others, teaching people through the first six perfections so that they may practice them.
The preceding four sections have specifically clarified the causes of the body; this section concludes by summarizing the accumulation of merit and virtue over incalculable eons.
The preceding section was the first, clarifying the cultivation of the requisites; from here on is the second, manifesting the excellence of the retribution.
This contains two parts:
first, in contrast to the causes for purifying the buddha-land cultivated above, it clarifies the attainment of excellent retribution, which is the fruit of the superior support (*adhiṣṭhāna-phala*).

Second, from "or as a householder or lay devotee" onwards, in contrast to the aforementioned causes for the Dharma-body, it clarifies the attainment of a superior retribution and the attainment of the supreme, correct fruit.

Regarding the first part of the middle section, the statement "In whatever place one is born, immeasurable treasuries of jewels will spontaneously manifest according to one's mental desires" means that one personally attains superior wealth.
The character "zai" (在) here signifies "to rely upon" or "to be at ease."
"Transforming and establishing others so that they abide in the right path" means gathering others through material gifts to lead them back to the True Dharma.
Herein, the first part clarifies the fruit of merit;
the subsequent section, "attaining mastery over all phenomena," clarifies the fruit of wisdom.
Within the fruits of merit, there is first the detailed exposition and subsequently the summary.
In the detailed exposition, there are four parts:
first, the excellence of the physical retribution;
2. From "Constantly making offerings with the four requisites" onwards, [the text describes] conduct arising based on the body;
3. From "The breath of the mouth" onwards, the physical retribution is subtle and wondrous—within this section, the three phrases have their textual structure clearly intelligible;
4. From "From the hands emerge" onwards, it describes the function of conduct arising based on the body: the hands produce offering implements to worship the Buddhas.
The preceding section concludes the specific exposition.
The phrase "those such as these surpass all devas and humans" serves as a general summary and praise; through this, the fruit of wisdom may be known.
Above, the practice was clarified; from here on, the second part clarifies that which is accomplished—namely, the attainment of the fruit of the Dharma-body and the Pure Land.
However, as for what has been accomplished here, it corresponds respectively to the previous forty-eight great vows; this can be clearly understood from the manifest text.
Within the text there are two parts:
first, a brief clarification of what has been accomplished; [second, a detailed explanation].
Second, from "The Buddha told Ānanda: 'The majestic spiritual power of Amitāyus Buddha... onwards, the accomplishment is explained in detail.
This section consists of four parts:
first, Ānanda asks regarding his own person whether he has already attained Buddhahood or not, and the Tathāgata answers in full.
2. From "That Buddha-field" onwards, the land is elucidated by way of its characteristics;
3. From "Again he asked" onwards, Ānanda again inquires regarding his own body concerning the duration since [the Buddha] attained enlightenment, and the Tathāgata answers in full;
4. From "In that land, the seven jewels appear spontaneously" onwards, the land is elucidated by way of its characteristics.
Within the first section, Ānanda first asks whether the Dharma-treasury Bhikṣu has already attained Buddhahood or has not yet manifested it;
this question is posed by distinguishing between the three periods of time.
The Buddha’s answer can be understood.
In the second section, the names of those buddha-lands are listed directly without yet distinguishing their characteristics.
In the third section, the text is clear and understandable, as it first poses questions and subsequently provides answers.
In the fourth section, first the "possessions" are clarified.
The passage beginning with "Furthermore, in that land there is no Mount Sumeru" clarifies what is absent.
Within the clarification of the possessions, the phrase "spontaneously formed of jewels" clarifies its essential nature and characteristics.
"Vast and expansive" clarifies the aspect of its magnitude.
"All are intermingled," and so forth, clarifies the aspect of adornment.
Regarding the clarification of what is non-existent, the former first provides the formal analysis;
From "Ānanda said" onwards, the question and answer further clarify [the preceding points].

In the initial formal exposition, it was first shown that there are no mountains and so forth; next, that there are no four realms of rebirth; and finally, that there are no distinctions such as the four seasons of spring, autumn, and so on.
In the subsequent section on further clarification, there are three distinct parts:
first, Ānanda asks,
"If Mount Sumeru did not exist, upon what would the Four Heavenly Kings and the others rely for their abode?"
1. The Tathāgata poses a counter-question.
2. Ānanda provides the correct answer, and the Tathāgata summarizes it to reveal that matter.
3. Ānanda clarifies that he asked for the sake of others, not because he himself was ignorant.
The preceding section concludes the brief exposition.
Regarding the following extensive exposition, there are four distinct parts:
first, clarifying the Buddha’s body; second, clarifying his retinue based on that body; third, clarifying the land; and fourth, clarifying the inhabitants based on that land.
Within the first section, one should first explain the meaning of the three types of Buddhas and subsequently interpret the text.
The meaning is as discussed in a separate chapter.
In the text, the characteristics of the Buddha’s radiance are clarified first, followed by the manifestation of his lifespan.
In the preceding section on "Radiant Light," it was marvelously praised and manifested; first through individual distinctions and subsequently through a summary.
Within the distinctions, there are four parts:
first, Śākyamuni’s own praise;
2. From "If there are sentient beings who encounter this light" onwards, it clarifies the benefits for all sentient beings who see or hear [it].
3. From "The light of Amitāyus shines resplendently" onwards, the various sages collectively offer praise.
4. From "If there are sentient beings who hear within that light" onwards, it again clarifies the benefits obtained by sentient beings who see or hear [it].
The first part has three sections:
First, distinguishing the superior from the inferior, wherein the radiance of Amitāyus Buddha is supreme.
Second, from the passage "the radiance of all other Buddhas cannot reach it" onwards, the inferior is cited to manifest the superior.
The Buddha’s light is indeed equal [to all], being thus because it accords with his transformative teachings.
Third, from the words “Therefore” onwards, there are twelve phrases that praise and manifest its excellence.
First, “immeasurable light, boundless, and unimpeded”—these three types are praised according to their respective characteristics.
"Immeasurable" means much;
"boundless" means vast;
"unimpeded" means sovereign.
"Unrivaled" (*pratigha*) and "flaming king" (*jvalanarāja*): these two terms are employed to manifest its excellence.
Because other lights cannot rival it, it is called "unrivaled light.
Because this light surpasses all others, it is called "flaming king light."
"Purity, joy, wisdom, and non-interruption"—these four qualities should be praised according to their respective characteristics.
Being free from defilement is called purity; being able to gladden the minds of those who see it is called joy.
Skillfully illuminating phenomena is called the light of wisdom.
Constantly shining without ceasing is called the uninterrupted light.
These three types—“inconceivable,” “incomparable,” and “surpassing the light of the sun and moon”—are designated in contrast to manifest their excellence.
Because its mental conceptions transcend the world, it is called "inconceivable.
Because its verbal expressions transcend the world, it is named "Ineffable Radiance.
Because its physical forms transcend the world, it is named "Surpassing the Sun and Moon."
The preceding section was the first, in which Śākyamuni praised himself; from here on is the second, concerning the benefits obtained through seeing and hearing.
First, the phrase "Those who encounter it have their three impurities extinguished" clarifies the benefit of removing hindrances.
This refers to the three poisons being designated as the "three impurities.
The phrase "warmth of body and mind" and so forth clarifies the benefit of generating wholesome states.
The section beginning with "If one is in [the three realms]" and below clarifies the benefit of extinguishing suffering.
The section beginning with "After the end of life" clarifies the benefit of attaining happiness.
The third part, the shared praise, is clear in its text and thus easily understood.

Within the fourth part, which again clarifies the attainment of benefits: first, it clarifies that one will be proclaimed to be reborn according to one's wishes; second, it shows that all the sages together offer praise and acclaim; and finally, it clarifies that one attains the universal praise of all Buddhas.
The preceding section constitutes the specific praise.
From the passage beginning with "The Buddha said: 'I speak of the light of Amitāyus Buddha,'" onwards, it serves as the general concluding praise.
From the section beginning with "The preceding [section] clarified the light," onwards, it clarifies the Buddha’s lifespan; the text is explicit and thus easily understood.
The preceding section was the first, clarifying the Buddha’s body; from here below is the second, clarifying the assembly in relation to that body.
This section contains four parts:
first, clarifying that the lifespan of the people in that land is exceedingly long, as in the case of Amitāyus.
1. The section beginning with "Furthermore, the śrāvakas... clarifies their great number; 2.
The section beginning with "Their divine wisdom penetrates... manifests the excellence of their virtues; 3.
The fourth section again manifests their great number.
Furthermore, we shall first manifest its manifold characteristics based on the initial assembly; the others cannot be discussed here.

Regarding the statement, "In the first assembly, the śrāvakas were beyond measure and calculation, and the bodhisattvas were likewise," one need not analyze these manifold characteristics further; it is sufficient to demonstrate them through the fact that Maudgalyāyana could not know [their number].
Among these, the first clarifies that Maudgalyāyana did not know;
from the phrase "like the great ocean" onwards, it illustrates this by means of an analogy.
The Buddha first established a metaphor and posed a counter-question to Ānanda.
Next, Ānanda replies;
the Buddha then restricts him [in his response] to clarify the extent of what Maudgalyāyana knows.
From here on, the third section elucidates that land.
Within this, one should first explain the meaning of the Pure Land, and subsequently interpret the text; the meaning is as discussed in a separate chapter.
In the text, there is a general discussion of the three types of adornment:
first, the adornment of phenomena (*vastu-vyūha*), consisting of the excellence of the five objects of desire, such as form, fragrance, flavor, and so forth.
There are two kinds of adornment: the adornment of the sublime Dharma, which consists solely of the exposition of the wondrous Dharma;
and the adornment of the people, wherein superior and virtuous sentient beings dwell.

In what is now clarified, the excellence of this land includes the adornment of things and the adornment of the Dharma; the fourth section below concerns the excellence of the populace, which constitutes the adornment of the people.
However, the wondrous adornments within that land cannot be fully detailed; for now, this text briefly cites four matters: first, the elucidation of the jewel trees;
second, the elucidation of the musical instruments; third, the elucidation of matters such as the lecture halls and palaces; and fourth, the elucidation of the jewel ponds.

Regarding the trees, first there is a general clarification of all trees; second, a specific clarification of the tree of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); and third, a comprehensive evaluation of them to manifest its superiority.
Within the initial general clarification, there is first a listing of the trees, followed by an explanation of the sounds they emit.
Regarding the arrangement among the trees: "The precious trees of that land fill the entire world" serves as a general heading.
The mention of "gold and silver trees" and so forth clarifies that these are trees composed entirely of precious substances.
The section beginning with "Or two treasures" clarifies the various jewel-trees.
Regarding the sounds produced by them, "producing the five notes" refers to the five types of musical tones, namely gong (gōng), shāng (shāng), jué (jué), zhǐ (zhǐ), and yǔ (yǔ).

Regarding the second section clarifying the Bodhi tree within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it first clarifies the characteristics of the tree, next clarifies the emission of sound, and finally clarifies how sentient beings obtain benefit upon seeing and hearing it.
Within the initial clarification of the tree, it first clarifies its dimensions and characteristics.
"Composed spontaneously of all manner of jewels" clarifies its essential nature and characteristics.
"By moonlight," and so forth, clarifies its marks of adornment.
Its sound issues forth and can be known.

Within the context of clarifying how benefit is obtained through seeing and hearing, the first section clarifies that the six sense faculties—seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing—all obtain benefit; the subsequent section clarifies the differences in the various levels of attaining patience (*kṣānti*).
"The devas and humans of that land all attain the three patiences" is the general heading.
To have a mind of wisdom that rests in the Dharma is called "patience.
According to its varying degrees of depth, patience is divided into three; these three names are now listed in sequence.
To awaken to understanding by following sounds and knowing that sound is like an echo is called the "patience of resonance" (*ghoṣānugā-kṣānti*), pertaining to the stages from the third downward;
to abandon conventional designations and proceed toward the ultimate reality is called the "patience of compliance" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), pertaining to the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages;
and to realize reality and be free from all marks is called the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), pertaining to the seventh stage and above.
The following clarifies the reasons why sentient beings attain patience.
Regarding the phrase "all [attain this] through the majestic spiritual power of Amitāyus": it is because of the present majestic power of that Tathāgata that they obtain the three kinds of patience.
Regarding "the power of the original vow" and so forth: by virtue of the power of his past original vows, he attained the three types of patience (*kṣānti*).
The original vow is the general [cause], while the other four are the specific [causes].
"Vow of Fulfillment" means the aspiration of the mind is perfectly complete.
"Vow of Clarity" means the seeking of the mind is manifest.
"Vow of Firmness" means it cannot be destroyed by conditions.
"Ultimate vow" means that one ultimately achieves non-retrogression.
By virtue of this vow, all those born in that land attain the three types of patience (*kṣānti*).
Having previously explained the various trees, he now specifically explains the tree of his place of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The following passage proceeds by means of comparative evaluation to manifest its excellence, specifically highlighting the superiority of the sounds produced within the trees;
the meaning of the text is clear and may be understood accordingly.
Having thus explained the trees, the second section below clarifies the musical instruments.
"Furthermore, there are naturally occurring ten thousand kinds of musical performances," which serves as a general heading.
"Moreover, the sounds of those instruments are none other than the Dharma," and so forth, which reveals the excellence of their sounds.
The phrase "the worlds of the ten directions" and so forth demonstrates the excellence of its sound, which surpasses all sounds throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
From here below begins the third section, clarifying matters such as the lecture hall and the palace.
"The lecture halls, vihāras, palaces, and towers are all composed of the seven treasures" clarifies their essential form (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).
"Furthermore, with pearls," and so forth, clarifies their aspect of adornment (*vyūha-lakṣaṇa*).
From here below, the fourth section clarifies the characteristics of the pond.
Within this, first the characteristics of the pond are distinguished, followed by the explanation of the sounds it emits.
In distinguishing the characteristics of the pond, there are four textual divisions:
First, the characteristics of their dimensions:
the various ponds in that land measure ten yojanas, twenty, thirty, or even up to a hundred thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Second, the characteristics of the water.
It possesses eight meritorious qualities:
it is clear, odorless, light, cool, soft, delicious, pleasant when drinking, and free from ailment after drinking; these are the eight.
The sense-sphere of pure visible form, the sense-sphere of odorless fragrance, and the five sense-spheres of tangibles—namely softness, coldness, and smoothness;
what is delicious is the sense-sphere of taste;
and that which is harmonious when drinking and free from affliction after drinking—these two are the sense-spheres of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
These eight are the functional capacities of the water-element, and are thus called "capacities" (guǒngōng);
they are the virtues of the water-element, and are thus called "virtues" (dé).
In the text, the initial statement that "the water of eight virtues is serene and overflowing" introduces them collectively.
"Pure" refers to the purity among the eight [qualities].
"Fragrant and clean" refers to the fragrance among the eight.
"Its taste is like nectar" refers to the excellence among the eight.
3. Below "Golden," the characteristics of the various jewels and other adornments are clarified.
4. Below "Those Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas Enter," the characteristic of their unimpeded utilization is manifested.

Among these, there are five phrases: first, the unimpeded nature of the shallow and the deep; second, attaining the middle way between cold and warmth; third, releasing the spirit to eliminate defilements; fourth, purity free from blemish; and fifth, the circulation of the flow, where its speed and slowness reach their proper state.
The preceding section clarifies the pond; the following section clarifies the emergence of sound.
This contains four parts:
first, the manifestation of immeasurable, spontaneous, and wondrous sounds, which properly clarifies the emergence of sound.
2. From "according to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*) onwards, there is the hearing of the various fruits corresponding to sentient beings.
Within this, there is first a general statement, followed by a detailed explanation, and finally a conclusion.
3. From "having conformed to purity and abandoned desire" (*anuloma-viśuddhi-vītarāga*) onwards, it clarifies that which can give rise to the wholesome.
"Conforming to the true meaning of purity, detachment, and quiescence" accords with *nirvāṇa*.
"Conforming to the powers and fearlessnesses of the Three Jewels," and so forth, accords with *bodhi*.
The preceding section concerns the concordant fruit (*anuloma-phala*).
"The path practiced by Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas who accord with supernormal knowledge" refers to the concordance with its cause.
From the passage beginning with "the four absences of the three miserable realms," it clarifies that which can produce happiness.
The passage beginning with "There are no three miserable realms" clarifies the absence of suffering.
The passage beginning with "There is only self... clarifies the presence of bliss.
From "Therefore" onwards, the conclusion summarizes and extols the excellence [of this land].
The preceding four sections together constitute the third [part], which elucidates its land.
From here on, the fourth [part] distinguishes its inhabitants.
This contains four [subsections]:
First, it clarifies that the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of those newly reborn from other directions is subtle and exquisite;
second, from "the palaces they inhabit" onwards, it clarifies that their secondary environment (*upabhoga*) is sublime;
third, from "all those who have heard the *saṃghāṭa*" onwards, it clarifies that the primary retribution of those who have long resided there is subtle and exquisite.
4. From the passage "The garments of those devas and humans" onwards, the excellence of the *adhiṣṭhāna* (environmental retribution) is shown.
At the beginning, "possessing a perfectly pure physical body" clarifies the excellence of the body.
“Various exquisite sounds” clarifies the excellence of the mouth.
“The merit of supernormal powers” clarifies the excellence of the mind.
In the second section, “the palaces, garments, and other articles he dwells in are like those of the Sixth Heaven” clarifies the excellence of his requisites.
The phrase "if one wishes to eat," and so forth, concerns the excellence of sustenance; this is discussed specifically with reference to food.
The passage beginning with "that Buddha-land is pure and peaceful" is a general eulogy that reveals its excellence.
Next, regarding the path of unconditioned *nirvāṇa*—
*nirvāṇa* and *niepan* are originally one name, with only the phonetic transmission differing— the third section,

concerning the superiority of the long-dwelling sentient beings, states: "Those śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans whose wisdom is lofty and brilliant, and whose supernatural powers are penetrating and pervasive," thereby clarifying the excellence of their virtues.
From "All are identical" (*xián tóng yī*) onwards, the excellence of their bodies is revealed.

Within this, the initial statement—"All are of one kind without any difference in appearance; they are designated as 'gods' or 'humans' only in accordance with other regions"—clarifies that their bodies are uniform and equal.
Below the phrase "handsome countenance," the superiority of the body is clarified.
The passage "his countenance was upright and handsome, surpassing anything rare in the world" distinguishes his excellence through the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
From "The Buddha said" onwards, his excellence is revealed through comparative evaluation.

There are five comparisons within this: first, comparing a poor person to a minor king; second, comparing a minor king to a wheel-turning monarch; third, comparing a wheel-turning monarch to a king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; fourth, comparing a king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to a king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; and fifth, comparing the king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven to all the devas and humans of Amitāyus—yet in the end, they do not equal him.
In the first section on "Comparative Measurement," there are three textual divisions:
first, the Buddha takes a poor man and a minor king (kṣudraka-rāja) to cross-examine Ānanda;
second, Ānanda provides the formal answer.

"Even if this person were by the side of a sovereign," there would be no analogy to describe it; it is hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions of times beyond measure, clearly showing that the poor man cannot compare to the sovereign.

The section beginning with "The reason for this" clarifies the cause by which that poor man was unable to attain [the Dharma]: it is because he lacked merit in his previous lives; the meaning of the text is clear and may be understood accordingly.

The passage beginning with "Therefore, the emperors of the world" explains the reason why those emperors excel others: it is because they cultivated merit in their past lives; the meaning of the text is likewise clear.
The three Tathāgatas express their approval.
The remaining four sections concerning comparative measurement are clear in their phrasing and easy to understand.

Within the fourth section, which further clarifies the excellence of the environment (*niśraya-vipāka*), it is first explained that all matters such as clothing and food in that land are commensurate with the bodies [of its inhabitants].
"Or a single jewel," and so forth, clarifies the excellence by way of specific distinctions.
Within this, there are five parts;
the first explains how all jewels manifest before one according to the mind.
Second, robes made of the two jewels are spread upon the ground;
third, nets of the three jewels cover [the space];
fourth, from the word "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*) downward, it is fanned by winds of virtue.
5. From "Furthermore, the assembly" below, precious flowers fill [the space].
Regarding the fourth wind, the phrase "naturally, a gentle breeze slowly rises and stirs slightly" refers to the trees as a whole; what follows distinguishes them individually.
There are four further aspects:

first, the substance of the wind is harmonious, with its speed being perfectly suited; second, it blows through the nets and moves the trees, producing subtle and wondrous sounds; third, upon touching the body, it generates bliss; fourth, it blows away and scatters various flowers, filling the entire land.
Within the fifth section on flowers, there are four distinct points:
first, it clarifies that jewel-flowers pervade the world;
second, it clarifies that each flower possesses numerous petals.
The third [section], "Each of the various flowers emits many rays of light," clarifies that each flower produces numerous beams of radiance;
the fourth, from "Within each individual flower, thirty [Buddhas appear]" onwards, clarifies that within each of the flowers, many Buddhas respectively emerge.
Within this, there are four further points:
first, it clarifies that from each of the aforementioned individual rays of light, many more rays emerge, stating: "thirty-six hundred thousand koṭis of rays emerge.
Second, it clarifies that from each of the aforementioned individual flowers, many Buddhas emerge, stating: "thirty-six hundred thousand koṭis of Buddhas emerge."
The third clarifies that each of the aforementioned Buddhas individually emits manifold rays of light.
The fourth clarifies that each of the aforementioned Buddhas universally expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the sake of the ten directions.
Among these, the first section clarifies what is taught.
The passage beginning with "In this way, each of these Buddhas" demonstrates the benefits of the teaching.
From here on, the third section clarifies what is subsumed therein.
He gathers sentient beings with whom he has a karmic connection throughout the ten directions to go together to that land, transforming and benefiting them through the Dharma.
Thus, those gathered below correspond precisely to the forty-eight vows made above; by matching each one individually, their correspondence becomes clearly manifest.
The text contains four sections:
first, the inclusion of those of inferior capacity so that they may be born together in that land;
second, from the passage "The majestic virtue of Amitāyus Buddha is infinite" onwards, the inclusion of those of superior capacity so that they may likewise go to that land.
3. From "The bodhisattvas in that land shall all ultimately reach the final birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*) onwards, those of lower capacity are again gathered to be reborn together in that land;
4. From "Maitreya asked the Buddha: 'How many bodhisattvas in this world will be born there? onwards, those of higher capacity are again gathered to be reborn together in that land.
What is the distinction between the first and the third sections?

In the first section, the generation of the aspiration, the karmic actions, the teachings, and the cultivation for rebirth are fully explained; in the third section, one is encouraged toward rebirth by citing both attainments and failures. Since there is this difference in meaning, they must be distinguished.
What is the difference between the second and the fourth?

In the preceding second section, it was taught that one gathers people to go together; in the fourth section, it is taught that one gathers people to be born together. Because there is this distinction, they must be explained separately.
The inclusion of those of inferior capacity clearly demonstrates the benefits received;
the inclusion of those of superior capacity reveals the excellence of that land, increasing their longing and aspiration.
Within the first part, there are three sections:
First, it demonstrates that those born there abide in the stage of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), causing people to aspire toward it;

second, from the passage "The Buddhas of the ten directions all praise [it]" onwards, it shows that all who hear the name attain rebirth there, increasing people's resolve to depart [from this world].
Third, from "The Buddha said to Ānanda" onwards, the text correctly distinguishes the karmic activities for birth [in the Pure Land] and teaches the cultivation of rebirth there.
Within this section, the initial statement, "Those who are born in that land all abide in right concentration," clearly elucidates what is encompassed [by the practice].
Human beings are categorized into three groups:
first, those fixed in the wrong; second, those fixed in the right; and third, those who are not fixed. Regarding these, the explanations differ within the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, ordinary worldlings who are constantly submerged [in saṃsāra] are termed "fixed in the wrong."

The five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣkambhaṇa-citta*), the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and the two minds of "heat" and "summit" (*ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*) are called "unfixed.
Because these states are subject to regression, they are termed "unfixed."
When the mind of forbearance (*kṣānti*) has already transcended this stage and is firm and non-regressive, it is called "right determination" (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, ordinary worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) who constantly sink back are called "wrongly determined" (*mithyātva-niyāma*);
because their wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*) may still undergo regression, they are said to be "subject to regression."
The five contemplations for settling the mind are called the wisdom of hearing;
the general and specific applications of mindfulness are called the wisdom of reflection;
and from the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) upward, they are termed the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*).
Directly perceiving the emptiness of phenomena, they never regress and are all established in right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma, those prior to the stage of the "wholesome destiny" (*sugati*) are termed "wrongly determined" (*mithyātva-niyāma*);
those within the stage of the wholesome destiny, who advance and retreat repeatedly, are described as "undetermined" (*aniyata*).
Once the stage of the lineage of practice has been transcended, one’s rank is non-retrogressive and is termed "rightly settled.
Regardless of whether they belong to the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, all sentient beings born in that land abide in right determination.
The section beginning with "Therefore" provides the explanation.
Because that [land] lacks the categories of those with wrong resolve (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*) and those of indeterminate resolve (*aniyata-rāśi*), all are of right resolve (*samyaktva-niyata*).
In the second section, it is first clarified that the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all together praise the Buddha of Immeasurable Life (*Amitāyus*).
Next, it is explained that sentient beings who hear the name, believe with faith, dedicate their merit, and make vows shall all attain rebirth;
as for the distinction made below, it is only those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the True Dharma who are excluded, while all others may be reborn.

As for the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), they are: killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and shedding the blood of a Buddha; these are the five.
These five are all offenses against those who have shown kindness, as well as violations of the field of merit; therefore, they are called "rebellious acts" (*ānantarya*).
The first two are both offenses against those who have shown kindness, while the latter three violate the field of merit.
To establish what is false and to disparage what is correct is termed "slandering the Dharma."
These are heavy obstacles, which is why they must be eliminated.
Question: In that *Contemplation Sūtra*, it is stated that even those who have committed the five heinous crimes and so forth can all attain rebirth [in the Pure Land].
In this sutra, it is stated that "rebirth cannot be attained.
What does this statement mean?
There are two interpretations for its explanation:
First, distinguishing by way of persons: there are two kinds of persons.
The first are those who have long since resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind but encounter conditions that lead them to commit a heinous offense, such as King Ajātaśatru and others.

Although this person has committed a heinous offense, if they certainly feel deep remorse and resolve their mind to seek liberation, they can extinguish that grave sin; it is for this reason that they are able to be reborn, as the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* relies upon this principle.

Second, those who previously failed to resolve upon the Great Mind, yet now commit an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), for the most part lack profound repentance and are unable to decisively resolve upon Bodhicitta; because such a mind does not arise, this sutra is based on this case.
Second, regarding the classification by practice, there are both concentrated and distracted practices.

Even if someone has committed a grave offense (ānantarya), if they can cultivate the roots of goodness of the sixteen right contemplations and deeply contemplate the Buddha’s virtues to eliminate their heavy sins, they will attain rebirth; the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* is based on this case.

If a person commits an act of immediate retribution (ānantarya), they cannot cultivate the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha; although they may perform other wholesome deeds, they cannot extinguish their transgressions and therefore will not attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]. This sutra is based on this principle.
From here below is the third section, which correctly explains the practices for generating the karma to be taught so as to achieve rebirth in that land.
Within this, the initial statement—"In the worlds of the ten directions, there are three grades of devas and humans who vow to be born in that land"—serves as a general introduction.
As stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, these are divided into three coarse categories and nine subtle categories.
Regarding the three coarse divisions, they are termed superior, middling, and inferior.
Among those of the Mahāyāna, those from the stage of the "seed of practice" (*śikṣā-bīja*) upward are designated as superior;
Among those of the Hīnayāna, from the external ordinary person observing the precepts up to the Anāgāmin, these are considered the middle grade;
among those of the Mahāyāna, the external ordinary person in the fortunate realms is termed the lower grade.
Regarding the ninefold subdivision: within the aforementioned "superior" category, there is a further threefold subdivision, namely, superior-superior, superior-middle, and superior-inferior.
Those from the fourth bhūmi upward are designated as "superior-superior," because upon being born there, one immediately attains the realization of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

The first, second, and third stages are designated as "superior-middle. Having been born in that land, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) after a minor kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
Because the days in that land are long, one attains the patience of non-arising after a minor kalpa;
whereas in this realm, it would take immeasurable kalpas before one could attain the patience of non-arising.

The stages of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and practice (*caryā*) are termed "upper" and "lower. Once born in that land, after three minor kalpas have passed, one attains the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas (*śatadharma-vidyāmukha*) and dwells in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
Thus we know that even prior to the [first] stage, because the time spent in that land is vast and long, one reaches the first stage after three minor kalpas;
whereas in this world-system, it would take immeasurable kalpas.
Those of medium capacity are also divided into three types: namely, superior-medium, middle-medium, and inferior-medium.
Those from the stage of the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) upward are called superior-medium, because upon being born there, they immediately attain the fruit of Arhatship.
Those of the inner ordinary stage are called "middling-middling," for upon being born there, they immediately attain the stage of *srotāpanna*.
The four mental states of *uṣmagata* and so forth are termed the "inner ordinary" stage.
Those of the outer ordinary stage who maintain the precepts are called "lower-middling," for after being born in that land, they attain the stage of *arhat* after the passage of one small kalpa.

The lowest grade of persons is also divided into three: namely, the lower-high, the lower-middle, and the lower-lowest; these are distinguished according to the lightness or gravity of the offenses committed, rather than according to their rank.

Among those, there are nine grades; these are now consolidated into three. The three persons of the superior grade are combined into the Superior Assembly; the three persons of the middle grade are combined into the Middle Assembly; and the three persons of the inferior grade are combined into the Inferior Assembly.

Nevertheless, although these three classes differ in their human status, when it comes to seeking rebirth there, they must all equally resolve their minds to seek great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), single-mindedly recollect that Buddha, and dedicate their merits while making vows; only then will they attain rebirth.
Therefore, this is discussed here.
A question is asked:
Vasubandhu composed the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-gāthā*, stating that "women, those with impaired faculties, and those of the two vehicles' lineage are all unable to be reborn [there]."
The *Amitābha Sūtra* proclaims that even sentient beings of the Hīnayāna can attain rebirth there.
What is the meaning of this?
To explain:

The statement that women and those with impaired faculties cannot be reborn there refers to the time of receiving retribution within that land, for in that land there are no women and no one with impaired faculties.

As for the statement that those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha) lineages cannot be reborn there, this refers to the time of departing from this land; although small-vehicle sentient beings may have previously practiced the Small Vehicle, at the moment they are about to depart, they must resolve upon the Great Mind before they can attain rebirth there. If one seeks rebirth in that land using a small mind, there is no principle by which they could go.
Regarding this statement by Vasubandhu that those of the two vehicles cannot attain rebirth there,
it is asked:
If one departs by means of the great mind (mahācitta), for what reason does one realize and enter the fruits of the small vehicle upon reaching that place?
The commentary states:
This is because they have long been habituated to the Hīnayāna.

Having previously dwelt here and extensively studied the contemplation of suffering, impermanence, and so forth, when they arrive there and hear the teaching on suffering, impermanence, and so forth, they immediately attain realization; thus, they realize the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.

Because they originally set out on the [Hīnayāna] vehicle but ultimately resolve to seek birth in that [Pure Land] by generating the Mahāyāna mind, once they have attained arhatship within that land, they immediately seek the Great [Vehicle].
The above provides a general summary; below, it is explained in detail.
Within the section on the superior class of practitioners, there is first a general introduction, secondly a detailed analysis, and finally a comprehensive praise of the Dharma.
Within the analysis, there are three parts:
the first clarifies the causes of their practice;
2. From "These [beings]" onwards, they collectively achieve rebirth;
3. From "Abiding in non-retrogression" onwards, they obtain benefits upon being born there.
Within the first section on practicing the causes, there are five distinct points:

First, renouncing the secular world to leave home; second, generating the bodhicitta; third, single-mindedly and exclusively recollecting Amitāyus Buddha; fourth, cultivating various meritorious virtues; and fifth, employing these aforementioned good roots to vow rebirth in that land.
Regarding rebirth, from the passage beginning "They welcome him here and he immediately follows" onwards, this refers to going from here to there.
Regarding the attainment of benefits, "abiding in non-retrogression" signifies that one's stage is firm and stable.
The phrase "Wisdom and Courage" (*prajñā-vīrya*) and so forth indicates the excellence of the perfected virtues.
Having first raised the topic and subsequently analyzed it, the section beginning with "Therefore" concludes by praising the practice.
Within the section on the middle grade, there is first a general introduction followed by a detailed exposition.
In the exposition, it first clarifies the causal practices, next clarifies the rebirth, and finally manifests the benefits obtained.
In the preceding clarification of the causes, the phrase "If there are devas and humans of the ten directions who, with a sincere heart, wish to be born in that land" serves as a general heading.
The subsequent passage, "Even though they cannot practice by becoming śramaṇas," and so forth, distinguishes these individuals from those of the superior grade.
According to the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, these are followers of the Hīnayāna; therefore, they are unable to cultivate those great merits.
The section beginning with "They should arouse" correctly explains the causes for this.
Within this, there are four points:

first, generating the bodhicitta; second, single-mindedly recollecting that Amitāyus Buddha; third, practicing even a small amount of meritorious virtue; and fourth, dedicating [the merit] with the vow to be reborn [in that land].
Although this person may have previously studied the Hīnayāna, if they truly desire to be reborn there, they must practice these four modes of conduct; only then will they attain rebirth.
Regarding the process of rebirth, first the other world comes to meet them here, and subsequently, they are born there from here.
The benefits obtained can be understood from this.
Within the section on the lowest grade of aspirants, there is first a general introduction and then a detailed exposition.
In the exposition, it first clarifies the causal practices, next clarifies the rebirth [in the Pure Land], and finally manifests the benefits obtained.
In the preceding explanation of the causes, the phrase "If there are devas and humans of the ten directions who with a sincere heart desire to be born in that land" serves as a general heading.
The subsequent statement, "Even if they are unable to perform various meritorious deeds," distinguishes this from the middle grade of aspirants.
As in the *Contemplation Sūtra*, faults were cited for the sake of distinction; here, they are omitted.
From the phrase "one should generate" [the aspiration] onwards, the causes are correctly explained.
Within this, there are four phrases:
First, to resolve once for all upon bodhicitta;
second, to single-mindedly recollect that Amitāyus Buddha, even for ten recitations, vowing to be born in his land;
third, to hear the profound Dharma and, with joy and faith, believe and delight in it without giving rise to doubt.
Fourth, even those with a single thought of utmost sincerity who mindfully recollect that Buddha and vow to be born in that land will also attain rebirth there.
Within the context of rebirth, it is further clarified that even those who see that Buddha in a dream during sleep will also attain rebirth.
The benefits gained are thus evident.

Above, the first section clarified the inclusion of those of inferior capacity; below, the second section clarifies the inclusion of those of superior capacity who likewise attain rebirth in that land.
This is presented to manifest the excellence of Amitābha’s land, thereby further increasing the aspiration for rebirth among those of inferior capacity mentioned previously.
Within this, first there is a brief exposition in prose, followed by an extensive discussion in verse.
In the preceding prose section, the text is divided into two parts:
first, the collective praise of all Buddhas; [the second part follows].
Second, from "In the eastern direction" onwards, Bodhisattvas are born there together.
The subsequent verse provides a specific eulogy, which should be carefully noted and understood.
Within the preceding praise by the Buddha, it first says: "The Buddha told Ānanda:"
"The majestic spiritual power of Amitāyus Buddha is infinite," Śākyamuni said in self-praise.
From "The worlds of the ten directions" onwards, the other Buddhas join in praise.
The following section is a distinct verse; this too must be noted and understood.
In the following sections concerning their departure, the eastern direction is listed first, followed by the other directions.

Within the listing of the eastern direction, the passage beginning with "From those Buddha-lands in the east, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, countless bodhisattvas all proceeded to the Buddha Amitāyus" marks its commencement.
"Respectfully making offerings to the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas" is the middle stage;
"listening to and receiving the Dharma, and proclaiming its transformative teachings" is the final stage.
As it is with the eastern direction, so it is with the remaining directions.
These [verses] concerning the beginning, middle, and end are also to be understood as being specifically recited in the following verse.
The sūtra compiler has arranged the sequence, stating: "The World-Honored One recited in verse."
The following verses provide a formal summary consisting of thirty stanzas.
The first fifteen stanzas summarize the latter section concerning the Bodhisattvas' collective departure;
the latter fifteen stanzas summarize the former section concerning the simultaneous praise of all Buddhas.
Within the preceding fifteen [verses], the first two verses praise the previous account of traveling together;
the next five verses praise the previous passage on respectful offerings;
and the final eight verses praise the previous account of listening to the Dharma and proclaiming its transformative teachings.
Within the preceding two verses, the first verse praises the previous account of traveling together toward the east;
the latter verse praises the aforementioned journey to the other directions together to pay homage to Amitāyus Buddha. For this reason, it is titled "Contemplating the Immeasurable Enlightenment."
Within the subsequent five verses, the first four describe making offerings upon seeing the Buddha,
while the final one describes seeking and aspiring for the buddha-field.
Within the first four verses, the initial two concern external offerings;
The latter two verses concern internal offerings.
Within the previous section on external matters, the phrase "each bringing exquisite flowers" refers to the offering of flowers;
"jewels" refers to the offering of jewels.
"Perfume" refers to offerings of incense.
"Priceless garments" refers to making offerings with clothing.
"Performing celestial music," and so forth, refers to offerings of instrumental music.
Within the sounds of music and song, the virtues of the Buddha are chanted and praised.
In the subsequent section on internal matters, the first one and a half verses consist of verbal praise and offerings;
the final half-verse consists of physical reverence and offerings.
Within the section on oral praise, the first verse praises the Buddha’s own virtues, while the latter half-verse praises his altruistic benefit for others.

Within the praise of his own virtues, the phrase "having thoroughly attained supernormal wisdom and entering deeply into the profound Dharma" praises two kinds of virtues: the Buddha’s wisdom (*jñāna*) and his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Wisdom is the basis of the supernormal powers (abhijñā), and the supernormal powers are the function of wisdom; since these two require one another, they are praised together as the perfection of supernormal wisdom.
"Ultimate" (jìngjiù) means thorough investigation, and "penetrating" (dòngdá) means complete penetration.
Since both this supernormal power (*abhijñā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are established based upon the Dharma, he further clarifies their engagement with the profound Dharma.
"Engaging" (*you*) refers to relying on contemplation; "entering" (*ru*) signifies exhausting the fundamental source.
By attaining entry into the gateway of the dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu*, one is able to manifest supreme supernormal powers.
"Entering the gateway of wisdom regarding the dependent origination of the dharma-realm, one is able to give rise to supreme insight.
"Possessing a treasury of merit, with wondrous wisdom beyond compare," praises the Buddha’s two types of practice: merit and wisdom.
Merit is the provision for wisdom, and wisdom is the guide for merit; as these two require one another, they are praised together.
When the practice of merit is perfected and complete, it is called "possessing merit";
when the practice of wisdom is preeminent, it is called "unequaled knowledge."
"Thou" (偷) refers to a peer; it denotes being a companion in service.
The Buddha has no peer, hence he is named "Unequaled.
Within the section on benefiting others, "The sun of wisdom illuminates the world" means that he transforms sentient beings and gives rise to their wisdom.
Wisdom can open and enlighten, illuminating the world like the sun; it causes people to give rise to understanding and is called "brightening the world.
It eliminates birth and death, transforming people so they may leave behind all obstructions.
Obscured by birth and death, it is metaphorically termed a "cloud.
Physical reverence may be understood accordingly.
The four preceding verses describe seeing the Buddha and making offerings.
The following verse concerns the vision of the land and the aspiration for it; its meaning is clear and may be understood directly.
From here on, the eight verses praise the aforementioned hearing of the Dharma and the proclamation of the transformative teachings.
Within this section, the first two verses describe the manifestation of signs by the Tathāgata Amitābha to inspire the practitioner.
Next follows one verse in which Avalokiteśvara asks out of wonder;
this is followed by five verses in which that Buddha provides a detailed answer.
"The Brahma-voice is like thunder, and the eight qualities of sound are exquisitely refined" answers to the excellence of the voice.
Regarding the eight kinds of Brahma-sounds, they are as described in the *Brahmāyu Sūtra*:
first, the most exquisite sound, whose tone is plaintive and sublime; [and so forth].
Second, the easily understood voice, whose words and phrases are distinct and clear;
third, the harmonious voice, whose volume is moderate;
fourth, the gentle voice, whose tone is soft and supple.
Fifth, his voice is not erroneous, meaning his speech is free from mistakes;
sixth, he does not have a feminine voice, for his voice is majestic and resonant;
seventh, it is a voice of venerable wisdom, meaning his speech possesses a dignified gravity like that of the World-Honored One, possessing the voice of a person of wisdom.
The eighth is the profound and far-reaching voice; its sound is deep and resonant, like the roll of thunder.
With this wondrous voice, he replied to Avalokiteśvara:
"You shall receive the prediction of bodhisattvahood; now I shall speak, so listen attentively. Thus he commanded him to listen and granted his permission to speak.
The term "bestowal of prophecy" (vyākaraṇa) has its meaning explained as above.
Now I shall explain this; you, virtuous ones, listen attentively.
From here on, the four verses clearly elucidate what is being taught.
Among these, the first verse cites his vow-mind and prophesies that he will certainly become a Buddha.
The second single verse cites his wisdom-vow and prophesies that he will certainly attain a buddha-field.
"Awakening to all things as being like dreams and illusions," and so forth, refers to wisdom (*jñāna*).
"Fulfilling all vows" refers to the vow (*praṇidhāna*).
"Accomplishing such a land" refers to the attainment of the buddha-field (*kṣetra*).
The third verse, consisting of a single stanza, cites his wisdom and conduct to prophesy that he will certainly attain Buddhahood.
"Knowing dharmas to be like lightning" cites his wisdom;
"thoroughly investigating the bodhisattva path and possessing all roots of virtue" cites his conduct.
"Receiving the prediction to become a Buddha" refers to the bestowal of the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood.
The fourth single verse cites his wisdom and vows, prophesying that he will certainly obtain a buddha-field.
"Thoroughly penetrating that the nature of phenomena is entirely empty and non-existent" is the citation of his wisdom.
“Previously realizing that all things are like dreams and illusions,” and so forth, refers to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
“This penetration [reveals] that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is entirely empty and non-existent” refers to ultimate knowledge (*paramārtha-jñāna*).
"Seeking exclusively for the Pure Land" refers to the aspiration;
"necessarily accomplishing this land" records the attainment of that realm.
The following fifteen verses praise the aforementioned passage concerning the collective eulogies of all Buddhas.
The first five verses praise the preceding section on how the Buddhas of the ten directions collectively extol [the land];
the subsequent ten verses praise the preceding passage in which Śākyamuni himself extols it.
Within the first five verses, the line "The Buddhas inform the Bodhisattvas, commanding them to visit the Land of Peaceful Nurturing" is a direct exhortation to go there.
"Listening to the Dharma and practicing it accordingly" clarifies what was done in the past.
"Swiftly attaining" and the following clarify the accomplishment of benefit.

"Swiftly attaining a pure realm" clarifies the benefit of having previously listened to the Dharma and practiced it accordingly; that one personally attains a wondrous and pure land in the future is called "attaining a pure realm."
The following four verses clarify the benefits of going forward to visit the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
There are five kinds of benefits:
first, the benefit of attaining supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) upon reaching that land; this is indicated by the first half-verse.
The second [visit] concerns the benefit of receiving the prediction of enlightenment; this is the subsequent half-verse.
This refers to the aforementioned matter of that Buddha bestowing the prediction upon the Bodhisattva.
The third [visit] concerns the benefit of attaining non-retrogression; this is the subsequent single verse.
The preceding statement that one is born there and dwells within the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) refers precisely to this matter.
Regarding the fourth benefit—arousing the aspiration to go there—the following single verse provides it.
"The Bodhisattva arouses the aspiration" is the general heading; what follows below is a specific praise thereof.
Regarding the phrase "wishing that one's own land be no different [from Sukhāvatī]" within the section on distinctions: this is the vow for seeking a pure land.
It is the wish that one may attain a land identical to that of Amitābha Buddha; thus, it is called "the land being no different."
"Universally delivering all" is the vow to transform sentient beings.
"Its name manifesting throughout the ten directions" is the vow to seek the Buddha-body, wishing that when one attains Buddhahood, one's name shall reach the ten directions.
The fifth section concerns the benefit of going there to extensively make offerings to many Buddhas and initiate practice; this is contained in the final verse.
The ten verses following this are Śākyamuni’s own praise, intended to lead others to go along with him.
Within this, there are three sections:
first, there are three verses that cite the sutra’s rarity and encourage joyful practice;
next, there are four verses that praise Amitābha Buddha’s bestowal of predictions upon bodhisattvas, illustrating the excellence of the Buddha’s wisdom and virtue to lead people toward him.
The final three verses exhort through both principle and teaching.
Within the first three verses, the initial half-verse cites the absence of virtuous people who do not hear this sutra, thereby manifesting the profound gravity of the scripture;
the subsequent one and a half verses cite the presence of virtuous people who are then able to hear it, thereby revealing the subtle and wondrous nature of the scripture.
Within this, it is first clarified that only those who possess virtue will hear this sutra.
From the passage beginning "I have previously seen," it is clarified that only those who have seen the Buddha will believe, revere, rejoice, and practice accordingly.
Next follows a half-verse which cites those who are evil and do not believe in this Dharma, thereby demonstrating the profound gravity of the sutra.
The subsequent half-verse cites those who are virtuous and delight in hearing this teaching, thereby revealing the subtle and wondrous nature of the sutra.
By exposing evil, one prevents it from being heard, causing people to abandon and distance themselves from it;
by promoting good, one ensures it is heard, leading people to admire and cultivate it.
Furthermore, within this text, the profound gravity of the sutra is revealed, removing people's frivolous slanders.
This reveals the subtle profundity of the sutra, giving rise to faith and reverence in people.
Below are four verses praising the extraordinary wisdom and virtue of Amitābha Buddha, leading people to take refuge in him.
Among these, the first seven lines clarify that the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas cannot fathom [the Buddha’s wisdom].
The initial principle, the subsequent analogy, and the final application may be understood accordingly.
Next, there is one sentence clarifying that the Buddha alone has full realization.
