Following that, there are six sentences clarifying that all people can attain the noble path, yet they do not know it through collective reflection.
"Even if all"—this refers to the great number of people.
"All fully attain the Way"—this refers to the excellence of their practice and virtue.
"Pure wisdom reaches the source"—this refers to the depth of their understanding of emptiness.
"To contemplate the Buddha for billions of kalpas" means that one contemplates him for a long time; "to exhaust one's strength in exposition" means that one speaks to the ultimate limit.
Even though this is so, "one will not know him even throughout the remainder of one's life."
Below is a half-verse that concludes with a praise to manifest its excellence:
"The Buddha’s wisdom is boundless" praises the vastness of the Buddha's knowledge;
"thus attained purity" praises the purity of the Buddha's virtues.
"Attaining" (*zhì*) means "reaching.
Because one reaches the ultimate purity of the *dharmatā* of *nirvāṇa*, it is difficult to fathom or know.
Below are three verses which exhort by means of both principle and teaching.
Among these, the first verse raises those three difficulties and exhorts people to seek [the Dharma] with diligence.
That "life is difficult to obtain" is the first difficulty;
that "it is difficult to encounter the age of a Buddha" is the second difficulty.
The third difficulty is that it is difficult to possess both faith and wisdom.
Having now encountered these three difficulties, one should diligently seek this sutra upon hearing it.
The second verse follows, citing those who have seen and heard it to show that they can obtain great benefit, thereby exhorting others to resolve their minds [to practice].
"Never forgetting what has been heard" means that in the presence of Amitābha Buddha, one hears the Dharma and does not forget it.
"Seeing and revering" means that upon seeing Amitābha Buddha, a heart of profound respect arises.
Regarding "attaining great celebration": this clarifies that by hearing the Dharma and seeing the Buddha with reverence as previously described, one attains wholesome benefit.
Attaining what is wholesome and joyful is termed "attaining great celebration."
"Then he is my good friend" refers to being embraced by the Buddha.
To act in accordance with Śākyamuni is called having a "good friend"; therefore, one should arouse a resolute resolve and exhort others to do so.
The final verse instructs him to go resolutely:
"Even if the world were filled with fire, one must pass through it to hear the Dharma. This demonstrates his firm resolve to depart.
"I shall surely attain Buddhahood and extensively save those in the cycle of birth and death" clarifies the purpose for his departure.
"To surely attain Buddhahood" refers to seeking the fruit of self-benefit;
"to extensively save those in birth and death" refers to seeking the fruit of benefiting others.
From this point downward is the third section, which gathers those of inferior capacity and causes them to be born together in that land.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, an extensive presentation of the supreme and wondrous matters of the Land of Immeasurable Life, intended to inspire people’s aspiration and seeking;

second, from the passage beginning with "The worldlings are vulgar and superficial" onwards, an elucidation of how the Sahā world is filled with filth and evil, intended to cause people to feel weary of it and renounce it.

Third, from the section "Extensively Praising the Infinite Life" (*Guǎng lǐ wúliàngshòu*) onwards, the text distinguishes between attainment and loss regarding Amitābha’s land, leading people to practice renunciation.
This initial part has two sections:

first, a detailed presentation of the superior joys of the Land of Infinite Life; second, [the subsequent discussion]. Regarding the first: [it begins with] a broad enumeration of the matters concerning the supreme bliss of the Land of Infinite Life.
Second, from "The Buddha told Maitreya and all the devas and humans" onwards, there is the exhortation for people to be reborn [in that land].

Within this section, there are eight parts: first, manifesting the long duration of life in that land; second, manifesting the extraordinary and wondrous radiance of its assembly; third, manifesting the complete physical marks of the beings therein; fourth, manifesting the supreme wisdom and virtue of the assembly; fifth, manifesting that those born there are forever free from the evil realms; sixth, manifesting the abundance of offerings made in that land; seventh, manifesting that the hearing of the Dharma is uninterrupted for those born there; and eighth, manifesting the perfect fulfillment of the practices and virtues of the bodhisattvas.
Within the first section, it is revealed that those bodhisattvas shall all ultimately reach the stage of being "in their final birth" (ekajātipratibaddha).
It clarifies that their lifespans are long and far-reaching, such that they do not suffer premature death, except when they voluntarily assume bodies in other realms for the sake of sentient beings.

In the second section, first it is shown that the bodily radiance of the śrāvakas in that land extends for one fathom, and next it is shown that the light of the other bodhisattvas in that land illuminates a hundred yojanas.
One *yojana* is forty *li*.
Illuminating one hundred *yojanas* amounts to four thousand *li*.
The three lights of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta pervade the trichiliocosm.
Among these, the first section provides a general analysis.
The passage beginning with "Ānanda addressed the Buddha" analyzes their names and titles.
The passage beginning with "These two bodhisattvas, in this land... demonstrates their birth here and their existence there.
In the third section, it is revealed that those sentient beings possess complete physical characteristics, being endowed with all thirty-two marks, as extensively explained in the sutra.
The passage beginning with "the perfection of wisdom" constitutes the fourth section, which reveals the extraordinary excellence of those sentient beings' intellectual virtue.
There are four distinct points:
first, the perfection of wisdom.

This involves penetrating deeply into all phenomena, realizing and harmonizing with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), thoroughly elucidating the essential subtleties, and fully mastering the meaning of the teachings.
Second, the two supernormal knowledges are unimpeded;
third, the faculties are clear and sharp;
fourth, the attainment of patience differs.
Those of dull faculties accomplish two types of patience, namely, the patience of resonance and the patience of compliance.
Those of sharp faculties attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), numbering as many as incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons, until they achieve Buddhahood.
The section beginning with "Furthermore, they attain" constitutes the fifth segment, demonstrating that those born there are forever free from the evil realms (*apāya*).

Within this, it is first clarified that those born in that land shall not again enter the evil realms until they attain Buddhahood; they possess sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), constantly remember their past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*), and subsequently manifest births in other regions for the sake of sentient beings.
Śākyamuni speaks for himself, saying that they are like the various bodhisattvas within my own land.
The section beginning with "He said to Ānanda" is the sixth segment, which demonstrates that those who are born there are able to perform extensive offerings.

Within this, first it clarifies his journey to the worlds of the ten directions to make extensive offerings to many Buddhas; next, it clarifies his receiving of the Dharma from them; and finally, it clarifies that after making these offerings, before partaking of food, he returned to his own country.
The first four verses of the preceding section are as follows:
First, it is shown that the bodhisattvas of that land travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions in the time it takes to eat a single meal to universally make offerings to all Buddhas.

Second, from the verse beginning with "according to their minds" (*svecchā*), it clarifies that the various offering implements are manifested through transformation in accordance with their intentions.
3. From "In the void" onwards, it clarifies that within the void they transform into flower canopies.
4. From "Those bodhisattvas" onwards, it clarifies that all the bodhisattvas together play celestial music and sing praises of the Buddha's virtues.
"Qian" means "all.
When the multitude were all filled with joy and leaping for joy, it was called "Qianxin Yue" (All Rejoiced).
After making further offerings to the Buddha, they returned to their own country before the meal.
From here below is the seventh section, which demonstrates that those who are born hear the Dharma without interruption.
Within this, the first part clarifies the time when the assembly gathers in the lecture hall and the Tathāgata preaches for them.
From "There was none who did not... onwards, it clarifies that through the teaching they attained benefit and their minds were liberated to realize the Way.
From "At that very moment" onwards, it describes the making of offerings to the Buddha.
Within this section, first there is the sound of trees swaying in the wind;
Next, they blow exquisite flowers;
thereafter, the various devas and others hold flowers, incense, and music to offer worship and present offerings, providing infinite entertainment.
From this point down to the eighth section, it demonstrates that the bodhisattva’s practice and virtues are perfectly complete.
Within this, there is first a detailed exposition and later a summary.
The detailed exposition contains seven parts:
first, practicing conduct while remaining free from faults;
2. From "Endowed with" (*samanvāgata*) onwards, the perfection of virtues is accomplished;
3. From "Equally contemplating the three realms as empty and non-existent" onwards, the fulfillment of practice is achieved;
4. From "The ultimate One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*) onwards, the excellence of accomplished virtues is realized.
5. From "Destroying Envy" onwards, there is the progressive cultivation of practice;
6. From "The Power of Causes" onwards, there is the perfection of all powers;
7. From "The Merit of Physical Color, Marks, and Signs" onwards, there is a general praise and manifestation of excellence based on all virtues.
The section on "Distinctions" first provides specific explanations and subsequently offers a general summary.

Within the specific explanations, the initial statement, "That which is expounded always proclaims what is correct," etc., concerns the purification of conduct through transformation and the avoidance of faults.
In the section beginning with "In that land," [the author] first explains his own practice as being free from error.
Within this, the initial portion clarifies the inclusion of remedies;
the section beginning with "extinguishing afflictions" clarifies the departure from all faults.
In the preceding section on "Compendium of Antidotes," it was clarified that the cultivation of the six perfections serves as their respective antidotes.
First is the cultivation of the practice of relinquishment (*tyāga*);
*tyāga* is synonymous with generosity (*dāna*).
"Having no sense of 'mine' regarding all things within that land" clarifies his freedom from views;
"having a mind free from attachment" reveals his freedom from craving.
To abandon these two is called the practice of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
Next, one cultivates the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The phrase "in coming, going, advancing, and halting, the mind has no attachments and is free and sovereign according to its will" clarifies the departure from faults of the body.
"Neither partiality nor aversion; neither 'other' nor 'self'" clarifies the transcendence of mental faults.
Regarding sentient beings, there is no partiality that treats some as intimate, nor aversion that treats others as distant; this is called "neither partiality nor aversion."
"Non-contention and non-litigation" clarifies the departure from verbal transgressions.
Next, one cultivates the practice of patience.
"Attaining a mind of great compassion and altruism toward all sentient beings, which is supple and subdued," correctly clarifies the capacity for patience.
“Absence of anger and resentment” and so forth refer to being free from the obstacles to patience.
Next, one cultivates diligence.
Seeking the wholesome without ceasing is called “absence of weariness and indolence.”
Because one practices all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) with uniformity, it is called the "equal mind" (*samacitta*).
Because that which is practiced is supreme, it is called the "superior mind" (*viśiṣṭacitta*).
Because the seeking of the mind is earnest and profound, it is called the "deep mind" (*adhyāśaya* / *gambhīracitta*).
Next, one cultivates the practice of dhyāna;
because it distances one from distracted thoughts, it is called "concentrated mind.
Below this, one cultivates the practice of prajñā.
To attain attachment to the Dharma is called "loving the Dharma"; this refers to the ultimate stage.
To experience the joy of the nectar upon hearing it is called "delighting in the Dharma"; this refers to the intermediate stage.
The joy felt when seeking [the Dharma] is called "delighting in the Dharma" (*dharmārāma*); this refers to the beginning.
What has preceded clarifies the cultivation and purification; what follows clarifies the departure from faults.
"Extinguishing all afflictions" (*sarvakleśapraśamana*) refers to being free from afflictions.
"Detaching from the mind of the evil destinies" means the elimination of unwholesome karma.
The foregoing concludes the individual [explanations].
"Ultimately fulfilling all bodhisattva practices" serves as the general conclusion.
The preceding first section concerned the cultivation of practice to eliminate faults; from here on, the second section concerns the perfect fulfillment of accomplished virtues.
"Possessing immeasurable virtues" serves as a general introduction, which will be specifically elucidated below.
Within this section, the first part clarifies the merit of self-benefit.
The passage beginning with "By means of non-obstruction" clarifies the merit of benefiting others.

Within the preceding section on self-benefit, the phrase "attaining profound meditative concentration, the various supernormal powers, and clear wisdom, and sporting in the virtues of the seven factors of enlightenment" refers to the merits of one's own stage (*svabhāva*).
"Dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas.
"Samādhi" refers to the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and so forth.
"Abhijñās" refers to the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
"Clear knowledge" (vidyā) refers to the three clear knowings:
knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and the exhaustion of outflows.
"Wisdom" (prajñā) refers to the three types of wisdom: [wisdom arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation].
Regarding hearing, reflection, and cultivation:
as for the "seven factors of enlightenment," they are mindfulness, wisdom, diligence, pliancy, joy, concentration, and equanimity; these are the seven.
From "Cultivating the Mind" (*xiūxīn*) onwards are the merits of progressive advancement (*śeṣavardhana*).
"Cultivating the Buddha’s Virtues" (*xiūxīn fódé*) refers to seeking the virtues of a Buddha above.

From "Fleshly Eye" (*ròuyuǎn*) onwards are the immeasurable merits of accomplishment; here, the meaning of the five eyes is briefly cited as it is explained extensively in a separate chapter and should be discussed in full therein.
Now, to explain the text: "The fleshly eye is clear and penetrating, discerning all without exception"—this refers to the excellence of the fleshly eye.
That which is composed of physical skin is called "flesh.
When the faculty of pure flesh is capable of illuminating and observing, it is termed the "eye."
Within that land, his retributive physical eye perceives clearly through countless worlds; this is called "purity and clarity.
Because what he sees is lucid and discerning, there is nothing he does not understand.
This is the ability to illuminate and perceive present forms and images, which is called the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*).
"The divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) penetrates the immeasurable and the limitless" refers to the superiority of the divine eye.

All meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) are termed "abodes of the gods" (*deva-vihāra*). Because one attains the eye based on these divine states, it is called the "divine eye" (*divya-cakṣus*); it is able to see sentient beings dying here and being born there.
Because that which is seen is vast and manifold, it is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
Because what is seen extends far into the distance, it is called "unlimited.
Regarding the statement, "The Dharma-eye observes the ultimate of all paths," the Dharma-eye is preeminent.
Because wisdom can illuminate phenomena, it is named the Dharma-eye.
One is able to perceive the faculties, desires, natures, and minds of all sentient beings, and simultaneously knows all methods for transforming sentient beings.
When such knowledge reaches its ultimate limit, it is called "ultimate" (niṣṭhā).
To thoroughly understand the distinctions among the dharmas of the paths of the three vehicles is called "perfecting all paths.
"Seeing the truth with the wisdom-eye and being able to cross to the other shore" refers to the excellence of the wisdom-eye.
The wisdom that illuminates emptiness and reality, which perceives the principle, is called the "eye.
Because it is able to perceive true emptiness, it is termed "seeing the truth.
Because it eliminates and abandons signs of existence to reach the shore of equality and signlessness, it is termed "crossing to the other shore."
“The Buddha-eye fully realizes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)”: this refers to the superiority of the Buddha-eye.
The preceding four [eyes] are specific, while the Buddha-eye is general.
Because its vision of objects is all-encompassing, it is said to be "fully endowed" (paripūrṇa).
Furthermore, the Buddha-eye is able to perceive the non-empty, true nature within the Tathāgatagarbha; this is called "comprehending the dharma-nature," which constitutes the virtue of self-benefit.
To expound [this truth] for others by means of unimpeded wisdom constitutes the virtue of benefiting others.
From here below is the third section, which clarifies the perfection of cultivation.
Within this, there are two pairs: self-benefit and benefiting others.
The first pair concerns the beginning of cultivation; the latter pair concerns the culmination of cultivation.
From the beginning up to "extinguishing the afflictions" (*kleśa*), all constitute the first pair;
from "the Tathāgata" onwards, these constitute the latter pair.
Within the former, the initial statement—"equanimously contemplating the three realms as empty and non-existent, and aspiring to seek the Buddha-dharma"—constitutes his self-benefit (*svārtha*).
"Equally contemplating that the three realms are empty and non-existent" refers to the practice of departing from birth and death.
"Resolutely seeking the Buddha-dharma" refers to the practice of proceeding toward Bodhi.
From "possessing all forms of eloquence" onwards, it clarifies his practice of benefiting others.
"Possessing all forms of eloquence" clarifies the virtue of transforming others.
"Eliminating the afflictions and sufferings of sentient beings" clarifies the benefit of transforming others.
Within the latter pair [of verses], the former clarifies self-benefit;
The section beginning with "That great compassion" clarifies its benefit for others.
Within the context of self-benefit, the text is divided into four parts:
first, the understanding of one's own portion;...
2. From "Practicing all virtues" onwards is the practice of self-benefit;
3. From "Hearing the profound" onwards is the understanding of superior progress;
4. From "Constantly able to practice" onwards is the practice of superior progress.
Within the explanation of self-analysis, the phrase "the dharma of understanding arises from the Tathāgata as suchness" refers to this comprehension.
Understanding is produced through the Tathāgata’s teaching; therefore, it is said to arise from the Tathāgata.
Śūnyatā-samatā is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
To understand and know that all phenomena (dharmas) are entirely suchness is termed "understanding Suchness-Suchness.
"Skillfully knowing the habitual tendencies" and so forth constitute its instructional explanation.
The teaching of cultivating goodness is called "cultivating sounds";
the teaching of extinguishing evil is called "extinguishing sounds.
A bodhisattva is able to skillfully understand both of these, and is therefore said to be "well-knowing."
Because one possesses skillful knowledge therein, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Because one is able to understand the noble teachings well, "one does not delight in worldly discourse, but takes pleasure in correct treatises."
Within the practice of one's own level, "cultivating all roots of goodness and aspiring to honor the Buddha-way" refers to the practice of proceeding toward Bodhi.
"Knowing that all dharmas are entirely quiescent, such that both the remaining traces of the birth-body and afflictions are exhausted" refers to the practice of extinguishing birth and death.
"Knowing that all phenomena are entirely quiescent" refers to the cultivation of purification through the contemplation of emptiness.
"The two remaining residues of the afflictions of the birth-body are both exhausted" refers to the accomplishment of purification through the removal of hindrances.
The retribution of suffering in the physical body and the causes of afflictive delusions— these two remnants are all completely extinguished.
Within the superior progress of understanding, the phrase "hearing the profound Dharma without doubt or fear" means that he does not doubt because he can understand the profound,
and he does not fear because he can penetrate the profound.
Regarding "constantly able to practice" during the process of superior progress, it means that one does not cease practicing the profound Dharma of the Buddha.
The preceding section concerned self-benefit; this clarifies the benefit of others.
"The one of great compassion" serves as a general heading, which is then specifically elucidated below.
"Profound and subtle" refers to the depth of the compassionate mind;
"nothing left uncovered or unsupported" refers to the breadth of compassion for all beings.
This concludes the third section.
From here on follows the fourth section, the excellence of the accomplishment of virtues.
Within this, first the virtue of self-benefit is elucidated.
The section beginning with "As in the Mahāyāna" clarifies the virtue of benefiting others.
Within the virtues pertaining to oneself, the first part clarifies the excellence of gathering wholesome qualities;
the section beginning with "Illuminating all merits" clarifies the excellence of being free from faults.
Within the excellence of gathering wholesome qualities, "the ultimate One Vehicle" refers to the fulfillment of the virtues of enlightenment.
A "vehicle" (yāna) is a functional application; because its practice can transport one to the goal, it is called a vehicle.
Although many vehicles are taught according to the needs of those to be transformed, they are not distinct when viewed from the perspective of ultimate reality; therefore, they are said to be "one.
Regarding this single meaning, there are generally four ways of explaining it:
first, "one" as a term used for distinction.
Within those three baskets of the teachings, the Tathāgata divided them according to the needs of those to be converted: for those seeking the state of a śrāvaka, he taught the Four Noble Truths;
for those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha, he taught dependent origination;

and for those seeking the Mahāyāna, he taught the Six Perfections. He proclaimed that bodhisattvas practice the six impure pāramitās throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and in the single body of their final birth, they sever the fetters and attain Buddhahood.
To distinguish those three, the term "one" is used.
This "one" sublates the individual names [of the three].
Although the Tathāgata taught the three vehicles in accordance with the capacities of those to be converted, worldly people have dogmatically clung to them as being real.
To distinguish them from those three, it is said that there is "one.
Therefore, the Sūtra states: "Only this one is real; all others are not true.
They are like a conjured city, not a true place of rest."
The three assemblies have one distinct name:
although the Tathāgata’s Fundamental Section is divided into three, they return to the source as one;
therefore, it is called "one," as explained in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
The four [vehicles] have no distinct names; they are one.
When discussing reality from the perspective of ultimate reality, they have been without distinction since the beginning, and are therefore called "one.
Within this Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), one exhaustively reaches the ultimate limit, arriving at the other shore, the pinnacle of the fruit of nirvāṇa.
These two pairs decisively sever the net of doubt.
That "wisdom emerges from the mind" is its verification.
To eliminate the false and manifest the true is called severing the net of doubt.
When true understanding arises from within, it is called the emergence of the wisdom-mind.
"The Buddha’s teachings encompass all things without exception" refers to the knowledge derived from these teachings.
To exhaustively understand them without remainder is what is meant by "encompassing all without exception."
This realization and the teaching form a pair.
"Wisdom like the ocean" clarifies that his wisdom is profound and vast;
"samādhi like a mountain" manifests that his concentration is lofty and supreme.
"The radiance of wisdom is pure and surpasses that of the sun and moon" reveals the brilliance of his wisdom.
"The pure and white dharmas are perfectly fulfilled, like the Snowy Mountains" manifests the purity of his meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This concentration and wisdom further constitute a pair.
What precedes summarizes the cultivation of virtue; what follows reveals the departure from faults.
"Illuminating all merits as equally pure" is the explanation in terms of the Dharma.
All virtues are pure; this is called "equality in purity.
The following uses metaphors to clarify this.
There are six distinct metaphors, which can be understood from the text and its illustrations.
The former [the first three lines] clarifies self-benefit, while the latter [the subsequent ten lines] elucidates benefiting others.
There are thirteen phrases, all of which reveal the meaning through metaphors.

Regarding the phrase, "Just as the Great Vehicle carries the multitudes of sentient beings": the world designates a great carriage as the "Great Vehicle" (Mahāyāna). The merit of those Bodhisattvas in benefiting others is like that worldly great carriage; it is called the Great Vehicle because it transports the multitudes of sentient beings out of birth and death.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
This concludes the fourth [section].
From here below begins the fifth: the cultivation of progressive advancement.
Among these, each of the five pairs first clarifies the benefit of others and subsequently elucidates self-benefit.
How do these five pairs differ?
The first two constitute the stage of maintenance (*svabhāva*), while the latter three represent the stage of excellence (*viśeṣa*).
Within one's own being, the first pair initiates the application of skillful means.
"To destroy the mind of envy so as not to resent the superior" constitutes the skillful means for benefiting others.
Because the mind harbors jealousy and envy, it is unable to benefit others; therefore, these must be eradicated.
"Dedicatedly delighting in seeking the Dharma without satiety" is the expedient means for self-benefit.
Next is the correct cultivation.
The passage beginning with "Constantly desiring to explain extensively, his resolve never weary" and so forth correctly clarifies benefiting others.
"Constantly desiring to explain extensively, his resolve never wearying" indicates the excellence of the mind that initiates the teaching.
Regarding the phrase "beating the Dharma drum" and so forth, the Dharma taught is supreme.
To speak of "beating the Dharma drum" is a metaphor for the Dharma of hearing-wisdom (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
that the sound of the teaching reaches afar is called "beating the Dharma drum."
"Raising the Dharma Banner" is a metaphor for the Dharma of the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);
"establishing" refers to the formulation of propositions, while "proposition" gives rise to the "banner.

As for the phrase "Shining the Sun of Wisdom to Remove the Darkness of Ignorance," this explains the Dharma of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) which opens the way for sentient beings.
"Cultivating the six points of respectful harmony" correctly clarifies self-benefit.
When one’s practice becomes identical to that of others and one’s feelings are free from discord, it is called the "six points of respectful harmony.
The identity of body, speech, and mind constitutes its three harmonies.
Sharing the same precepts, sharing the same acts of giving, and transforming others through shared views—these are the six bases of harmony.
When these six are harmonized, one comes to regard each other with intimacy and respect; this is called the "respectful harmony of the six bases."
Within the section on "inferior advancement," the first corresponds to the beginning of cultivation, the second to the sequence of cultivation, and the third to the completion of cultivation.
Regarding the first correspondence, "constantly practicing the gift of Dharma" constitutes the beginning of benefiting others.
“With a mind of courageous diligence, do not face weakness” refers to the beginning of one’s own practice.
In the second pair, “acting as a lamp for the world and a most excellent field,” and so forth, refers to the subsequent stage of benefiting others.
“Acting as the lamp and illumination for the world and the most supreme field of merit” clarifies the excellence of his transformative virtue.
Being inherently endowed with wisdom and able to engender understanding in sentient beings, he is called the Lamp and Illumination of the World.
"Being inherently endowed with merit and able to produce goodness in sentient beings, he is called a supreme field of blessings.
"Constantly acting as a guide, equal toward all without hatred or affection," clarifies that his transformative benefits are supreme.
To enlighten others through wisdom is what defines a "Teacher.
Because one’s merit and goodness provide universal relief and nourishment, there is neither hatred nor attachment.
"Delighting solely in the Right Path, without other joys or sorrows" refers to the sequence of one's own practice.
Delighting in the Way and cultivating goodness, one is free from all remaining faults.
Within the third pair, "extracting the thorns of desire" and so forth, refers to the accomplishment of benefiting others.
"Extracting the thorns of all desires to bring peace to sentient beings" means transforming people so they may leave behind their transgressions.
"His merit and wisdom are so preeminent that there are none who do not revere him," meaning that transformed beings follow what is good.
"The extinction of the three impurities," and so forth, refers to the perfection of one's own practice.
"The extinction of the obstacles of the three impurities" constitutes the accomplishment of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
Greed, hatred, and delusion—these are the three defilements that constitute obstacles.
"Wandering through the various supernormal powers" refers to the accomplishment of conduct and virtue.
This concludes the fifth [section].
From here below is the sixth section, "Endowment with All Powers," which first distinguishes the individual powers and concludes with a summary.
Within the distinction, the first part clarifies the endowment of one's own power;
from the phrase "harmonizing according to the Dharma" onwards, it clarifies the endowment of the power to transform others.
From this central point, we shall proceed by means of seven gates.
"The power of causes and the power of conditions" constitutes the first gate, serving as the basis for initiating cultivation.
All virtuous practices cultivated in the past that are capable of producing present goodness are termed the "power of causes."
Associating with virtuous friends and hearing the true Dharma is called the power of conditions.
"The power of intention and the power of aspiration" constitute the second gate, which gives rise to the skillful means of cultivation.
The mind that seeks Buddhahood is called the power of intention (*āśaya-bala*).
The vow to initiate practice is called the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*).
"The power of skillful means, the constant power, and the wholesome power" constitutes the third section: preparatory application and correct cultivation.
Skillful cultivation in accordance with the Dharma is called the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*).
Constant cultivation in accordance with the Dharma is called the power of constancy (*nitya-bala*).
Right cultivation in accordance with the Dharma is called the power of goodness (*kuśala-bala*).
"The power of concentration and the power of wisdom" constitute the fourth section, which concerns the accomplishment of mental cultivation.
The accomplishment of practicing *śamatha* (calm abiding) is called the power of concentration;
the accomplishment of practicing *vipaśyanā* (insight) is called the power of wisdom.
The preceding four gates are distinguished according to cultivation.
"The power of extensive learning" constitutes the fifth gate, which is the understanding that gives rise to practice.

"The powers of giving, morality, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom" constitute the sixth gate, clarifying the practices that are initiated; these practices refer to the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā).
These two gates are distinguished according to practice.
"The power of right mindfulness, right contemplation, and the various supernormal knowledges and clarities" constitutes the seventh gate, wherein virtues are accomplished based on practice.
Abandoning signs and entering into reality is termed "right mindfulness."
To see phenomena free from delusion is called right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).

Based on these two types [of wisdom], one accomplishes the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) and attains the three insights (*tisro vidyāḥ*); this is termed the power of supernormal knowledge and insight (*abhijñā-vidyā-bala*).
This latter section distinguishes [the powers] according to their qualities.
The preceding section concerns self-benefit.
The phrase "the power to bring all sentient beings to fulfillment according to the Dharma" clarifies his benefit for others.
Thus ends the individual exposition.
"Thus, all such powers are fully possessed"—this serves as a general conclusion.
This concludes the sixth [section].
From here on, the seventh [section] generally praises and reveals the excellence by means of all the virtues.
Within this, there are four points:
first, the excellence of his own virtues; second, being praised by the Buddhas; third, the ultimate Mahāyāna; and fourth, transcending the Hīnayāna.

Regarding the first, the phrase "endowed with physical beauty, the marks and signs, merit, and eloquence, such that none can equal him" refers to what is accomplished through his own efforts (*svabhāva-siddha*).
"The physical form, color, and marks are peerless" clarifies the excellence of his body;
"merit and eloquence are peerless" clarifies the excellence of his virtue.
The term "endowed" clarifies the perfection of merit;
the term "adorned" clarifies the adornment of the body.
"Respectfully making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas" refers to that which arises from superior progress.
The second [section] contains the Buddha’s praise, through which the [bodhisattva] marks are manifest and can be known.
In the third section, the phrase “the bodhisattva brings the various pāramitās to ultimate fulfillment” indicates that the practice has reached completion.
The passage beginning with “cultivating the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, which are neither arising nor ceasing,” refers to the fulfillment of the realization of practice.
In the fourth section, the transcendence of the two vehicles is clearly evident from the text.
The preceding section constitutes the specific praise.
The passage beginning with "Those bodhisattvas have accomplished such [qualities]" serves as the general concluding praise.
The eight preceding sections together form the first part, which sets forth the matters concerning the superior bliss of Amitābha’s land.
From here below is the second section, which exhorts others to be reborn [in the Pure Land].
"The Buddha addressed Maitreya" indicates the person to whom he spoke;
"the various devas and humans" identifies those for whose sake he spoke.
"The merit and wisdom of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas in the Land of Immeasurable Life are beyond measure," and so forth, reiterates what has been analyzed above.
"The merit and wisdom of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas are beyond description" reiterates the individuals analyzed in the preceding text.
"Furthermore, its land is so subtle, peaceful, blissful, and pure," this restates the land as analyzed in the preceding text.
"Why not exert yourself... and below, this is the formal exhortation to be reborn there.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the formal exhortation to be reborn there;
second, from "It is easy to go" onwards, the Tathāgata’s expression of lamentation; [and third, the description of the splendors of that land].
3. From "Why not abandon [evil]" onwards, there is a renewed exhortation to seek rebirth.
In the preceding section on the formal exhortation, "Why do you not strive to do good? was the formal exhortation to cultivate the causes.
"What is it that you do not strive to cultivate goodness and seek birth? refers to the power of cultivating goodness.
From "mindfulness of the Way" (*nian dao*) onwards, it clarifies the benefits of cultivation.
One who is mindful of the Way will naturally attain rebirth; this is called "mindfulness of spontaneity" (*nian ziran*).

However, as long as one can mindfully contemplate the Way and manifest the practice of virtue, one will be reborn in the Pure Land regardless of high or low status; thus it is said, "clinging to that which is without superior or inferior."
If one is born there, one’s supernormal powers will penetrate all things without limit; thus it is said, "penetratingly reaching the boundless.
The phrase "each should diligently strive to seek this" is a repeated exhortation to cultivate the causes.
The phrase "will certainly transcend" below serves to reiterate the benefits of cultivation.
"Will certainly transcend and surpass" clarifies that which is exited;
"reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing" manifests that which is reached.
"Transversely cutting off the five evils, the evil destinies are naturally closed," clarifies that which is abandoned.
Among the three miserable paths and the human and celestial realms, these constitute the five destinies (*gati*).
To distinguish among them: the lower three evil paths are called the "evil destinies," while the two paths of humans and devas are called the "fortunate destinies."
Now, in reference to the Pure Land of Amitābha, the five destinies of this Sahā world are collectively termed "evil realms" (*durgati*).
Hell, hungry ghosts, and animals are called evil realms because they are destinations of pure evil;
the humans and devas of the Sahā world are also called evil realms because they are destinations of mixed evil.

If one practices according to this method to effect abandonment, first one abandons the delusions of view, thereby departing from the causes of the three miserable realms and extinguishing their results; subsequently, one abandons the delusions of cultivation, thereby departing from the causes of human and celestial rebirth and severing their results.
Gradual elimination is not called "horizontal severance";
if one attains rebirth in Amitābha’s Pure Land, the five realms of existence in this Sahā world are abandoned all at once, and thus it is called "horizontal severance."
"Cutting off the five evil destinies" refers to cutting off their results.
"The evil destinies close of themselves" refers to closing off their causes.
This clarifies that which is to be abandoned.
"Ascending the Way to the Infinite" reveals what has been attained.
Because the attainment of the Way is profound and vast, it is without limit or end.
The preceding section constitutes the first part, which is the formal exhortation to be reborn [in the Pure Land].
From this point downward is the second section, in which the Tathāgata expresses lamentation, desiring to inspire worldly people to exert themselves in order to attain rebirth there.
The initial statement, "It is easy to go, yet no one does," is precisely intended as an expression of lamentation.
To practice the causes and immediately depart is called "easy to go.
Because there are no people who practice the causes, those who attain rebirth are few; hence it is said, "no people.
The phrase "that land does not oppose or contradict" clarifies the aforementioned ease of going.
"Drawn by what is natural" indicates that there is no person [acting as an agent] prior to this.
The sentient beings of the Sahā world are shrouded by the veils and fetters of literary habit; they are naturally bound and constrained by these, unable to escape, and thus there is no such person.
From here below is the third section, an earnest exhortation to be reborn [in the Pure Land].
“Why not abandon worldly affairs and diligently seek the Way and its Virtue? This exhorts one to cultivate the cause.
“One may thereby attain longevity, with life and happiness that are limitless. This clarifies the fruit obtained through cultivation.
The preceding first section sets forth the matters of the supreme bliss of Amitābha’s land, causing people to aspire toward it.
From here on, the second section reveals that the Sahā world is filled with impurity and evil, causing people to feel weary of it and seek renunciation.
Within this, there are four parts:

first, enumerating the faults of the afflictions of the three poisons; second, exhorting people to practice equanimity (*upekṣā*); third, enumerating the faults of the suffering of the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings; and fourth, exhorting people to practice equanimity.
Within the first section, the faults of greed are clarified first;
from "the people of the world, fathers and sons" onwards, the faults of anger are clarified;
and from "in this way, worldly people do not believe" onwards, the faults of ignorance are clarified.
Regarding greed, there are three parts:
first, a general explanation of the faults of greed as understood by worldly people;
second, from "Noble and Dignified" onwards, a specific explanation of the faults of greed as they pertain to the wealthy and powerful.
Third, from "The Poor" onwards, the text specifically addresses the lowly and destitute to clarify the faults of greed.
Within the first section, the phrase "worldly people, base and vulgar, contend over matters that are not urgent," clarifies their possession of evil.
This means that the people of this world are negligent regarding social customs and contend over worldly matters that are not urgent.
The phrase "In this [state of] distress" and below demonstrates that they possess suffering.
Within suffering there are three aspects:
first, the suffering of seeking wealth;
second, from the phrase "having fields" onwards, the suffering of guarding and protecting it.
Third, from "横為" (crosswise for) onwards, the suffering of dissipation is clarified.

Within the initial category of the suffering of seeking, the phrase "amidst this intense suffering, one diligently applies physical labor to provide for oneself" refers to seeking for the sake of the body.
The phrase "without distinction of high or low" and so forth refers to seeking [the goal] for the sake of others.
"Without high or low, without poor or rich" identifies those who seek;
"young or old, male or female" and so forth identifies those for whom they act.
The following clarifies the existence of suffering.
The phrase "sharing in anxiety over wealth" and so forth clarifies mental suffering;
"running after the mind" and so forth clarifies physical suffering.
Regarding the protection against suffering, the passage "there is anxiety over fields, and there is anxiety over houses" and so forth specifically clarifies those various sufferings.
The section beginning with "reflecting deeply" concludes [the discussion].
Within the suffering of loss, the phrase "unwarrantedly [suffering] from the impermanence of water, fire, and thieves," etc., clarifies the suffering of losing wealth.
The phrase "or being crushed while sitting," etc., clarifies the suffering of losing one's body.
Next, the faults of greed are elucidated by means of wealth and nobility; the text is explicit and thus easily understood.
Within the section elucidating the faults of greed by means of poverty and low status, there are three distinct parts:
first, the suffering of seeking wealth.
2. From "Sometimes sitting" onwards, it clarifies the suffering of losing one's body;
3. From "Unwilling" onwards, it clarifies future suffering.
Regarding the suffering among the pursuits for wealth,
there are five distinct textual sections:
first, the arising of suffering from worrying about matters that do not yet exist.
2. From "Just when there is one... onwards, the suffering of insufficiency is clarified within the context of minor matters;
3. From "Just as one wishes to complete... onwards, the suffering of loss is clarified within the context of things already obtained;
4. From "One must seek again... onwards, the suffering of non-attainment during the process of further seeking is clarified.
5. From "Furthermore, they form groups" onwards, it clarifies the sufferings of cold, heat, and so forth during the time of seeking.
These five [points] together constitute the suffering of seeking wealth.
The suffering of losing one's body and future suffering are clear and can be understood from the text.
In the section clarifying the faults of anger, the text is divided into three parts:
first, exhortation through reasoning and teaching:

"You should treat one another with affection and not harbor increased jealousy; share both presence and absence, and do not be greedy or stingy; let your speech and countenance always be harmonious, and do not be in opposition or conflict."
2. From "Or mental strife" onwards, the faults of anger are explained in detail;
3. From "Why not abandon" onwards, one is exhorted to practice relinquishment.
Within the second section on the faults, there are specifically three types:
First, it clarifies the fault of future enmity and harm;
second, from "A person in the world" onwards, it clarifies the fault of future rebirth in the evil realms;
third, from "The place of birth is dark and obscure" onwards, it clarifies the fault of separation and the difficulty of reunion.
In the third section, the exhortation to abandon [ignorance] is clear.
Within the explanation of the faults of ignorance (*moha*), the text is divided into two parts:
first, the demonstration that ignorance exists; [the second follows].
Second, from "The constant path of birth and death turns ever more severe" onwards, it clarifies the fault of ignorance (*moha*).
Within the preceding section, there are two parts:
first, it clarifies that ignorant people lack right faith themselves;...
Regarding the second section, from "mutually gazing" (*gengxiang zhan*) onwards, [the text] focuses on receiving the words of others.
Within the section "lacking faith oneself," the first part provides a specific analysis.
From "merely sitting thus" (*danzuo shi*) onwards, it summarizes and reveals the faults.
It is their fault that, due to a lack of faith, they stubbornly cling to their own views.
Within the words received from others, they "glance at one another, with the same behavior before and after," imitating and practicing what they have learned from others.
Regarding the phrase "successive transmission" (*zhuanxiangcheng*) below, it refers to the practice of following one's ancestors.
Within this, the initial statement, "successively receiving and inheriting the remaining instructions of the father," clarifies that the son, being ignorant, receives the father’s erroneous words.
Regarding the phrase "the ancestors and forefathers," it illustrates that because the father was foolish and stubborn, the son became ignorant.
Within this, there are four phrases:
the first states, "The grandfather never practiced goodness," clarifying his lack of virtuous conduct.
Second, "not knowing the Way and its Virtue" (moral truth) reveals their lack of understanding.

Third, "the body is ignorant and the spirit dark; the mind is blocked and the will closed; they cannot perceive for themselves the good and evil of birth and death, and there is no one to speak to them," which further clarifies their lack of understanding.
The former phrase lacks understanding, for one does not recognize the path to liberation;
this phrase lacks understanding, for one does not know the causes and effects of good and evil in the world.
One cannot perceive for oneself the course of birth and death, as one does not recognize their results.
The paths of good and evil cannot be seen by themselves; one does not know their causes.
Since one does not recognize this cause and effect within one's own mind, and others have no words to explain it, one will never understand.
4. Regarding the phrase "Good and ill fortune, calamity and blessing, each arise in competition; there is not a single anomaly": this reiterates the state of non-action.
The preceding sentence’s "non-action" manifested the failure to perform good deeds;
this sentence’s "non-doing" clarifies the commission of evil.
"Though one commits evil oneself, others may remain silent; therefore, one is not eternally separated from it.
The preceding section clarifies the existence of delusion (*moha*); the following clarifies the faults of delusion.
Within this, there are four parts:
First, due to delusion, fathers and sons weep for one another;
second, from the passage "such a person" onwards, it clarifies that due to delusion one commits evil and undergoes suffering;
third, from the passage "or the household" onwards, it clarifies that due to delusion relatives long for one another.
4. From "The General Summary" onwards, it is clarified that one creates evil and undergoes suffering due to ignorance (*moha*).
At the beginning, the mutual weeping of father and son is first explained.
From "Instruction and Speech" onwards, it clarifies that they are difficult to enlighten; thus, they transmigrate through birth and death without end, revolving in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
In the second section, there are five distinct points:
first, it clarifies that these deluded people are ignorant and obstinate, failing to believe in the sutras and the Dharma, each acting solely according to their own whims;
second, they are confused by sensual desire and fail to comprehend the Way and its Virtue.
Third, they are deluded by anger and greedily crave wealth and sensual pleasures;
fourth, remaining bound by these three, they fail to attain the Right Path and undergo manifold sufferings.
They shall further fall into evil realms, where manifest suffering is heavy.
Birth and death are endless; it is clear that there is profound suffering.
From the words "Alas! onwards, the Tathāgata expresses lamentation to cause people to feel weary of and renounce [samsara].
Within this third section, there are three distinct parts:
First, due to delusion, one cannot be dissuaded from cherishing memories of kinsmen;
second, from the section on "thoughts" (*saṃjñā*) downward, it clarifies that because of such cherishing, one is unable to cultivate goodness;
third, from the section on "walking about" (*caṅkrama*) downward, it shows that because one does not cultivate goodness, one cannot attain the Path.
In the fourth section, there are four distinct points:
first, due to delusion (*moha*), they give rise to greed (*rāga*) and pursue worldly affairs, as expressed in the passage beginning with “confused, turbid, and agitated by greedy desire and craving”;
second, from the passage beginning with “each harboring thoughts of killing,” due to delusion, they give rise to hatred (*dveṣa*) and mutually harm one another.
"Each harbors the poison of killing, their evil breath is dark and murky, and they engage in deluded deeds," and so forth.
Third, from "spontaneously" (*svabhāva*) onwards, it clarifies that one undergoes suffering and finds it difficult to escape due to the aforementioned evils.
For those who commit sins, by the power of their past offenses, unlawful and evil conditions naturally gather and follow them, allowing them to act as they please.
When their transgressions reach their limit, [the karmic force] suddenly seizes them and exhausts it, leading them into the evil realms to undergo boundless suffering.
4. From "The suffering is unbearable" onwards, the Tathāgata expresses lamentation to inspire in people a sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*).
Having extensively set forth the faults of the three poisons (*trivisa*) above, from here on is the second section: the exhortation to cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*) through effort.
Within this, there are four sections:
first, the formal exhortation to cultivate equanimity; second, Maitreya’s comprehension of the teaching; third, the further cultivation of equanimity; and fourth, Maitreya’s commitment to practice.
In the first [section], there are two parts:
First, exhorting people to practice;
second, from "Should there be any doubts" onwards, exhorting people to inquire.
There are three ways of exhorting practice:
First, he cites the aforementioned faults to exhort people to cultivate abandonment.
When it says, "The Buddha told Maitreya that because of worldly matters, one cannot attain the Way while sitting," this cites the aforementioned faults.
"Worldly affairs" refers to the aforementioned matters of the three poisons.
"By means of" (yòng) means "thereby.
"Because of" (zuò) means "due to."
Because worldly people are occupied with these three poisons, they are unable to attain the Way.
The passage beginning with "should mature" is an exhortation.
"One should maturely contemplate and distance oneself from all evils" exhorts people to abandon faults, meaning to leave behind the aforementioned evils of the three poisons.
"Select and practice what is good" exhorts the cultivation of remedies.
From "Lustful desires" downward, it cites the faults of the impermanence of the five worldly desires, exhorting people to cultivate renunciation.
Third, from "The Buddha is currently present" onwards, the text cites the Buddha’s current presence to exhort people to practice diligently.
Within this section, it first cites the Buddha’s current presence as a direct exhortation to practice.
The section beginning with "Those who have aspirations" below clarifies the benefits and encourages practice.
"Attaining wisdom and clear penetration" refers to the excellence of *jñāna* (knowledge).
"Excellence of merit" refers to the excellence of *puṇya* (fortune).
From "Do not" onwards, there is the citation of prohibitions as warnings against harm.
The preceding sections on exhorting practice and exhorting inquiry can be understood accordingly.
From here below is the second section: Maitreya’s summary and understanding.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the formal comprehension;
second, from "Now I have encountered" onwards, the expression of joy and self-congratulation.
The preceding section has four parts.
First is the praise of the Buddha for his swift speech.
By reflecting upon it with a focused mind, one realizes that "the people of the world are indeed thus," thereby fulfilling the previous statement regarding the swiftness of his speech.
"Guan" (pervasion) means "to penetrate.
To penetrate with the mind and contemplate: worldly people truly follow the affairs of the three poisons and thus sit unable to attain the Way; this is what is meant by "reality" (shi).
Second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, [the text] receives the Buddha’s compassionate transformation.
3. From "The Buddha’s Words and Teachings" onwards, there is a repeated praise of the Buddha’s discourse as being profound and excellent.
Within this section, the praise for the profundity and excellence of the teaching comes first.
The passage beginning with "Wisdom is luminous" cites his wisdom to establish the excellence of his discourse.
4. From "Now, as for why our assembly has received [benefit]" onwards, the Buddha's grace is reiterated through verse.
From "Now, as for why our assembly has attained liberation," the specific cause is correctly set forth below.
"Because the Buddha diligently practiced the Way through his past lives and has now attained the fruit of Buddhahood to transform and guide us, we have obtained liberation.
The phrase "all is due to the humility and austerity he practiced while seeking the Way in his previous lives" cites the causes of the Buddha's attainment.
"Universal in grace and virtue," and so forth, manifest the fruit of Buddhahood.
"Grace and virtue universally cover" is a general enumeration of the Buddha's virtues;
"Blessings and fortune majestic," and so forth, reveal them specifically.
The passage beginning with “The Buddha is the Honored Sovereign of the Dharma, transcending all sages” serves as a general conclusion and eulogy.
Within the specific details, the initial statement, “His fortune and glory are towering and his radiance shines through all,” refers to the excellence of his own merit.
“Reaching the ultimate of emptiness” refers to the excellence of one’s own wisdom.
“Opening the way into Nirvana and grasping the principles of instruction” refers to benefiting others through wisdom.
“Opening the way into Nirvana” means leading people to realize extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (Compendium of Training) instructs people to give rise to the Path.
The Dharma of the Path that instructs the world is called "instruction" (*śikṣā*).
Because this scripture compiles essential meanings from various sources to enable their study and practice, it is termed a "compendium" (*samuccaya*).
"Subduing through majestic power and causing dissolution," etc., refers to benefiting others through the transformation of merit.

For those sentient beings who are stubborn and fierce, one subdues them with majestic virtue, causing them to be tamed and subdued so that they turn toward and follow the holy transformation; therefore, it is called "subduing through majestic power and causing dissolution."
He skillfully moistens sentient beings and gathers them in through the power of his compassion.
This is called "moving the ten directions"; those with whom he has a karmic affinity are gathered in, which is termed "inexhaustible.
The concluding praise may be understood accordingly.

Having thus understood and accepted [the teaching], we have now encountered the Buddha and heard of Amitāyus; there is none among us who does not rejoice, our minds are opened and enlightened, and we celebrate this joy within ourselves.
This second section consists of Maitreya’s summary understanding.
Below this is the third section, the repeated exhortation to practice relinquishment,
which contains four parts:
First, a praise of Maitreya’s prior bearing of the Buddha’s grace;

second, from “Maitreya, you should know that since countless kalpas past” onwards, a celebration of Maitreya’s prior encounter with the Buddha and hearing of the Dharma, as well as his hearing the name of Amitāyus;
third, from “You should now likewise weary of [saṃsāra] yourself” onwards, the formal exhortation to practice.
4. From "You all should each exert yourselves with diligence" onwards, he exhorts them to abandon doubt.
At the beginning of this section, "The Buddha told you that this is so," confirms his previous statement.
Maitreya stepped forward and praised the Buddha’s teaching, saying it was "excellent, profound, and most virtuous. Because these words accord with the truth, he said, "It is so.
From the phrase "If there is compassion" onwards, he praises Maitreya’s previous reception and bearing of the Buddha’s grace.
Maitreya, because in a former life he took pity on sentient beings and, through diligent and arduous effort, sought the Buddha-way for their sake, he was named Cifó (Buddha of Compassion).
Because he reverently bore the Buddha’s grace, he was named Jingfó (Buddha of Reverence).
"This is truly a great good.
The passage "In the long course of time, a Buddha appears in the world" below cites the benefits of the Buddha’s transformation of beings to elaborate upon what was previously stated.
"In the long course of time, a Buddha again appears in the world" demonstrates that it is difficult to encounter a Buddha.
From "Now I" onwards, it clarifies that [the Buddha] has already completed his transformative benefit.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, manifesting that he has already become a Buddha and transforming the world through the Dharma.
Second, from "severing all" onwards, it describes how the Buddha manifests transformations to teach all sentient beings to sever the causes of death.
By "severing the net of doubts and uprooting the source of craving," he causes them to be free from afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Block the source of all evils" means to cause one to depart from unwholesome karma.
"Block" (du) is synonymous with "obstruct" (sai).
Unwholesome karma is the fundamental root of all evil paths; thus, it is called the "source of all evils."
To issue commands that cut off and block [obstructions] is termed "blocking" (du).
Below the third section, "Wandering Steps" (youbu), it is revealed that he has already attained Buddhahood and transforms the world through the Dharma.
"Wandering through the three realms without any restriction or hindrance" refers to the transformation of the bodily karma (kāyakarma).
Because the body is transformed with mastery, there is no obstruction.
"Mastering the essentials of the various paths through wisdom" refers to the transformation of mental karma (*manas-karman*).
Being skillfully able to understand the scriptures and comprehensively grasping their manifold meanings is called "mastering wisdom."
Skillfully knowing the essentials of the practices of the Three Vehicles is called "the Essentials of the Various Paths.
"Holding fast to the guiding cords and illuminating them clearly to reveal the five destinies" refers to the transformation through the karma of speech.
Upholding the Dharma and sustaining the assembly is called "maintaining the guiding cords.
Discerning and rectifying the heterodox and the deviant is called "illuminating with clarity.
Employing transformation for all classes of beings is called "opening the five destinies."
4. Regarding the section "Delivering those not yet delivered" and below: the Buddha transforms the world and teaches all sentient beings to emerge from the fruits of birth and death.
"Delivering those not yet delivered" means to decisively rectify birth and death, thereby causing them to emerge from birth and death.
"The Way of Nirvāṇa" refers to bringing about the attainment of nirvāṇa.
This passage cites these transformative benefits to recount what was previously praised and understood by Maitreya.
This concludes the first section.
From here begins the second section, which celebrates Maitreya’s previous encounters with Buddhas, his hearing of the Dharma, and his hearing of the name of Amitāyus.
This section contains three parts;
the first demonstrates that Maitreya has practiced for a vast duration of time.
The second section, beginning with "Even unto," clarifies that he has now encountered the Buddha and heard of the Infinite Life [Amitāyus].
The third section, beginning with "How joyful!", expresses the Tathāgata’s congratulation.

Within the first part, the initial statement, "From incalculable kalpas past you have practiced with the desire to deliver sentient beings; how long it has been! indicates that the duration of his cultivation is long.
“From the time you attained the Way until your entry into *nirvāṇa*, [the number of beings] is beyond measure”—this shows that the Sage has come from afar.

“You and all the devas and humans of the ten directions have, since eternal kalpas past, undergone sorrow, fear, and arduous suffering that cannot be fully described”—this shows that such arduous suffering is vast.
"Everlasting" (*yong*) means "long-lasting.
By virtue of these many causes, one now encounters the Buddha and hears of Amitāyus; this is indeed a cause for celebration.
The latter two [points] are easily understood.
This concludes the second section.
From here on follows the third section, which is the formal exhortation to practice;
while addressed to Maitreya, its intent encompasses all beings.
Within this, the first part is the formal exhortation to practice;
from "Although it is but one lifetime" onwards, it demonstrates the benefits to exhort sentient beings.
The former section contains three parts:
First, exhorting the abandonment of faults;
second, from "upright body" (*kāya-samprajāna*) onwards, exhorting the cultivation of wholesome dharmas;
third, from "if a person can [transform themselves]" (*puruṣaḥ śaknoti*) onwards, exhorting the benefiting of sentient beings.

Regarding the exhortation to renounce transgressions beyond the [proper time]: "You should cultivate self-disgust for birth, old age, and sickness," and so forth; this exhorts the arising of a mind of revulsion.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death constitute the internal sufferings.
The term "suffering" refers to external suffering. The statement, "Impurities are foul and not to be relished;
one should resolve this for oneself," reveals the faults [of such things] so that they may be abandoned.
Among the exhortations to cultivate goodness, "upright body and correct conduct" refers to the goodness of stilling (*śamatha*).
"Increasing the performance of various good deeds" refers to the goodness of action (*pravṛtti*).
"Cultivating oneself to purify the person and washing away the defilements of the mind" exhorts the cultivation of mental conduct (*manas-karma*).
Cultivating [wholesome conduct] constitutes active goodness (*kriyā-kuśala*); the remainder constitutes the goodness of restraint (*saṃvara-kuśala*).
"Sincerity and trustworthiness in speech and action, with inner and outer corresponding" encourages the cultivation of verbal conduct.
"Sincerity and trustworthiness in speech and action" refers to its active goodness.
"Correspondence between the external and internal" constitutes the excellence of his stillness (*śamatha*).
To say that the heart corresponds to the internal means that his speech does not contradict his mind; thus they correspond.
Within the exhortation to benefit others, the phrase "if a person can save themselves" reiterates the aforementioned virtue of self-cultivation.
The phrase "mutually rescuing one another" and so forth primarily exhorts the practice of benefiting others.
"Mutually rescuing and aiding one another" refers to transforming others so they may leave behind transgressions.
"Vigorously seeking and making vows" refers to accumulating the roots of goodness and transforming people to achieve virtue.
"Vigorously seeking and aspiring" transforms and gives rise to aspiration;
"accumulating the roots of goodness" transforms and gives rise to practice.
The above has been an exhortation to cultivation.
The following section cites the benefits to encourage people to practice and study.
"Though one undergoes diligent toil for but a brief moment in this single lifetime" indicates that the duration of cultivation is short.
The passage beginning with "in future lives" describes the benefits obtained.
Among these, the first clarifies that the attainment of benefit is long-lasting.
The phrase "The unconditioned spontaneity follows nirvāṇa" indicates that the attainment of benefit is particularly sublime.
Within this long-term attainment of benefit, there are four distinct points:
The first statement, "In a future life one will be born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, where happiness is infinite," refers to the lengthening of one’s cherished desires.
The second, "For long shall one be united with the clarity of the Way and its Virtue," refers to the lengthening of the perfection of one’s virtues.
When the body and merit coexist, it is called the union of virtue and the Way.
When the mind and wisdom coexist, it is called the union with clarity.
Phrases such as "the three are forever uprooted" describe the prolongation of the state free from transgressions.
Within this, "permanently uprooting the root of birth and death" means long-term separation from the causes of karma;
"having no further craving," and so forth, means long-term separation from afflictions;
and "being without the calamity of suffering and distress" means long-term separation from the retribution of suffering.
4. "Desiring long life," and so forth, refers to a long lifespan.
This concludes the third [section].
From here below is the fourth, which exhorts the abandonment of doubt and confusion.
"Each of you should diligently seek what you desire," he exhorts them to practice with single-minded devotion.
"Do not harbor doubts," and so forth, he exhorts them to abandon uncertainty.
From the passage beginning "If you are born in those borderlands," below, he reveals the faults [of doubt] to urge them to relinquish it.
The preceding section was the third, the repeated exhortation to practice relinquishment.
From here below is the fourth, Maitreya’s reception of the practice.

Within this, the initial statement—“Having received the Buddha’s weighty instruction, I shall apply myself with diligence to study and practice according to the teaching”—accepts the Buddha’s previous words of exhortation to practice and demonstrates that he has already undertaken their implementation.
Regarding "dare not doubt": this acknowledges the Buddha’s previous exhortation to abandon doubt and demonstrates that [the speaker] himself no longer doubts.

From here on, the third section extensively enumerates the faults of the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings—the sufferings of karmic retribution—to cause people to feel weary of them and renounce them.
Among these, the first part is general;
the section beginning with "What are... is specific;
and the section beginning with "The Buddha told Maitreya, 'I say to you... is a further general explanation.
Within the first general section, the text is divided into two parts:
first, praising what precedes to introduce what follows—specifically, praising Maitreya’s reception of the teaching and his practice;

second, from the words "Now I," below, revealing the intent of one's own transformation, which is to transform sentient beings so that they may leave behind the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, and so that they may uphold the five virtues and obtain the five blessings.

Regarding the initial statement in the first part—that "in this evil world, to maintain an upright mind and correct intention while refraining from all evils is the ultimate virtue"—this is a direct praise of its characteristics.
The phrase "unsurpassed and peerless throughout the worlds of the ten directions" is used by way of contrast to manifest its excellence.
The section beginning with "Therefore" provides an explanation, first posing a question and then offering a resolution.

By stating that "the Buddha-lands are naturally virtuous, do not greatly produce evil, and are easily transformed," the text highlights the easy to manifest the difficult, thereby establishing this as superior.
Within the latter section, the phrase "I have now become a Buddha in this world" demonstrates that he has already attained Buddhahood;
the phrase "dwelling amidst the five evils," etc., reveals the places where he manifests his transformation.

The passage beginning with "Causing them to abandon the five" clarifies the intent of his own transformation: for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he causes them to have something from which to emerge and something to be attained.
That which they are caused to emerge from is the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, which are what the five precepts prevent.
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking intoxicants—these are the five evils.
To commit these five evils, one is punished by royal law in the present life and the body encounters calamities; these are called the five pains.
Because of these five evils, one will receive retribution in the three miserable realms in future lives; these are called the "five burnings.
[The Buddha] causes all beings to emerge from them.
Within that which they have attained, he subdues and transforms their minds, causing them to submit and follow the Dharma, and causing them to uphold the five virtues.
The so-called five precepts are the opposites of the five evils.
Regarding "attaining their blessings": by observing the five precepts, one experiences physical peace and freedom from suffering in the present life, which is the opposite of the five types of pain.

Regarding the phrase "the path of Nirvana for longevity and transcendence of the world," it means that by being reborn in the Land of Amitābha, one ultimately attains Nirvana; this reverses the aforementioned five types of burning.

Within the second specific section, the passage beginning with "What are the five evils, the five pains, and the burnings? poses a question to introduce what follows, which is then explained in response below. In each of these sections, the evil is first clarified, followed by the clarification of the corresponding good.
Within the first section, the faults are first elucidated, followed by the clarification of virtues through their inversion.

Regarding the faults, the initial phrase "the first fault" introduces them collectively; this is then analyzed, followed by the application of the teaching, and finally illustrated through a metaphor to reveal the transgressions.
In the first part of this analysis, the evil of killing is first elucidated.
The section beginning with "The world has its constant ways and the laws of kings" explains suffering by way of killing.
The section beginning with "When life ends" explains burning by way of killing.
In the previous explanation of evil, the phrase "all devas and humans" and so forth clarifies those who commit evil;
"desiring to do evil" and so forth explicitly clarifies the act of committing evil;
and the section beginning with "not knowing how to practice" clarifies the faults of committing evil, wherein the faults themselves are first explicitly set forth.
The section beginning with "Furthermore, those who are noble and honorable" below cites what has been attained to reveal what has been lost.
That they are "tormented by pain" can be known [from this].
"This is called" concludes the passage.
The phrase "For example, as follows" and so forth uses a simile to clarify the characteristic of burning.
Within the exposition on the wholesome, there is first an analysis and subsequently a conclusion.

In the initial passage of the *Vibhaṅga*, the statement "If a person can single-mindedly restrain themselves therein," etc., precisely clarifies the performance of wholesome deeds as a counterpoint to the preceding unwholesome ones.
The phrase "The body alone attains liberation and gains its merit" counters the preceding suffering and counters the preceding burning.
The section beginning with "This is" concludes [the preceding].
Within the second section, the unwholesome precedes the wholesome.
Regarding the unwholesome, first it is introduced, then analyzed, followed by the Dharma-exposition, and finally illustrated by an analogy below.
In the first section of the *Vibhaṅga*, "Now, in this present world, there already exists the law of kings" and below, the second part clarifies suffering (*duḥkha*).
"Because of their lack of faith in previous lives" and below, the third part clarifies burning (*ādīpana*).
Within the section on evil, the first part clarifies the person who commits evil.
The passage beginning with "utterly devoid of meaning" correctly clarifies the commission of evil.
The section beginning with "ruining the family" clarifies the transgressions resulting from committing evil.
While actually committing evil, the phrase "utterly devoid of principle and contrary to the laws of dharma" clarifies his lack of goodness;
"luxury, lust, and arrogance," etc., clarify his commission of evil.
"Indulging in lust, arrogance, and self-indulgence, each desiring to gratify their own whims," and "engaging in theft"—these refer to the acts committed.
"Acting according to one's own heart and will, mutually deceiving one another," and so forth, precisely clarify the act of robbery and theft.
The remaining text may be understood by itself.
Within the third section, [the sequence] proceeds from evil to good.
Regarding the evil, first it is introduced, then analyzed, and finally established through doctrine; subsequently, a metaphor is used to illustrate it.
Regarding the first of the evils in the "Discrimination" section: from "nor does he fear the king's law" downward is "Suffering.
From "such evil being attached to" downward is "Burning. Within these, the first clarifies the person who commits evil.
The phrase "constantly harboring depravity" below correctly clarifies the commission of the evil of sexual misconduct.
The phrase "forming associations and gathering" below clarifies the transgression of committing evil;
to commit acts such as killing and stealing for the sake of lust is precisely that transgression.
The remaining text is easily understood.
Within the fourth section, the sequence proceeds from evil to good.
Regarding the evil, it first introduces the subject, then analyzes it, and finally concludes; subsequently, it clarifies this through a metaphor.
In the initial section on "Distinguishing Evil," the passage beginning with "Thus the various evil celestial deities record" clarifies their suffering;
the passage beginning with "the end of their lifespan" clarifies their burning.
Regarding the first of the evils, the person who commits evil is clarified.
From the phrase "not mindful of cultivation" onwards, the actual commission of the evil of false speech is clarified.
Because the four verbal transgressions do not accord with the Dharma, they are collectively termed "false speech."
