The section beginning with "Increasing jealousy toward the virtuous" clarifies the transgressions of committing evil.

Among these sufferings, it is explained that one's past roots of goodness are extinguished and protective deities abandon and distance themselves; thus, the body has no support and encounters many calamities—this is what constitutes such suffering.

"Being burned" clarifies that one is led by one's evil karma and seized by spirits and deities, being brought into the evil realms to undergo the suffering of scorching and burning; this is what is meant by "burning.
The rest of the text is self-evident.
In the fifth section, there is evil at the beginning and goodness at the end.
Within the section on evil, there is first the presentation, followed by the analysis, and finally the teaching; below this, a simile is used to clarify it.
In the analysis, evil comes first; from the passage "The minds of such people in the world" onwards, there is suffering.
The passage beginning with "When his great life is about to end, he feels regret and fear" describes the burning [of the body].
The section beginning with "He lingers about, indolent, and unwilling" specifically clarifies the commissioning of the evil of drinking alcohol.
Those who drink alcohol do not cultivate virtuous conduct nor attend to their household duties; they violate the teachings.

Furthermore, when combined with anger, it incites strife, leads to ingratitude and the rejection of righteousness, and results in deception, arrogance, and defiance. These points shall be discussed together.
The passage beginning with "肆心蕩逸魯扈抵" (indulging the mind in dissipation and acting with reckless arrogance) clarifies the transgressions of committing evil.
Although the manifestations of these transgressions are numerous, they are fully revealed within the text.
Among the sufferings, it clarifies that he currently possesses ignorance; his mind is shrouded by dark obstructions and he lacks understanding—this is what constitutes suffering.
There should also be the application of royal law to punish such offenses, but the text omits this for brevity.
Incineration and other methods may be inferred.
What has preceded is a detailed discussion; what follows is a general analysis.
Within this, the first section again clarifies the five evils.
From the passage "The Buddha said to Maitreya, 'In such a world, all Buddhas feel compassion,'" onwards, the evils are reversed to clarify the virtues.
Regarding the evils, it first provides a general explanation of how the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings arise from one another in succession.
The section beginning with "But having done" explains this specifically.
Within this specific explanation, there are two parts:
first, it clarifies how suffering arises and burning arises from evil.
The section following "Upon the death of the body" clarifies that from burning arises evil and suffering.
Within the preceding part, the initial statement, "One merely commits various evils and does not cultivate the roots of goodness," clarifies his wickedness.
"Everyone naturally enters the various evil realms" clarifies the arising of burning;
"or they may first suffer calamity in this present life," and so forth, clarifies the arising of pain.
Regarding the initial passage in the middle section of the latter part, which states, "After death, one follows [one's karma] into the three evil realms," this clarifies their burning.
From the phrase "When it has lasted for a long time" onwards, it describes how evil arises from that burning.
"After a long time, they together form a bond of enmity; arising from a minor slight, it eventually becomes a great resentment," thus giving rise to the evil of killing.
"All because of greedy attachment and an inability to practice generosity," thus giving rise to the evil of theft.
"Driven by delusion and desire, following the dictates of one's thoughts," and so forth, gives rise to the evil of sexual misconduct.
"Seeking to enrich oneself and contending for profit without any sense of reflection or restraint," gives rise to the evil of false speech.
The passage beginning with “Wealth, nobility, and splendor cannot endure the fleeting pleasure of the moment” gives rise to the evil of drinking alcohol;
such things give rise to evil.
From the phrase “sitting in the body” onwards, suffering arises from that evil.
Sitting before these five evils, one’s body undergoes toil and suffering; as this suffering increases without ceasing, it is called "long-lasting, vast, and intense.
The following clarifies the characteristics of this intensity.
Generally, within the world, the principles of the universe are naturally established; therefore, this is termed the "spreading out of the Way of Heaven" (*tiantao shizhang*).
When evil is committed, it inevitably becomes manifest; this is called "self-reproach.
When one's person falls within the net of the Dharma, it is therefore called the "net of the guiding principles.
From the noble to the humble, from the superior to the subordinate, there are none who do not follow the Dharma; therefore, it is called "the correspondence between high and low."
The transgressors return to it, having no companion or peer; hence it is said, "Alone and trembling, one shall enter therein.
The phrase "Throughout antiquity and today" concludes the passage to manifest the fault.
The preceding section clarifies evil; the following section, by contrast, clarifies goodness.
"The Buddha said to Maitreya, 'The world is thus,'" reiterates the aforementioned evils; "the Buddha pities them all" demonstrates his own compassion.
The section beginning with "By means of majestic spiritual power" teaches the extinction of prior evils and transforms beings to follow the good.
The phrase "Crush all evils and cause them all to attain goodness" teaches the cultivation of worldly virtues.
The passage beginning with “Abandoning what is contemplated and upholding the sūtra” and so forth teaches the cultivation of transcendence.
From the initial point up to “no loss,” it clarifies the cause for transcending the world;
from “finally attaining” onwards, it establishes the fruit of transcending the world.
The above was the third section, clarifying the faults of the suffering resulting from the five evil karmas and so forth.
From here on is the fourth section, exhorting people to practice renunciation.
Within this, there are two parts:
First, the Tathāgata’s exhortation to practice;
second, Maitreya’s comprehension and understanding.
Within the former, there are three parts:
First, exhortation through rectifying with principle;
second, from "I pity you" onwards, exhortation by citing the benefits of transformation achieved during his own present life;
third, from "When I have passed away" onwards, exhortation by citing the decline and loss that will follow after his extinction.
The beginning and middle have two parts:
first, exhorting through correct reasoning;
second, from the passage "You all shall extensively plant roots of virtue" onwards, manifesting the excellence of this cultivation to increase the resolve for study among people.
Within the preceding section on "Exhortation to Practice," the initial portion exhorts one's own practice.
From the words, "Having attained the sutras, you should reflect upon them thoroughly; rectify your mind and cultivate correct conduct, O Sovereign," and below, it exhorts one to transform others.
"May the Sovereign perform good and lead his subordinates through transformation," and so forth, refers to transforming others to cultivate goodness.
"One should seek transcendence of the world to uproot birth and death," and so forth, refers to transforming others to abandon evil.

Within this exposition of excellence, the first part clarifies that practicing virtue for a single day in this world is superior to practicing virtue for a hundred years in the Land of Immeasurable Life;
the section beginning with "The reason why" provides the explanation.
The following clarifies that practicing virtue for ten days in this realm is superior to practicing virtue for a thousand years in other Buddha-lands;
the section beginning with "The reason why" provides the explanation.
Within the first segment, the phrase "You all shall extensively plant the roots of merit therein" serves as a general heading.
"Bestowing grace," and so forth, distinguishes [the two types of practice].
Within this distinction, the initial mention of the six *pāramitās* constitutes the practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha-caryā*).

"Bestowing grace" is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*); "not transgressing" is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); "patience" is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); "vigor" is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*); "single-mindedness" is the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); and "wisdom" is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*). "Transforming and mutually teaching one another" constitutes the practice for the benefit of others (*parārtha-caryā*).
"To establish virtue and perform good" serves as the general conclusion.
What has been described above constitutes "active goodness";
rectifying the mind and intention through fasting and purification constitutes "restraining goodness."
Because this practice is difficult to cultivate, it is superior to spending a hundred years performing good deeds for Amitāyus in a single day.
Within the second section, which exhorts by citing present instances of transformative benefit, the first part clarifies that transformed beings cultivate goodness and attain happiness;
from the words "The Buddha said" onwards, it clarifies how those transformed beings extinguish evil and depart from suffering.
Regarding the third section below, which exhorts [the practitioner] regarding the decline after cessation, the first part presents the matter of decline after cessation;
from "Speak to Maitreya" onwards, it exhorts people to practice abandonment.
Above, the Buddha exhorted; below, Maitreya receives and practices this instruction.
"Maitreya said to the Buddha:
'What you have taught is most excellent; it is indeed so for the people of the world. This constitutes his reception and understanding.
The passage beginning with “the Tathāgata’s compassion” demonstrates that [the Buddha] has already practiced it.
The preceding four sections together constitute the second broad exposition of the impurities and evils of the Sahā world, intended to cause people to feel weary of them and renounce them.
From here below is the third section, which examines both the gains and losses regarding Amitāyus to encourage people to practice equanimity.
This section contains five parts:
first, the Buddha exhorts Ānanda to pay homage to Amitāyus;
1. Second, Ānanda, having received the command, respectfully prostrated to that Buddha and expressed his aspiration to behold him; 2.
Third, due to the previous request, Amitāyus Buddha emitted light that shone everywhere; 3.
Fourth, by means of the Buddha’s radiance, they were able to see one another.
The five causes and characteristics reveal in full the matters of gain and loss in that land, leading people to practice equanimity.
Within the first section, the Buddha first instructs Ānanda to pay homage to that Buddha;
from the words "the lands of the ten directions" onwards, he cites the Buddhas' collective praise to facilitate this prostration.
In the second section, the first part clarifies Ānanda’s reception of the command to perform the rites;
from the words "He addressed [the Buddha]" onwards, he petitions for an audience.
"I wish to see that Buddha" is a request to see the principal teacher of the transformation.
Regarding "the Land of Peace and Bliss," one seeks to see its location.
Regarding "the bodhisattvas" and so forth, one seeks to see that assembly.
In the third section, first there is an explanation by way of the Dharma.
The Buddha emits a radiance that universally illuminates all things, making them all of one single color.
This is first clarified through metaphors, and subsequently applied to the specific case.
In the fourth section, first this sees that, and later that sees this.
Within that, first Ānanda sees it, and subsequently the great assembly sees it.
In the fifth section, first his attainment is revealed to inspire people’s aspiration;
subsequently his failure is manifested to cause people to feel weary of and abandon it.
Regarding the manifestation of his attainment, the Tathāgata asked three times and Ānanda answered three times; the text is explicit and thus easily understood.
Regarding the manifestation of his failure, first the faults of his womb-birth are revealed;
from the passage beginning "If there are sentient beings who recognize their fundamental offenses," it teaches people how to practice relinquishment.
The preceding section clarifying the loss of the middle [state] consists of four distinct parts:
first, it demonstrates that that land possesses the fruit of womb-birth;
second, from the passage beginning "Maitreya said," it distinguishes the causes to manifest the fruits.
3. From "Furthermore, Maitreya" onwards, the inferior is revealed in contrast to the superior;
4. From "Like a Wheel-Turning King" onwards, the faults are revealed based upon that [superior state].
Within the first section, the Tathāgata first asks: "Do you also see those among the people of that land who are born from a womb?"
Ānanda answered next, manifesting that he himself had already seen [the truth].
From the words "The Tathāgata" onwards, [the text] further provides a detailed analysis for his sake.

Within the second section, Maitreya first asks, "By what cause and by what condition do the people of that land undergo birth from a womb or miraculous birth? This primarily analyzes birth from a womb while illustrating it by means of miraculous birth; thus, it serves as a general inquiry.
The Buddha answers this below.
Within that response, he first clarifies the causes for birth from a womb;
the section beginning with "If there are sentient beings who clearly believe in the Buddha" clarifies the causes for transformation-birth (*upapāduka*).
Within the section on the causes of birth from a womb, the causes are first clarified.
The passage beginning with "These sentient beings are born there" clarifies how the result is obtained through those causes.
Within the clarification of the causes, the phrase "If there are sentient beings who, with a mind of doubt... briefly explains their faults.
"Cultivating various merits with the vow to be born in that land" briefly clarifies what is attained.
From "Failing to understand the Buddha" onwards, it extensively clarifies what is lost.
To harbor doubt and lack faith in the wisdom of that Buddha is the nature of such loss.
Among these, the initial phrase "not understanding the Buddha’s wisdom" is the general statement;
"inconceivable," and so forth, are the specific details.
Because the Buddha’s wisdom is profound and deep, such that others cannot fathom it, it is called "inconceivable wisdom."
The wisdom of the Buddha is manifold and cannot be exhausted by words;
thus it is called "incomparable. To know all dharma-gates to their ultimate limit is termed "vast wisdom."
Because his rank and position are so exalted, he is named "The Peerless and Supreme Victorious Wisdom.
The section beginning with "In this regard" concludes [the preceding discussion].
The section beginning with "Yet he still believes" extensively elucidates his virtues.
Within the section on attaining the fruits, the analysis comes first and the teaching follows.
Within the clarification of birth by transformation (*upapāduka*), its cause is clarified first.
From the words "These various births" onwards, it clarifies how the fruit is attained through that cause.
From here below is the third section, which contrasts the superior with the inferior.

Within this, first the superiority of birth by transformation (*aupapāduka*) is presented, followed by the inferiority of birth from a womb (*jarāyuja*), as can be understood from the explicit wording of the text.
From here below, the fourth section clarifies the defects of birth from a womb, illustrating them through analogies.
The Tathāgata first establishes an analogy and poses a counter-question, to which Maitreya subsequently replies.
"No," he answers in summary.
The section beginning with "But various kinds" distinguishes this by means of specific illustrations.
From the words "The Buddha told" onwards, the Tathāgata provides an explanation.

He clarifies that for those born from a womb, there are no other forms of suffering; rather, their sole suffering is that for five hundred years they do not see the Three Jewels and cannot practice the good. This is what constitutes their suffering.
Because of this suffering, even pleasure is not pleasurable.
The preceding four sections together constitute the first part, clarifying the defects of birth from a womb.
From here on is the second part, teaching the cultivation of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

"If these sentient beings recognize their fundamental transgressions and deeply repent and reproach themselves, seeking to leave that place," this correctly teaches the cultivation of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
Recognizing the fundamental transgression of doubting the Buddha's wisdom, they should deeply repent and reproach themselves.
The section beginning with "Immediately one attains" clarifies the attainment through cultivation.
The section beginning with "Maitreya, you should know that such a person exists" concludes by exhorting one to practice and study;
it exhorts by pointing out what is lost to reveal what is attained.

The preceding third section clarified the inclusion of inferior persons for rebirth in that land; from here on, the fourth section again clarifies the inclusion of superior persons for rebirth in that land.
Within this, it first clarifies the rebirth in that land of bodhisattvas from this world.
Maitreya asked first, and the Tathāgata subsequently explained.
From the passage beginning "The Buddha told Maitreya, 'Not only... onwards, there is a detailed exposition on the rebirth of bodhisattvas in other lands.
Among these, the first part provides a general summary;
from "The first" onwards, they are listed individually.
Thirteen countries of bodhisattvas who attain rebirth there, together with the previous Sahā world, are specifically enumerated as fourteen.

The passage beginning with "Not only this" collectively mentions other lands to clarify that all beings therein attain rebirth; they are so numerous and immeasurable that they cannot be fully described.
By citing these examples, it inspires people to seek rebirth there with single-minded devotion.
The preceding section constitutes the main body of the teaching;
from here on follows the dissemination.
Within this, there are four parts:
First, the Tathāgata praises the sūtra and exhorts study;
second, from "At that time the World-Honored One spoke this sūtra" onwards, it reveals the benefits of the teaching as various people realize the Way;
third, the earth shakes, light is emitted, flowers rain down, and music is played, increasing the deep faith of the assembly.
The benefits explained by the Four Illuminations are vast and manifold, and the great assembly rejoices together.
In the beginning, there are five parts:
first, citing the benefit of hearing [the teaching] to exhort people to receive and practice it.
Second, from "I now, for the sake of all sentient beings" onwards, he instructs people to request a definitive resolution;

third, from "In future ages, when the Way of the sutras shall perish" onwards, he reveals the essential point of how this Dharma of the sutra provides salvation and benefit, remaining alone for a hundred years;
fourth, from "The Buddha said to Maitreya" onwards, he cites the difficulty of hearing this sutra to engender profound respect in people.
5. "Therefore, my Dharma is thus practiced," and so forth, concludes with an exhortation to practice and study.
This section has two parts:
first, it cites how hearing the name of Amitāyus brings profound and vast benefit, thereby exhorting one to study this sutra.
Since the title was heard based on the sūtra, one is therefore exhorted to study it.

The passage beginning with "If there are sentient beings who hear this sūtra" clarifies that the benefits gained from hearing this sūtra are vast and great, thereby exhorting people to receive and practice it.

In the previous section clarifying the benefits gained from hearing of the Buddha, it was stated: "Should there be anyone who hears the name of that Buddha and leaps for joy, even for a single thought-moment, they shall obtain great benefit. This clarifies that the benefits derived from hearing the Buddha’s name are manifold.
From the words "Therefore" onwards, there is an exhortation to study this sutra.

Because this sutra speaks of Amitāyus and because one gains great benefit upon hearing it, even if a great fire were to fill the three thousandfold world system, one must pass through it to hear and receive this sutra, let alone other minor hardships.
The section beginning with "Therefore" provides the explanation.
It states that "there are many bodhisattvas who wish to hear this sutra but are unable to do so," and thus it is essential to listen.

Later, within the clarification of the benefits gained from hearing the sutra, it says, "If one hears this sutra, one will never regress from the unsurpassed path," thereby citing the benefit of hearing the sutra.
"Therefore, one should believe with single-minded devotion," and so forth; this exhorts people to practice and study.

The preceding section was the first, which cited the benefits of hearing [the teaching] to exhort people to accept and practice it; from here on is the second, which teaches people how to request clarification.
"I preach this sutra-dharma for the sake of sentient beings, so that they may see Amitāyus and all that exists within his land," thus manifesting the intent of his transformation.
"Whatever one ought to do may all be sought therein" is a direct exhortation to resolve [one's practice].
From "There shall be no... onwards, it precludes the doubts of future generations.
Below this, the third section clarifies that the essentials of this sutra alone shall remain for a hundred years.
Regarding the phrase "In a future age, the path of the sutras will perish," this refers to the event of the extinction of those future dharmas.

The True Dharma (*saddharma*) of Śākyamuni lasts for five hundred years, the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*) for one thousand years, and the Final Dharma (*paścimadharma*) for ten thousand years; when all of these have passed, it is termed "extinction."
The passage beginning with "I [act] with loving-kindness" clarifies that attention has already been focused.
Out of compassion and pity for sentient beings, the Buddha uniquely left this sutra behind for a hundred years after the extinction of the Dharma to provide salvation.
Because this sutra reveals the Pure Land and encourages people to seek rebirth there, it alone remains.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* manifests the Buddha-nature; among the teachings for the noble ones, it is the most profound. Since the noble ones have already vanished, it perished first.
This sutra teaches people to weary of suffering and seek happiness; as it is essential for the salvation of ordinary beings, it perished last.
The Dharma varies according to the individual; therefore, its cessation differs.
The statement, "Any sentient beings who encounter this sutra shall obtain all their aspirations," clarifies the benefit of its preservation.
Even those who hear [this teaching] a hundred years after the Dharma has been extinguished will still obtain benefit and be reborn in the Pure Land;
how much more so for those who hear it now—how could they not be reborn there?
"May the Buddha take heed: those who hear this sutra now and seek rebirth shall certainly attain it; do not harbor any doubts.
This concludes the fourth section, which cites the rarity of hearing this sutra to inspire profound reverence in people.
"The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter and difficult to behold" clarifies the difficulty of encountering a Buddha.
To be born at the time of a Buddha is called "encountering";
to see him with one's own eyes is termed "beholding."
All of these are difficult matters.
The passage beginning with "The sūtras and paths of the Buddhas are difficult to hear" clarifies that the Dharma is difficult to hear.
Within this, it first clarifies that the scriptural teachings are difficult to hear.
To obtain a sutra scroll with one's own hands is called "attaining" (de), while listening to it with the ears is called "hearing" (wen).
Furthermore, to master and recite it is termed "attaining," and to take it in through the ears is termed "hearing.
All of these are difficult.
The passage beginning with "The excellence of the Bodhisattva" clarifies that it is extremely difficult to hear the methods of his practice.
The phrase "To encounter a virtuous friend and be able to practice is also difficult" clarifies the difficulty of cultivation.
The preceding was a general statement.
As for the passage, "If one hears this sutra and believes, delights in, and accepts it," etc., this is the most difficult among difficulties.
In comparison with the previous three, it clarifies that practicing and studying within this sutra is the most difficult of all.

While other meanings and dharmas are proclaimed and elucidated here and there, this single sutra alone reveals the Pure Land and teaches people to be reborn therein; therefore, it is the most difficult [to encounter].
From here on, the fifth section concludes with an exhortation to practice and study.
The phrase "therefore" means that because this Dharma of the sutra provides manifold benefits and because it is most difficult to encounter those who practice and study within it, I now proclaim it.
The phrase "my Dharma" refers to the Dharma of this sutra.

"Acting in such a manner" means that this sutra proclaims how Amitābha Tathāgata attained his body and his land through the cultivation of vows and practices; this is what is meant by "acting in such a manner."
"Thus spoken" means that what the Tathāgata has proclaimed for the sake of the assembly above is called "thus spoken.
"Thus taught" means that what the Tathāgata has instructed people regarding rebirth above is called "thus taught."
This summarizes the preceding teachings.
"One should believe and comply, practicing in accordance with the Dharma" concludes the exhortation to practice and study.
Thus ends the five preceding sections.
Taken together, this constitutes the first section: praising the sutra and exhorting study.
From here below is the second section, clarifying the benefits of its exposition.
"Immeasurable sentient beings give rise to the mind of perfect enlightenment" refers to the benefit arising from the arousal of vows.

Having heard that Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood through the practice of vows and established a Pure Land to gather and transform sentient beings, one aspires to share in this resolve; this is called the "Mind of Right Enlightenment.
The following clarifies the attainment of the Way, first through the Small Vehicle and subsequently through the Great Vehicle.
Sentient beings of the Hīnayāna, upon hearing that the Sahā world is defiled, evil, and loathsome, develop a profound sense of weary detachment; thus, they attain the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.
Within this context, the initial statement "attaining the pure Dharma-eye" refers to their realization as *srotāpannas*.
To perceive the Four Noble Truths is called the pure Dharma-eye.
Next, one attains the stage of Anāgāmin, and subsequently, one attains Arhatship.

As for sentient beings of the Mahāyāna, having heard that Amitābha Buddha has perfected his virtues and extensively delivers others, they cultivate a firm resolve and seek rebirth; therefore, they attain the stage of non-retrogression.
Hearing this, he perceived its many benefits and vowed to deliver all beings, thus naming himself "Self-Adorned by Vow" (Shizizhuang).
Because he strove toward this fruit through these means, he shall attain perfect enlightenment in the future.

In the third section, the Tathāgata’s transformation is universal; in order to increase the veneration of sentient beings, he employs his supernormal powers to shake the earth, emit light, produce music, and rain down flowers.
The six types of earthquakes are as described above.
In the fourth section, it is clarified that the teaching extensively benefits all, satisfying the diverse capacities of sentient beings, and the great assembly rejoices together.
This concludes the lower fascicle of the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life*.
